title: Take-home Exercise 1: Geospatial Analytics for Public Safety
text:
4.4 Geometry validation
I checked the boundary polygon for validity before using it. It is a single valid polygon, so I did not need any multipart or self-intersection handling, though I ran st_make_valid anyway as a defensive step. For point-in-polygon assignment I used st_within rather than st_intersects, so a detection sitting exactly on the boundary arc is excluded rather than double-counted against a neighbouring regency. spatstat’s window conversion reported no points rejected as outside the window, which tells me my clip and the owin agree.
Two things here commonly go wrong and I handled them deliberately. First, I assigned regencies to parent provinces by testing containment of an interior representative point in a projected coordinate system, not by nearest-feature matching. Nearest feature would silently mis-assign any regency whose representative point fell marginally outside its own province, and I would never have noticed. Second, I read the 159 MB national ADM2 file through a bounding-box filter at the GDAL level rather than loading it and subsetting afterwards, so the full national geometry is never held in memory.

Table 10: Methodological decisions. The right-hand column records the alternative that was considered and not taken, which is the part that makes a decision reviewable.




Two of these deserve a note.
Border versus Ripley correction. Ripley’s isotropic correction is more efficient but costs substantially more computation, and the envelope procedure requires 199 re-computations. At 10,321 points the border correction’s loss of efficiency is immaterial, because the number of pairs contributing at each lag is very large. The choice is a compute trade-off, made explicitly rather than by default.
Global versus pointwise tests. A pointwise envelope is read at every one of several hundred values of \(r\), so the probability of at least one excursion under the null far exceeds the nominal level. Pointwise envelopes are still plotted, because they show where on the \(r\) axis the departure sits, which a single p-value cannot. Every claim of significance in this report is backed by the MAD or DCLF global test, not by the band.

Figure 2: Detection density across the 56 regencies and cities of Indonesian Borneo, 1 July to 25 September 2026, with Pulang Pisau outlined. The concentration in the southern peat belt of Central Kalimantan is the regional structure within which the study window sits. What I take from it: the choice of study window is not an outlier hunt. Pulang Pisau is the most intense cell of a coherent regional band running along the southern coastal peat domes, so findings about its internal structure plausibly transfer to its neighbours. The map also shows what the regency boundary does analytically: it cuts a continuous field of fire activity, which is why the edge corrections of Section 5 matter rather than being a formality.

Figure 3: The primary spatial pattern: one point per 375 m cell in which fire was detected. Colour shows the local date of first detection, so the map carries the season as well as the location. What I take from it: two things are immediately visible and both matter. The pattern is strongly concentrated in the southern two-thirds of the regency, which is the drained peat of the former Mega Rice Project, while the northern interior is nearly empty. Second, the colour gradient is not spatially random: earlier detections (lighter) sit disproportionately in the south and east, later ones spread north and west. That is a testable claim about space-time interaction rather than an impression, and Section 8 tests it.

Table 11: Chi-squared test of a homogeneous Poisson process, across quadrat resolutions. The variance-to-mean ratio (VMR) is 1 under complete spatial randomness. The verdict is identical at every resolution, which is the point: the test is not informative, it is merely arithmetically certain.




The chi-squared statistic exceeds its degrees of freedom by three to four orders of magnitude at every resolution tested, and the variance-to-mean ratio ranges from 79.2 to 1036.1 against a null value of 1. Complete spatial homogeneity is rejected with certainty.
This is reported for transparency and should persuade nobody of anything. The result was guaranteed by the data-generating process described in Section 1.1 and by the obvious geography: a regency that is half drained peatland and half comparatively intact landscape cannot possibly have uniform fire intensity. Quadrat counts also inherit an arbitrary origin and cell size, and they discard all within-quadrat information. Their only genuine use here is the VMR column, which quantifies how far from uniform the pattern is at each scale rather than asking a yes-or-no question already answered.

text:
6.4 Bandwidth selection, and why cross-validation was rejected
The substantive first-order tool is kernel density estimation, and the decision that determines what it shows is the bandwidth.


code
FO$bw_tab |> transmute(Selector = selector, `sigma (m)` = round(sigma_m),
                       `sigma (km)` = sigma_km) |> kable(align = "lrr")








Selector
sigma (m)

10543

Table 12: Bandwidth selectors compared on the primary pattern, ordered as computed. The spread is a factor of roughly eighteen from smallest to largest, which is why reporting a single surface without this table would conceal the most consequential choice in the first-order analysis.




The two cross-validation selectors return sub-kilometre bandwidths, 573 m for bw.ppl and 628 m for bw.diggle, and density.ppp emits a numerical-underflow warning at that scale over a window of 9,759 km². Neither was adopted, and the reason is not that the warning is inconvenient.
Cross-validation selectors are documented to choose very small bandwidths when a pattern is strongly clustered at short range. Their criteria reward a surface that reproduces the local bursts, so they interpret clustering as fine-grained intensity structure. That is a reasonable thing to want in some applications, and the wrong thing to want here, because the same estimate is used as the reference intensity for the second-order test in Section 7.3. If \(\hat{\lambda}(u)\) has already absorbed the sub-kilometre clustering, then asking whether clustering remains after removing \(\hat{\lambda}(u)\) is a rigged question, and the answer would be no by construction.
The adopted bandwidth is therefore fixed at 4,000 m, on a criterion stated before the surfaces were inspected: it must exceed the interaction range, so that trend and interaction are estimated by separate parts of the analysis rather than competing for the same signal. Four kilometres sits above the roughly 2 km interaction range that Section 7.3 goes on to find, inside the interval spanned by the two components of bw.scott (3,847 m and 10,543 m), and below bw.CvL (10,530 m).
This is a judgement, not an optimisation, and it is stated as one. The comparison below shows what each alternative would have produced, so a reader who disagrees can see the consequence rather than having to take the choice on trust.


code
bw_panels <- list(
  ppl   = glue("bw.ppl, {round(FO$sigma_ppl)} m (rejected)"),
  main  = glue("adopted, {fmt_n(FO$sigma_main)} m"),
  scott = glue("bw.scott x, {fmt_n(round(FO$sigma_scott[1]))} m"),
  CvL   = glue("bw.CvL, {fmt_n(round(FO$sigma_CvL))} m"))
bw_df <- bind_rows(lapply(names(bw_panels), function(k)
  im_df(FO$kde[[k]]) |> mutate(panel = bw_panels[[k]]))) |>
  mutate(v = per_1000km2(intensity))
bw_df$panel <- factor(bw_df$panel, levels = unlist(bw_panels))
ggplot(bw_df) +
  geom_raster(aes(x, y, fill = v)) +
  geom_sf(data = win_p, fill = NA, colour = PAL$ink, linewidth = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, nrow = 1) +
  scale_fill_intensity(v = bw_df$v) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA, expand = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "What the bandwidth decides") +
  theme_map(base_size = 9)








Figure 4: The same pattern under four bandwidths. Reading: the choice is not cosmetic. The cross-validated surface resolves individual fire complexes and, at this sample size, a great deal of structure no agency could act on; it is also the surface that would sabotage the second-order test, for the reason given above. The 10.5 km bw.CvL surface is stable but has smoothed away the distinction between the peat belt and its margins, which is the distinction of interest. The adopted 4 km surface and bw.scott’s 3.8 km are visually close, which is reassurance that the adopted value is not an idiosyncratic pick. The important disclosure is that all four agree on the location of the principal concentration and disagree on how many secondary concentrations exist, so no claim about secondary hotspots is made.

title: Where peat burns, and how close together
text:
6.5 The reported intensity surface


code
kde_main <- im_df(FO$kde$main) |> mutate(v = per_1000km2(intensity))
ggplot(kde_main) +
  geom_raster(aes(x, y, fill = v)) +
  geom_sf(data = win_p, fill = NA, colour = PAL$ink, linewidth = 0.45) +
  scale_fill_intensity(v = kde_main$v) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA, expand = FALSE) +
  scalebar_layer(bb) + north_layer(bb) +
  labs(title = "Fire intensity concentrates in the drained southern peat",
       subtitle = glue("Kernel intensity estimate, sigma = {fmt_n(FO$sigma_main)} m, Diggle edge correction")) +
  theme_map() + theme(legend.position = "right", legend.key.height = unit(34, "pt"),
                      legend.key.width = unit(9, "pt"))








Figure 5: Estimated first-order intensity of burned cells, Gaussian kernel with Diggle’s edge correction, at the adopted 4 km bandwidth. Reading: intensity is organised as a broad south-southeast band reaching a maximum in the lower third of the regency, with a secondary extension along the eastern margin. The empty northern interior is a real absence rather than an absence of observation: the same satellites observed it on the same days. The gradient is steep, spanning roughly two orders of magnitude between the peat belt and the northern interior, which means resource allocation proportional to intensity would be very unevenly distributed. That is the operational content of a first-order surface, and it is the strongest planning-relevant result the first-order analysis alone supports.





An adaptive estimator was computed as a check, since a fixed bandwidth over-smooths sparse areas and under-smooths dense ones. It reproduces the same principal concentration, which is the reassurance sought: the reported structure is not an artefact of assuming one bandwidth everywhere.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Geospatial Analytics for Public Safety
text:
6.6 Radiative power, not just counts
A count surface treats a barely detectable smouldering pixel and an intense flaming front as the same event, which bothered me. Fire radiative power is the sensor’s estimate of radiative output in megawatts, so smoothing that instead answers a different and arguably more useful question.


code
frp_df  <- im_df(FO$frp_smooth, "v") |> mutate(panel = "Mean FRP per detection (MW)")
frpt_df <- im_df(FO$frp_total, "v") |> mutate(v = v * 1e6, panel = "Total FRP released (MW per km²)")
p1 <- ggplot(frp_df) + geom_raster(aes(x, y, fill = v)) +
  geom_sf(data = win_p, fill = NA, colour = PAL$ink, linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colours = PAL$seq, name = "MW") +
  coord_sf(datum = NA, expand = FALSE) + labs(subtitle = "Mean FRP per detection") + theme_map(9)
p2 <- ggplot(frpt_df) + geom_raster(aes(x, y, fill = v)) +
  geom_sf(data = win_p, fill = NA, colour = PAL$ink, linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colours = PAL$seq, trans = "sqrt", name = "MW/km\u00b2",
                       labels = label_number(big.mark = ",")) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA, expand = FALSE) + labs(subtitle = "Total FRP released") + theme_map(9)
p1 + p2 + plot_annotation(title = "Energy release has a different geography from event count",
                          theme = theme_ex01())








Figure 6: Left, mean fire radiative power per detection. Right, total radiative power released, which is intensity and mean power combined. What I take from it: the two panels separate two things a single count map conflates. Total power (right) closely tracks detection intensity, so the southern peat belt dominates energy release as well as event count. Mean power per detection (left) has a different geography: it is comparatively low across the core of the peat belt and higher on the margins and in the sparse north. That is consistent with the physical expectation that peat combustion is low-intensity and persistent while fires on mineral soil and in cleared vegetation burn hotter and shorter. It is also a caution to me: the places with the most detections are not the places with the most intense individual fires.

Figure 7: Daily count of burned cells with a centred seven-day mean, and the onset/peak split used later. What I take from it: the episode is not a plateau. Activity is negligible through early July, rises from late July, and escalates sharply through August to a maximum in the first half of September. The seven-day mean is shown because the raw series carries strong short-period structure from cloud cover and overpass geometry, not from fire: a single overcast day suppresses detection regardless of what is burning. I placed the split date by a rule I set in advance, the first day the seven-day mean reaches half its eventual maximum, rather than choosing it after seeing the surfaces I later use it to compare.







code
ggplot(FO$overpass, aes(hr_bin, n, fill = daynight)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.42) +
  facet_wrap(~platform, ncol = 2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(day = PAL$accent, night = PAL$cool), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 24, 4), limits = c(0, 24)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_number(big.mark = ",")) +
  labs(x = "Local solar time (WITA, UTC+8)", y = "Detections",
       title = "Four fixed overpasses, not a diurnal cycle") +
  theme_ex01()








Figure 8: Detections by local solar time of acquisition, split by platform. What I take from it: I put this figure in to stop myself making a mistake. The two platforms observe at four narrow fixed local times, so the apparent day and night counts are not a diurnal cycle of fire activity; they are two sampling windows. Peat fires smoulder continuously and their true diurnal variation cannot be recovered from these data at all. If I said ‘fires peak in the early afternoon’ I would be describing the satellite’s orbit, not the fires. I use the day and night split only as a detectability covariate, since night overpasses catch cooler anomalies against a cooler background.

section: 7.1 The straw man, tested and dismissed
text:
7.1 The straw man, tested and dismissed


code
mk_env_df <- function(e, lab) e |> mutate(panel = lab)
eg <- mk_env_df(SO$env_G, "G(r), nearest neighbour")
ef <- mk_env_df(SO$env_F, "F(r), empty space")
el <- SO$env_L |>
  mutate(across(c(obs, theo, lo, hi), ~ .x - r), panel = "L(r) - r, centred")
env_all <- bind_rows(eg, ef, el)
env_all$panel <- factor(env_all$panel, levels = c("G(r), nearest neighbour",
                                                  "F(r), empty space", "L(r) - r, centred"))
ggplot(env_all, aes(r)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = PAL$rule, alpha = 0.75) +
  geom_line(aes(y = theo), colour = PAL$muted, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_line(aes(y = obs), colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, scales = "free", nrow = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(scale = 1e-3, suffix = " km")) +
  labs(x = "r", y = NULL,
       title = "Against complete spatial randomness, everything is significant",
       subtitle = glue("Orange, observed. Grey band, envelope from {SO$nsim} CSR simulations. Dashed, theoretical CSR value.")) +
  theme_ex01(base_size = 9)








Figure 9: Nearest-neighbour G, empty-space F, and the centred L function, each against a complete spatial randomness envelope from 199 simulations. Reading: every statistic departs from the CSR envelope immediately and by an enormous margin. G rises far faster than expected, meaning nearest neighbours are much closer than random; F rises far slower, meaning empty gaps are much larger than random; L sits far above zero at every lag. Read naively this is overwhelming evidence of clustering. Read correctly it is evidence of almost nothing, because the sensor guarantees this result: a single fire produces adjacent detections. The figure is included to make that failure visible rather than to hide it, and the analysis that carries weight is in Section 7.3.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Geospatial Analytics for Public Safety
section: 7.2 What the pair correlation function reveals about the instrument
text:
7.2 What the pair correlation function reveals about the instrument
\(K\) and \(L\) are cumulative, so a departure at one lag propagates into every larger one and the location of the effect is invisible. The pair correlation function \(g(r)\) is a density, and it separates scales. That distinction matters more here than I expected.


code
pcf_df <- SO$pcf_obs |> filter(is.finite(trans), r > 0)
ggplot(pcf_df, aes(r, trans)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, colour = PAL$muted, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = DEDUP_GRID_M, colour = PAL$cool, linetype = "12", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_line(colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.7) +
  annotate("text", x = DEDUP_GRID_M + 60, y = max(pcf_df$trans) * 0.85,
           label = "375 m pixel", hjust = 0, size = 2.9, colour = PAL$cool,
           family = "Helvetica") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(scale = 1e-3, suffix = " km")) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "r", y = "g(r), log scale",
       title = "The sensor's footprint is visible in the statistic",
       subtitle = "Suppression below one pixel width is an instrument property, not fire behaviour.") +
  theme_ex01()








Figure 10: Pair correlation function of the primary pattern, log scale. The dotted line marks the 375 m VIIRS pixel dimension. What I take from it: g(r) is suppressed at very short range and peaks at about 460 m, immediately above the pixel width. This is not fires avoiding one another. It is the sensor’s resolution: two detections cannot be much closer than one pixel, because one pixel yields one detection. That short-range suppression is an instrument artefact and is the clearest single piece of evidence that this pattern records observation rather than events. Above the peak, g(r) decays slowly and is still above 3 at 2.9 km, nowhere near its asymptote of 1. So spatial dependence extends well beyond the 5 km range I plot here, which is what pushed me to the extended range in Section 7.6.

title: Where peat burns, and how close together
text:
7.3 The test that can fail
These are the statistics I trust. The null is an inhomogeneous Poisson process whose intensity is the kernel estimate from Section 6.5, so everything the first-order analysis established sits inside the null already. A departure now means residual interaction, not large-scale variation. That is Q3.


code
# An envelope built from `simulate=` has no theoretical curve, only the simulation
# mean, so the reference is set explicitly: 0 for the centred L function and 1 for
# the pair correlation function.
li <- SO$env_Linhom |> mutate(across(c(obs, lo, hi), ~ .x - r),
                              ref = 0, panel = "L_inhom(r) - r")
gi <- SO$env_pcfinhom |> filter(r > 0) |> mutate(ref = 1, panel = "g_inhom(r)")
ggplot(bind_rows(li, gi), aes(r)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = PAL$rule, alpha = 0.75) +
  geom_line(aes(y = ref), colour = PAL$muted, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_line(aes(y = obs), colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, scales = "free", nrow = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(scale = 1e-3, suffix = " km")) +
  labs(x = "r", y = NULL,
       title = "Clustering survives the honest null, and has a scale",
       subtitle = glue("Envelope from {SO$nsim} simulations of an inhomogeneous Poisson process with lambda re-estimated each time.")) +
  theme_ex01(base_size = 9)








Figure 11: Inhomogeneous centred L function and inhomogeneous pair correlation function, against envelopes from 199 simulations of an inhomogeneous Poisson process. The reference intensity is re-estimated for every simulated pattern. What I take from it: the departure survives, and it does not close. Both curves leave the envelope at about 100 m and remain outside it across the entire range plotted. g_inhom peaks near 5.9 at roughly 570 m and is still above 2 at 2.8 km, against an envelope ceiling near 1.4. So after accounting for the fact that fire is far more likely in the southern peat belt than in the north, burned cells still occur much closer together than that variation alone predicts. Note also that g_inhom falls below 1 at the shortest lags, the sensor floor surviving into the inhomogeneous statistic.







code
tibble::tribble(
  ~Test, ~Statistic, ~Null, ~`p-value`,
  "MAD",  "L(r)",       "complete spatial randomness",  fmt_p(SO$mad_L$p.value, 99),
  "MAD",  "L_inhom(r)", "inhomogeneous Poisson",        fmt_p(SO$mad_Linhom$p.value, 99),
  "DCLF", "L_inhom(r)", "inhomogeneous Poisson",        fmt_p(SO$dclf_Linhom$p.value, 99)
) |> kable(align = "lllr")

Table 13: Global Monte Carlo tests. The maximum absolute deviation (MAD) and Diggle-Cressie-Loosmore-Ford (DCLF) statistics each summarise the whole curve in one number, so these p-values are not inflated by reading a band at many lags. The Monte Carlo floor is 0.01 with 99 simulations.




Both global tests reject the inhomogeneous Poisson null at the Monte Carlo floor. The pattern is clustered beyond its first-order trend, which answers the first half of Q3.
Where the clustering ends is a different matter, and here a decision of mine got in the way. I capped r at 5 km on the reasoning that longer lags in an elongated window rest on too few pairs. Across that whole range both curves sit outside the envelope. All 5 km establishes is that dependence extends at least that far. Section 7.5 extends the range.
The direction of the remaining bias matters for how confidently this can be stated. As set out in assumption A6, estimating \(\hat{\lambda}\) from the pattern under test lets it absorb part of the clustering, which widens the envelope and makes the test harder to reject. The rejection therefore stands despite a conservative procedure, not because of a permissive one.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Geospatial Analytics for Public Safety
text:
7.5 Sensitivity to the event definition
My whole analysis rests on collapsing detections to cells, so I wanted to know whether the finding depends on that choice. If it did, it would be a finding about my choice rather than about fire.


code
sd_df <- bind_rows(
  SO$Linhom_cell |> transmute(r, v = border - r, pattern = "ppp_cell (reported)"),
  SO$Linhom_all  |> transmute(r, v = border - r, pattern = "ppp_all (un-thinned)"))
ggplot(sd_df, aes(r, v, colour = pattern)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = PAL$muted, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("ppp_cell (reported)" = PAL$accent,
                                 "ppp_all (un-thinned)" = PAL$cool), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(scale = 1e-3, suffix = " km")) +
  labs(x = "r", y = "L_inhom(r) - r",
       title = "The conclusion is robust, the magnitude is not",
       subtitle = glue("n = {fmt_n(SO$n_cell)} cells against n = {fmt_n(SO$n_all)} detections.")) +
  theme_ex01()








Figure 13: Inhomogeneous centred L function computed on the cell pattern and on the un-thinned detection pattern, on a common axis. What I take from it: both curves are positive, so the qualitative conclusion of residual clustering does not depend on the event definition. The magnitudes differ by roughly an order of magnitude, and the un-thinned pattern shows far stronger apparent clustering at every lag. That gap is the repeat-detection artefact measured directly. It is why I use the cell pattern for inference and the detection pattern only for this check. If I reported the upper curve I would be reporting the satellite revisit schedule as a fire-behaviour result.

title: Where peat burns, and how close together
section: 7.5 Extending the range, and what it costs to have been wrong
text:
7.5 Extending the range, and what it costs to have been wrong
The 5 km cap was set on the reasoning that long lags in an elongated window rest on few pairs. That reasoning is sound, but 5 km was more conservative than necessary: the rule stated in Section 5 caps \(r\) at a quarter of the window’s shortest dimension, and the window is 86 km wide, so 20 km was admissible all along. Extending to 20 km is not a post-hoc licence, it is applying the rule that was already stated.
Two practical constraints follow, and both are disclosed rather than absorbed. pcfinhom offers no border correction, and the translation correction over roughly seven million pairs per pattern did not complete in a workable time for 99 simulated patterns. So significance across the extended range rests on \(L_{inhom}\) with a border correction and a full envelope, while the shape of \(g_{inhom}\) across that range comes from a single translation-corrected curve with no simulations. No significance claim is made for \(g_{inhom}\) beyond 3 km.


code
Lx <- EX$env_L_ext |> mutate(across(c(obs, lo, hi), ~ .x - r), ref = 0,
                             panel = "L_inhom(r) - r, with envelope")
Gx <- EX$g_obs_ext |> filter(r > 0, is.finite(trans)) |>
  transmute(r, obs = trans, lo = NA_real_, hi = NA_real_, ref = 1,
            panel = "g_inhom(r), observed only")
ggplot(bind_rows(Lx, Gx), aes(r)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = PAL$rule, alpha = 0.75, na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_line(aes(y = ref), colour = PAL$muted, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_line(aes(y = obs), colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(data = tibble(panel = "g_inhom(r), observed only",
                           x = EX$summary_ext$r_g_within_10pct_of_1),
             aes(xintercept = x), colour = PAL$cool, linetype = "12", linewidth = 0.4) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, scales = "free", nrow = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(scale = 1e-3, suffix = " km")) +
  labs(x = "r", y = NULL,
       title = "Dependence is local, but a cumulative statistic cannot say so",
       subtitle = glue("Dotted line marks {round(EX$summary_ext$r_g_within_10pct_of_1/1000, 1)} km, where g_inhom first comes within 10% of 1.")) +
  theme_ex01(base_size = 9)








Figure 13: Left, inhomogeneous centred L function to 20 km with a 99-simulation envelope. Right, the observed inhomogeneous pair correlation function over the same range, with no envelope, on a log scale. Reading: the two panels answer different questions and disagree in an instructive way. g_inhom, which localises scale, peaks at about 440 m and decays steadily: it is 4.3 at 1 km, 2.7 at 2 km, 1.4 at 5 km, and reaches within 10% of its asymptote of 1 at about 7.2 km. L_inhom, which is cumulative, never re-enters its envelope within 20 km. Both are correct. The excess pair density is a local phenomenon that has largely dissipated by 7 km, and because L accumulates every excess at smaller lags it remains significantly elevated far beyond the range over which anything is actually happening.







code

  Lag = c("peak", "1 km", "2 km", "5 km", "10 km", "20 km"),

text:
8.2 Does the signature move between onset and peak?


code
rr_df <- im_df(ST$rr, "p")
share_peak <- as.numeric(ST$season_counts["peak"]) / sum(ST$season_counts)
ggplot(rr_df) +
  geom_raster(aes(x, y, fill = p)) +
  geom_sf(data = win_p, fill = NA, colour = PAL$ink, linewidth = 0.45) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = PAL$cool, mid = PAL$ground_alt, high = PAL$accent_dk,
                       midpoint = share_peak, name = "P(peak period)",
                       labels = label_percent(accuracy = 1)) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA, expand = FALSE) +
  scalebar_layer(bb) + north_layer(bb) +
  labs(title = "The episode expands rather than intensifies in place",
       subtitle = glue("Split at {format(ST$split_date, '%d %B')}. Midpoint of the scale is the overall peak share, {percent(share_peak, accuracy = 1)}.")) +
  theme_map()








Figure 16: Probability that a burned cell belongs to the peak period rather than the onset period, as a spatially varying surface. Values above the overall peak share indicate areas where fire arrived late; values below indicate areas that burned early. What I take from it: the surface is not flat, so the episode is not a uniform intensification of one fixed footprint. The southern and southeastern peat burned disproportionately early, while the northern and western margins of the active area contribute disproportionately to the peak period. Read together with the weekly trajectory below, this describes an episode that begins in the most degraded peat and expands outward from it. The operational implication I draw is that where fire is early in the season carries information about where it will appear later, which my static seasonal intensity map cannot convey.







code
tr <- ST$traj |> filter(n > 0)
p_sd <- ggplot(tr, aes(week_start, sd_km)) +
  geom_col(fill = PAL$accent_lt, width = 4.4) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Standard distance (km)", subtitle = "Dispersion of burned cells") +
  scale_x_date(date_labels = "%d %b") + theme_ex01()
p_step <- ggplot(tr |> filter(!is.na(step_km)), aes(week_start, step_km)) +
  geom_line(colour = PAL$accent_dk, linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_point(colour = PAL$accent_dk, size = 1.2) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Weekly shift of mean centre (km)", subtitle = "Movement of the mean centre") +
  scale_x_date(date_labels = "%d %b") + theme_ex01()
p_sd + p_step + plot_annotation(
  title = "The footprint widens as the season progresses", theme = theme_ex01())








Figure 17: Weekly mean centre of burned cells with the weekly dispersion about it, and the distance the centre moved each week. What I take from it: the mean centre is a crude summary and I use it only for what it does reliably, which is showing direction and spread over time. Dispersion widens as the season progresses, which confirms the expansion I read off the relative-risk surface. The weekly displacement of the centre is largest in the early weeks, when few cells dominate the mean, and settles to a few kilometres a week once activity is widespread. The caution I would attach is that the mean centre of a strongly non-convex, multi-modal pattern is not a place where anything is happening. It is a summary statistic and I would not put it on an operational map.

  geom_sf(data = win_p, fill = NA, colour = PAL$ink, linewidth = 0.22) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, nrow = 1) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colours = PAL$seq, name = "Relative intensity",
                       labels = label_percent(accuracy = 1)) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA, expand = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Fire spreads north and west from a southeastern origin") +
  theme_map(base_size = 8)








Figure 18: Space-time intensity at fortnightly reference days, estimated with a fixed spatial kernel and a Gaussian weight in time of five days’ standard deviation. Each panel is normalised to its own weights, so panels show where fire was concentrated at that moment rather than how much there was. What I take from it: the sequence makes the expansion explicit. Early July activity is confined to a small southeastern area. Through August the active area extends north and west along the peat belt while retaining the southern core. By mid-September activity covers most of the southern two-thirds of the regency. My estimator assumes separability, meaning the spatial kernel does not change shape over time. That is a simplification: the real footprint is elongating, and a separable estimator can only show that as a change in weights.

title: Where peat burns, and how close together
section: 10.1 What is the clustering organised around?
text:
10.1 What is the clustering organised around?
Peat fire here is human in ignition and made possible by drainage. Two mapped covariates proxy those mechanisms: distance to the road network for access and ignition opportunity, distance to mapped canals and waterways for drainage-driven desiccation.
I took the covariate geometry from a dated Geofabrik OpenStreetMap extract for Kalimantan rather than a live Overpass query. That was not my first choice. Overpass refused a bounding box this size repeatedly, and once I had switched I realised the extract is better anyway: a live query returns different data every time it runs, so it cannot be part of a reproducible pipeline. The extract gave me 28,515 road features and 3,061 waterway features within a 15 km buffer of the regency.
I compute distances on that buffered frame and only then crop to the analysis window. If I had computed them on the clipped window I would have biased every distance upward for cells near the boundary, because their nearest road is often outside the regency entirely.
The same reasoning caught a bug in my first land-cover attempt, and it is worth recording because it fails quietly. distmap returns distances on the enclosing frame of whatever you hand it. Handed the union of the landuse polygons, that frame is their own bounding box, so the covariate was undefined across 98% of the regency and ppm fitted on the 2% that remained. The AIC values it returned were in the hundreds against tens of thousands for the other models, which is the only reason I looked. Evaluating distfun over the analysis window fixes it. Nothing in the report rests on the broken version, but a less absurd set of numbers would have gone unnoticed.
The 3,061 waterway features against 28,515 road features is itself my first result here, and it is a warning rather than a finding. An area defined by an abandoned canal network has fewer mapped watercourses than roads. I come back to what that does to the drainage covariate below.


code
rho_to_df <- function(rh, lab) {
  if (is.null(rh)) return(NULL)
  d <- rh
  nm <- names(d)
  tibble(x = d[[1]], rho = d[["rho"]],
         lo = if ("lo" %in% nm) d[["lo"]] else NA_real_,
         hi = if ("hi" %in% nm) d[["hi"]] else NA_real_, panel = lab)
}
rho_df <- bind_rows(
  rho_to_df(CM$rho_road,  "Distance to nearest road"),
  rho_to_df(CM$rho_water, "Distance to nearest mapped waterway"))
mean_int <- P$ppp_cell$n / (P$area_km2 * 1e6)
if (!is.null(rho_df) && nrow(rho_df)) {
  ggplot(rho_df, aes(x / 1000)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = per_1000km2(mean_int) / 1e3 * 1e3,
               colour = PAL$muted, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.35) +
    geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = per_1000km2(lo), ymax = per_1000km2(hi)),
                fill = PAL$rule, alpha = 0.6) +
    geom_line(aes(y = per_1000km2(rho)), colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.7) +
    facet_wrap(~panel, scales = "free", nrow = 1) +
    labs(x = "Distance (km)", y = "Burned cells per 1,000 km²",
         title = "Access explains a great deal, mapped drainage very little",
         subtitle = "Dashed line, mean intensity over the window.") +
    theme_ex01(base_size = 9)
} else cat("Covariate estimation unavailable; see the limitations.\n")








Figure 21: Estimated intensity as a non-parametric function of distance to the nearest road and to the nearest mapped waterway, with 95% confidence bands. The horizontal line is the mean intensity over the window. What I take from it: intensity falls steeply with distance from a road, from well above the window mean within the first kilometre to below it beyond a few kilometres. That is a strong and monotone access effect, consistent with ignition being human. The waterway relationship is weaker and less monotone. This is my more interesting negative result. It does not show drainage is unimportant, it shows OpenStreetMap’s waterway layer is a poor proxy for it, because the dense minor canal network of the former Mega Rice Project is largely unmapped. My covariate is measuring mapping effort as much as hydrology, so I read the flat curve as absence of evidence.

The signs describe an agricultural frontier. Intensity rises steeply as you approach plantation and farmland (coefficient -0.0519, z = -29.3) and falls as you approach mapped forest (0.0135, z = 14.6). Fire sits near cultivated land and away from standing forest. For peat fire used in land clearing that is the expected pattern, and it is a more specific mechanism than proximity to a road.
The caveat from the drainage covariate applies again, with less force. OSM landuse is sparse here. Mapped forest covers 20.8% of the window and plantation or farmland 10.6%, from a few dozen polygons apiece. Distance to the nearest such polygon across a 9,759 km² regency is a coarse instrument, and part of what it measures is where mappers have drawn boundaries. The effect is large enough, and the signs coherent enough, that I do not think mapping effort explains it. I cannot rule it out.
None of this is causal. Roads, farmland and forest edges are all jointly determined by where people have cleared and worked the land. The model identifies association and orders the covariates by explanatory power. It does not tell me what would happen if any of them changed.

10.1.1 What the covariates still fail to explain


code
rk <- RK$res_K
ycol <- if ("bres" %in% names(rk)) "bres" else names(rk)[2]
ggplot(rk, aes(r, .data[[ycol]])) +

       title = "The covariates explain location, not contagion",
       subtitle = glue("Model: {RK$formula}")) +

Figure 23: Residual K function for the best-fitting Poisson model, which is the full model with road, water, forest and plantation distances. If the fitted trend explained the pattern this curve would sit on zero. What I take from it: it does not. A large positive residual remains at short lags, so the covariates account for a great deal of the first-order variation and none of the local interaction. Knowing how far a place is from cleared land tells me whether it is likely to burn. It does not tell me that burning spreads. A Poisson model cannot represent contagion by construction, which is what motivates the cluster process fitted next.

title: Where peat burns, and how close together
text:
10.2 How large is a cluster?
A significance test says clustering exists. A fitted cluster process says how big it is, which is the form a planner can use. Getting that number right meant discarding my first answer.
The first fit had no trend term. It returned a cluster standard deviation of 3,292 m, about 440 events per cluster, and an implied 24 parent locations across the whole regency. Twenty-three clusters of 440 events each is not a cluster scale. It is the southern peat belt re-described as a handful of enormous clusters, which is the only way a model without a trend term can represent large-scale intensity variation. Trend and interaction are not separately identifiable unless you make them so. Taken at face value the number would have given a confident and completely wrong operational radius.
The fix is to remove the trend before estimating the cluster parameters. My inhomogeneous pair correlation function already does exactly that, because it divides out \(\hat{\lambda}(u)\). So I fitted the Thomas pair correlation function
\[g(r) \;=\; 1 + \frac{1}{4\pi\kappa\sigma^{2}}\exp\!\left(-\frac{r^{2}}{4\sigma^{2}}\right)\]
directly to \(g_{inhom}\) by minimum contrast, minimising \(\sum_r \left(\hat{g}(r)^{q} - g_\theta(r)^{q}\right)^{2}\) with \(q = 1/4\) over \(r \in [200, 5,000]\) m. I set the lower limit to exclude lags governed by the 375 m sensor floor rather than by the cluster process. I wrote the fit out explicitly in R/07_cluster_scale.R rather than calling a packaged routine, because the objective function and the excluded range are the substance of the estimate and I wanted them visible.

TH$thomas_tab |> transmute(

  `sigma (m)` = round(sigma_m),
  `r95 (m)` = round(r95_m),
  `Parents in regency` = round(n_parents_implied),
  `Events per cluster` = round(mu_per_cluster)) |> kable(align = "lrrrr")

The contrast between the two rows is the finding: leaving the trend in the model inflates the estimated cluster scale by a factor of two, and the implied cluster sizes become absurd.

gobs <- EX$g_obs_ext |> filter(r > 0, r <= TH$RMAX, is.finite(trans))
ggplot() +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 0, xmax = TH$RMIN, ymin = 1, ymax = max(gobs$trans) * 1.05,
           fill = PAL$rule, alpha = 0.45) +

            linewidth = 0.55) +

  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "r", y = "g(r), log scale",
       title = "Removing the trend halves the estimated cluster scale",
       subtitle = "Orange, observed inhomogeneous pcf. Blue, fitted Thomas models. Shaded, lags excluded from the fit.") +
  theme_ex01()








Figure 24: Observed inhomogeneous pair correlation function with the two fitted Thomas models, log scale, over the range used for fitting. The shaded band marks lags below 200 m, excluded from the fit because they are governed by the sensor’s pixel size. What I take from it: the trend-removed fit tracks the observed curve closely from the peak outward, which is the range that matters for an operational radius. The fit that retains the trend is too flat and too wide, because its cluster component is doing work that belongs to the intensity surface. Neither fit captures the observed curve beyond about 4 km, where the observed g_inhom decays more slowly than a single Gaussian cluster kernel allows. That is a real limitation of my model: the pattern has structure at more than one scale, and a one-scale model cannot represent it.





My trend-removed fit gives a cluster standard deviation of 1,055 m, so about 95% of a cluster’s events fall within roughly 2,581 m of its centre, with 67 events per cluster and about 155 cluster centres across the regency.

10.2.1 How precise is that number
Minimum contrast gives no standard error, so the estimate above was unqualified until I bootstrapped it. My first attempt resampled points with replacement. That is not a valid bootstrap for a point process: it destroys the dependence being estimated and creates coincident points, which distorts the pair correlation function at exactly the short lags the fit uses. The symptom was unmistakable. The interval excluded the point estimate entirely, and in the wrong direction.
The interval below comes from a parametric bootstrap. I simulate from the fitted inhomogeneous Thomas process, re-estimate \(\hat{\lambda}\) on each simulation, recompute \(g_{inhom}\), and refit by the same minimum contrast.


code
BC$boot_compare |> transmute(

  `sigma point (m)` = round(point_sigma_m),
  `median (m)` = round(median_m),
  `95% interval (m)` = glue("{round(lo95_m)} to {round(hi95_m)}"),
  `r95 interval (m)` = glue("{round(r95_lo_m)} to {round(r95_hi_m)}")
) |> kable(align = "lrrll")

Table 24: Two bootstrap intervals on the cluster standard deviation. The non-parametric row is shown because it is wrong in an instructive way: an interval that excludes its own point estimate is a sign the resampling scheme does not respect the process.




The parametric interval puts the cluster standard deviation between 902 and 1,025 m, and the radius holding 95% of a cluster between 2.21 and 2.51 km. The refits sit a little below the point estimate, a known downward bias of minimum contrast under resimulation, so the point estimate lies just above its own interval. A cluster scale of about a kilometre, with roughly 2.2 to 2.5 km holding the bulk of one, is the summary I would defend. The kilometre-scale conclusion does not turn on which end of that range is right. That is consistent with my pair correlation function, which peaks at 438 m, and I got there by a different route: minimum contrast fitting of a mechanistic model rather than envelope testing.
Two estimates agreeing is stronger than either alone, but the agreement is only partial and I should say where it breaks. My fitted model has a single scale, and the figure below shows the observed curve decaying more slowly beyond about 4 km than a single Gaussian kernel allows. So the Thomas process describes the dominant local structure well and the longer tail of dependence out to roughly 7.2 km not at all. A multi-scale cluster process, or a log-Gaussian Cox process with a flexible covariance, would be the natural next model. Fitting one is beyond what I can do in this exercise, but it is the first thing I would try next.

10.3 Where is the single most unusual concentration?
This is the most directly practical question I ask anywhere in the report. Not whether clustering exists, but where the single most unusual concentration sits and whether it is more extreme than chance would produce.

  `p-value` = fmt_p(sc$p.value, 99),

) |> kable(align = "rrll")

It measures, at each location, how much better a model with an elevated rate inside a circle fits than a model with a constant rate, so it answers where I would look first rather than where fire is densest. The maximum sits in the southern peat belt, consistent with the kernel intensity estimate, and the statistic is significant at the Monte Carlo floor. What this adds over my intensity map is that it is explicitly comparative. The broad plateau shows several locations are nearly as unusual as the maximum, so I would over-read it if I treated the single peak as uniquely important.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Geospatial Analytics for Public Safety
text:
12.1 Consistency across approaches
My first-order and second-order analyses agree where they should and disagree in two places, and the disagreements taught me more than the agreement did.
They agree on the dominant scale. The inhomogeneous pair correlation function peaks at 438 m, and a Thomas process fitted to that same curve returns a cluster standard deviation of 1,055 m. Envelope testing and model fitting are different machinery, and both land near a kilometre. That agreement is why I am willing to quote the number at all.
They disagree about extent, and it is the cumulative statistic that misled me. \(L_{inhom}\) never re-enters its envelope within 20 km, which tempted me to conclude that dependence extends at least that far. \(g_{inhom}\), which localises scale instead of accumulating it, shows the excess is within 10% of nothing by about 7.2 km. Both computations are correct and the second is the one I report, because \(L\) accumulates every excess at smaller lags and therefore stays elevated long past the range over which anything is actually happening. This is a general property of \(K\) and \(L\) rather than a quirk of my data, and it is probably the single most useful thing I learned doing this exercise.
They disagree about sufficiency, and my first-order surface loses. My earlier version, capped at a 5 km lag, concluded that the intensity surface was an adequate description above about 2 km. That was wrong, and wrong because of a decision rather than a computation: my cap was too short to see where dependence ended. Corrected, the first-order surface is not a sufficient description at any lag below roughly 7.2 km. A smooth intensity map is still a reasonable tool for allocating resources across a regency. It is not a tool for anticipating what happens next around a fire that has already started.
The covariate models sharpen this. They improve on an intercept-only model by 3,550 AIC units, most of it from land cover, so a lot of the first-order variation is explained by where the cleared and cultivated ground is. The residual \(K\) function shows they capture none of the local interaction. Land cover explains where fire is likely. It does not explain the contagion.

title: Where peat burns, and how close together
text:
10.2 Where the analysis is weakest
Three places, in order of severity.
The event definition does the heavy lifting. Collapsing detections to cells is defensible and necessary, but it is a modelling decision presented as data preparation. A cell that burned for three weeks and a cell that burned for one overpass contribute identically to ppp_cell. An analysis weighting cells by persistence or by cumulative radiative power would answer a related but different question and might not reach the same conclusion about scale.
The inhomogeneous null is estimated from the data under test. The bias is in the conservative direction, so the rejection stands, but the magnitude of the excess clustering is not reliably estimated. Statements about how much clustering there is should be read as ordinal, not quantitative.
Detectability is confounded with intensity. Assumptions A1 and A2 cannot be discharged within this data source. Sub-surface peat smouldering, the mode of greatest public-health concern, is systematically under-detected, and cloud cover is not plausibly independent of location. The intensity surface is a surface of detected fire.
One analytical decision was simply wrong and had to be reversed. The r range was initially capped at 5 km. Every inhomogeneous statistic sat outside its envelope across the whole of that range, which means the cap could not answer the question it was set to answer, and the first draft of this report drew a conclusion from it that the extended analysis contradicts. The cap is recorded here rather than silently replaced, because a range chosen before seeing the curves and then revised when the curves demanded it is a different thing from a range chosen to produce a tidy answer, and a reader has no way to tell the two apart unless told.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Geospatial Analytics for Public Safety
text:
Contents

One argument running through all of it: a satellite hotspot is not a fire, and almost everything I did follows from taking that seriously.


The place, the data, and the window
Why a detection is not a fire
Where it burns

Two nulls: one meaningless, one that can fail

section: 1. A regency chosen by rule, not reputation
text:
1. A regency chosen by rule, not reputation













My rule, set first. Highest detection density among regencies above 5,000 km², the size floor I need for second-order estimation to a 5 km lag.
Pulang Pisau wins outright, at 3,656 per 1,000 km².
What I rejected. Ketapang leads on raw count (65,901) but is 3x the area. Kota Palangka Raya is denser but only 2,606 km².
My first pass picked it from a 7-day sample where it led on count. Over the full window it does not, so I restated the rule against the whole record.

section: 2. Data, and a constraint worth naming
text:
2. Data, and a constraint worth naming



413,182


rows downloaded, all Kalimantan




34,987


detections inside the regency




10,321


burned 375 m cells, the analysis unit




87


days, 1 Jul to 25 Sep



VIIRS 375 m Collection 2, both platforms. My window is the administrative polygon in UTM 49S, 9,759 km².
The temporal window was imposed on me, not chosen. The FIRMS area API retains near-real-time granules for roughly 90 days, and the standard-processing archive is not built for 2026. My Kalimantan-wide queries return exactly zero rows for every sampled date from January to 30 June, and non-zero from 1 July. Six months of zero detections across a 10° box is not credible, so I read that as absence of coverage, not absence of fire.
The cost: no wet-season baseline, so nothing here speaks to seasonal amplitude. It does span onset to peak, which is the period an agency acts on.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Geospatial Analytics for Public Safety
section: 2. A detection is not a fire
text:
2. A detection is not a fire













One large peat fire fills many 375 m pixels, and two satellites re-detect it about four times a day.
I measured it: the raw count overstates distinct burning locations by 3.4x.
So the pattern I started with partly measures the satellite’s revisit schedule, which means testing against complete spatial randomness was guaranteed to reject before I computed anything.
So I changed two things. The unit becomes the 375 m cell. The null becomes an inhomogeneous Poisson process.
That is the spine of everything else I did.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Geospatial Analytics for Public Safety
text:
3. Where it burns













Gaussian kernel, Diggle edge correction, bandwidth I fixed at 4 km.
Cross-validated selectors gave me about 0.6 km and I rejected them: they absorb the very clustering my second-order test exists to detect, which would have rigged the second-order test two slides on.
Intensity spans roughly two orders of magnitude between the southern peat belt and the northern interior.
So allocating in proportion to sub-district area is badly matched to risk. I think that is the most directly usable thing I found.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Geospatial Analytics for Public Safety
section: 4. When it burns, and what the orbit decides
text:
4. When it burns, and what the orbit decides













Heavily back-loaded: week 1 recorded 7 events, the week of 16 September recorded 8,087.
The day/night contrast is not a daily cycle, and I nearly read it as one. Both platforms observe at four narrow fixed local times, so if I claimed fire peaks at a given hour I would be describing the orbit.
I use the split only as a detectability covariate, since night overpasses catch cooler anomalies against a cooler background.

title: Where peat burns, and how close together
text:
6. Against CSR, everything is significant

Every statistic leaves the envelope immediately. This should persuade nobody, including me: the sensor guarantees it. I show it so the failure is visible rather than hidden.
My pair correlation function makes the point sharper. It is suppressed below 375 m, the pixel dimension. That apparent short-range inhibition is the instrument, not fires avoiding one another.

title: Where peat burns, and how close together
text:
7. The test that can fail













My null is an inhomogeneous Poisson process with intensity from the 4 km kernel estimate, so everything my first-order analysis found is already inside the null. I re-estimate the reference intensity for every simulated pattern.
The departure survives. Both global tests reject at the Monte Carlo floor.
The two panels disagree, and that was the lesson for me. L_inhom never re-enters its envelope in 20 km. g_inhom, which localises scale instead of accumulating it, peaks at 438 m and is within 10% of no-excess by 7.2 km.
L accumulates every excess at smaller lags, so it stays significant far past the range where anything is happening. My first draft capped r at 5 km and drew the wrong conclusion from exactly this.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Geospatial Analytics for Public Safety
section: 6. Space and time are not separable
text:
6. Space and time are not separable













Knox test. My null is random labelling: I hold locations and dates both fixed and permute only their pairing, across 999 permutations of 8,720,153 close pairs.
Because both marginals stay fixed, none of this can be explained away by the seasonal ramp or the spatial concentration.
Strongest at the tightest cell, decaying monotonically outward. I read that as short-range propagation: a cell that burns today raises the chance a neighbour burns tomorrow, and the effect is largely spent within days and a kilometre or two.
The decay is steeper in time than in space, which fits fire spreading over contiguous ground within days rather than recurring in the same place weeks apart.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Geospatial Analytics for Public Safety
section: 7. What it is organised around, and how big it is
text:
7. What it is organised around, and how big it is













Plantation, not access. Fitted alone, distance to plantation and farmland recovers 3,204 of the 3,550 AIC units the full model gains. Roads alone recover 1,991.
My first version had only roads and waterways and concluded access dominated. That was the thin covariate set talking.
But not the forest half of that story. Fitted alone, distance to forest explains less than roads (1,906), its curve is not monotone, and the median burned cell sits 20 km from any mapped forest. I reported it as a mechanism and it is not one.
Cluster scale 1055 m, parametric bootstrap 902 to 1025 m, with 2.2 to 2.5 km holding most of a cluster.
Resampling points with replacement gave an interval that excluded its own point estimate. That is not a valid bootstrap for a point process.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Geospatial Analytics for Public Safety
section: 9. What this supports, and what it does not
text:
9. What this supports, and what it does not


What I would act on
Reallocate by intensity, not by area. Two orders of magnitude separate the southern peat belt from the northern interior.
A containment geometry. First ring 2.2 to 2.5 km, elevation out to about 7.2 km, days not weeks.
A monitoring limit. I cannot resolve anything below 375 m. A finer answer needs a different sensor, not a different statistic.


What I would not claim
Roads as a policy lever. Roads follow worked land. I cannot tell from this whether access aids suppression or enables ignition, and the two point opposite ways.
Drainage, or land cover, as a lever. Both covariates are limited by OSM coverage, and cleared land, roads and forest edges are jointly determined.
Any claim about time of day. Four fixed overpasses.
That any of this describes a normal year. As the previous slide shows, 2026 is the second-worst season in fourteen years, so every scale here was measured under extreme conditions.

title: Where peat burns, and how close together
section: 1.1 The problem the data handed me
text:
1.1 The problem the data handed me
A VIIRS active-fire detection is not a fire. It is a 375 m pixel where a radiometer measured a thermal anomaly during one overpass. A peat fire covering ten square kilometres fills dozens of those pixels in a single pass, and between them the two satellites pass overhead about four times a day, so the same fire is recorded again and again. The detection set samples the sensor’s view of fire. Any statistic I compute on it is partly a measurement of the instrument.
That ruins the textbook second-order question. Asking whether the pattern is clustered relative to complete spatial randomness has an answer before I compute anything: yes, overwhelmingly, and it would still be yes if fires were sited at random, because each one produces a burst of adjacent detections. I did not want to build a report on a rejection that was guaranteed.
Two changes follow, and they are the methodological content of this exercise. The unit of analysis becomes the 375 m cell, not the detection. The null becomes an inhomogeneous Poisson process, not complete spatial randomness. Section 7 is where that earns its keep.

3.2 Why I chose this regency
I chose the study window with a rule applied to the whole island, after downloading data for all 56 Kalimantan regencies and cities and screening it for confidence. The rule: the highest detection density among regencies large enough to support second-order estimation to a 5 km lag, which I operationalised as an area above 5,000 km².
I used density rather than raw count because intensity relative to window area is what governs how much signal a point pattern carries. I added the size floor because a 5 km lag inside a small window starts to approach the window’s own dimension, and at that point edge effects dominate every second-order estimate I would compute.

Pulang Pisau wins on that rule outright, at 3656 detections per 1,000 km². Two alternatives were seriously considered and rejected, and the reasons are recorded because a choice is only reviewable alongside them.
Ketapang beat it on absolute count, with 65,901 detections against Pulang Pisau’s 35,679. I did not choose it because it covers 29,722 km², slightly over three times the area, and ranks second on density. Its bigger count is mostly just a bigger window.

My first pass picked the regency from a seven-day sample, where Pulang Pisau led on count. Over the full 87 days it does not. Ketapang does. I restated the rule against the complete record and applied it again. A rule chosen after you have seen which unit it favours is not a rule, so the sequence is recorded here for the reader to judge.

section: 3.6 My completeness audit, and a real outage
text:
3.6 My completeness audit, and a real outage
Counting downloaded rows does not establish completeness. The failure I was worried about is a request that returns empty, which looks exactly like a day on which nothing burned and would appear in the analysis as a drop in fire activity that never happened.
The audit is built around one expectation: across an 87-day dry season, each platform should record at least one detection somewhere in Kalimantan every day. An island-sized box is never entirely without fire. Any day where a platform contributes nothing is a candidate failure.

Table 4: Completeness audit. Local dates on which one VIIRS platform contributed no detection anywhere in the Kalimantan bounding box. Each was re-queried four times with backoff by R/01b_fill_gaps.R, and each returned empty again, so these are not failed requests.




Six of the seven dates are consecutive, which pointed at an outage rather than a flaky connection. Re-querying confirmed it. Suomi NPP returns empty for 11 to 16 July and for 3 August however many times I ask, so the absence is in the FIRMS record itself. On those seven days the analysis rests on NOAA-20 alone and counts are depressed by roughly one platform’s contribution.
The consequence is small, but I do not want to write it off as nothing. Those dates carry 51 of 23,576 events, or 0.22% of the record, and all of them fall in the near-zero early season before the dry-season ramp. Mean daily events on the affected dates are 7.3 against 10.8 on nearby unaffected July dates, which is consistent with losing one platform on very small counts. No conclusion I draw turns on those seven days, but the reader should treat the early-season part of my daily series as a slight underestimate.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Geospatial Analytics for Public Safety
section: 4.2 The missing type field, and what I replaced it with
text:
4.2 The missing type field, and what I replaced it with
This took the longest to solve. The FIRMS standard-processing product carries a type field separating vegetation fire (0) from active volcano (1), other static land source (2) and offshore (3). The NRT product does not, which I checked against the API response header: column present = FALSE. The screen it would have given me had to be rebuilt from other evidence.
I worked through the three cases separately:

Volcanoes (type 1) are not a risk at all. Borneo has no Holocene volcano, so this screen is unnecessary not approximated. I did not need to do anything.
Offshore (type 3) is already handled by my clip to the terrestrial polygon.
Other static land sources (type 2) are a genuine problem. Kalimantan has palm-oil mills, coal operations and gas flares, and all of them show up as persistent thermal anomalies. This is the case I actually had to solve.

My substitute is a persistence screen. The logic is that a vegetation fire burns out or moves, whereas a flare stack does not. So I score each 375 m cell by the number of distinct local dates on which it was detected, as a fraction of the 87-day window, and drop cells above a threshold as fixed installations.

4.3 My evidence that a detection is not a fire
The claim I made in Section 1.1 is checkable, so I checked it. If detections were independent events, most occupied cells would be detected exactly once. They are not.


code
mt <- P$multiplicity
ggplot(mt, aes(n_det, n_cells)) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = n_det, yend = 0), colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.35, alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = label_number(accuracy = 1)) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = label_number(big.mark = ",", accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(x = "Detections recorded in the cell", y = "Number of cells",
       title = "One fire, many detections",
       subtitle = glue("{fmt_n(sum(mt$n_cells))} occupied cells. Median {median(rep(mt$n_det, mt$n_cells))} detections per cell, ",
                       "maximum {max(mt$n_det)}.")) +
  theme_ex01()


Warning in scale_y_log10(labels = label_number(big.mark = ",", accuracy = 1)):
log-10 transformation introduced infinite values.








Figure 1: Detections per occupied 375 m cell over the 87-day window, log scale on both axes. If each detection were an independent event, the distribution would be concentrated at one. Instead a long tail of cells is detected tens or hundreds of times, which is the repeat-observation signature of persistent fire in a fixed pixel grid observed roughly four times daily.





Only 34.2% of occupied cells were detected exactly once. The mean is 3.4 detections per occupied cell, so the raw count overstates the number of distinct burning locations by a factor of about 3.4. That is the number that convinced me. Analysing the raw detections as a point pattern would mean analysing the satellite’s revisit schedule about as much as the fire regime, which is why I made ppp_cell the primary unit.

Table 10: The methodological decisions I made. The right-hand column records the alternative I considered and did not take, which I think is the part that makes a decision reviewable.




Two of these are worth explaining properly.
Border versus Ripley correction. Ripley’s isotropic correction is more efficient and much more expensive, and the envelope procedure needs 199 re-computations of it. At 10,321 points the efficiency lost to the border correction is immaterial: the number of pairs contributing at each lag is already very large. A compute trade-off, made deliberately.
Global versus pointwise tests. This one took me a while to get straight. A pointwise envelope gets read at every one of several hundred values of \(r\), so the probability of at least one excursion under the null is far above the nominal level. I still plot the pointwise envelopes, because they show me where on the \(r\) axis the departure sits and a single p-value cannot. But every claim of significance I make in this report is backed by the MAD or DCLF global test, not by the band.

Table 11: Chi-squared test of a homogeneous Poisson process, across quadrat resolutions. The variance-to-mean ratio (VMR) is 1 under complete spatial randomness. The verdict is identical at every resolution, which is the point: the test is not informative, it is merely arithmetically certain.




The chi-squared statistic exceeds its degrees of freedom by three to four orders of magnitude at every resolution, and the variance-to-mean ratio runs from 79.2 to 1036.1 against a null of 1. Complete spatial homogeneity is rejected with certainty.
It should persuade nobody. The result was guaranteed by the data-generating process in Section 1.1, and by the geography: a regency that is half drained peatland and half intact landscape cannot have uniform fire intensity. Quadrat counts also inherit an arbitrary origin and cell size and discard everything within a quadrat. The one useful column is the VMR, which says how far from uniform the pattern is at each scale instead of answering a question I already knew the answer to.

6.4 Bandwidth selection, and why I rejected cross-validation
Kernel density estimation does the work here, and the bandwidth decides what it shows. This took longer than any other single choice in the report.


code
FO$bw_tab |> transmute(Selector = selector, `sigma (m)` = round(sigma_m),
                       `sigma (km)` = sigma_km) |> kable(align = "lrr")








Selector
sigma (m)
sigma (km)

10530

10543

Table 12: Bandwidth selectors compared on the primary pattern, ordered as computed. The spread is a factor of roughly eighteen from smallest to largest, which is why reporting a single surface without this table would conceal the most consequential choice in the first-order analysis.




Both cross-validation selectors returned sub-kilometre bandwidths, 573 m for bw.ppl and 628 m for bw.diggle, and density.ppp threw a numerical-underflow warning at that scale over a 9,759 km² window. Neither was adopted, and not because of the warning.
Cross-validation selectors choose very small bandwidths when a pattern is strongly clustered at short range. Their criteria reward a surface that reproduces the local bursts, so clustering gets absorbed into the intensity estimate. For some purposes that is what you want. Not here. The same estimate becomes the reference intensity for the second-order test in Section 7.3, and if \(\hat{\lambda}(u)\) has already soaked up the sub-kilometre clustering then asking whether clustering survives its removal is rigged. The answer would be no by construction, and confidently wrong.
So I fixed the bandwidth at 4,000 m, on a criterion I set before looking at the surfaces: it has to exceed the interaction range, so that trend and interaction are estimated by separate parts of my analysis instead of competing for the same signal. Four kilometres sits above the interaction range Section 7 goes on to find, inside the interval spanned by the two components of bw.scott (3,847 m and 10,543 m), and below bw.CvL (10,530 m).
I want to be clear that this is a judgement and not an optimisation. The comparison below shows what each alternative would have given me, so anyone who disagrees can see the consequence rather than taking my word for it.


code
bw_panels <- list(
  ppl   = glue("bw.ppl, {round(FO$sigma_ppl)} m (rejected)"),
  main  = glue("adopted, {fmt_n(FO$sigma_main)} m"),
  scott = glue("bw.scott x, {fmt_n(round(FO$sigma_scott[1]))} m"),
  CvL   = glue("bw.CvL, {fmt_n(round(FO$sigma_CvL))} m"))
bw_df <- bind_rows(lapply(names(bw_panels), function(k)
  im_df(FO$kde[[k]]) |> mutate(panel = bw_panels[[k]]))) |>
  mutate(v = per_1000km2(intensity))
bw_df$panel <- factor(bw_df$panel, levels = unlist(bw_panels))
ggplot(bw_df) +
  geom_raster(aes(x, y, fill = v)) +
  geom_sf(data = win_p, fill = NA, colour = PAL$ink, linewidth = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, nrow = 1) +
  scale_fill_intensity(v = bw_df$v) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA, expand = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "What the bandwidth decides") +
  theme_map(base_size = 9)








Figure 4: The same pattern under four bandwidths. What I take from it: the choice is not cosmetic. The cross-validated surface resolves individual fire complexes and, at this sample size, a great deal of structure no agency could act on; it is also the surface that would sabotage the second-order test, for the reason given above. The 10.5 km bw.CvL surface is stable but has smoothed away the distinction between the peat belt and its margins, which is the distinction of interest. The adopted 4 km surface and bw.scott’s 3.8 km are visually close, which is reassurance that the adopted value is not an idiosyncratic pick. What I should disclose is that all four agree on where the principal concentration is and disagree on how many secondary ones exist, so I make no claim about secondary hotspots.

title: Where peat burns, and how close together
text:
6.5 The intensity surface I report


code
kde_main <- im_df(FO$kde$main) |> mutate(v = per_1000km2(intensity))
ggplot(kde_main) +
  geom_raster(aes(x, y, fill = v)) +
  geom_sf(data = win_p, fill = NA, colour = PAL$ink, linewidth = 0.45) +
  scale_fill_intensity(v = kde_main$v) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA, expand = FALSE) +
  scalebar_layer(bb) + north_layer(bb) +
  labs(title = "Fire intensity concentrates in the drained southern peat",
       subtitle = glue("Kernel intensity estimate, sigma = {fmt_n(FO$sigma_main)} m, Diggle edge correction")) +
  theme_map() + theme(legend.position = "right", legend.key.height = unit(34, "pt"),
                      legend.key.width = unit(9, "pt"))








Figure 5: Estimated first-order intensity of burned cells, Gaussian kernel with Diggle’s edge correction, at the adopted 4 km bandwidth. What I take from it: intensity is organised as a broad south-southeast band reaching a maximum in the lower third of the regency, with a secondary extension along the eastern margin. The empty northern interior is a real absence rather than an absence of observation: the same satellites observed it on the same days. The gradient is steep, spanning roughly two orders of magnitude between the peat belt and the northern interior, which means resource allocation proportional to intensity would be very unevenly distributed. That is the operational content of a first-order surface, and it is the strongest planning-relevant thing my first-order analysis alone supports.





I also computed an adaptive estimator as a check, because a fixed bandwidth over-smooths sparse areas and under-smooths dense ones. It reproduces the same principal concentration, which is the reassurance I was after: the structure I report is not an artefact of forcing one bandwidth everywhere.

title: Where peat burns, and how close together
section: 7.1 The straw man I had to test anyway
text:
7.1 The straw man I had to test anyway


code
mk_env_df <- function(e, lab) e |> mutate(panel = lab)
eg <- mk_env_df(SO$env_G, "G(r), nearest neighbour")
ef <- mk_env_df(SO$env_F, "F(r), empty space")
el <- SO$env_L |>
  mutate(across(c(obs, theo, lo, hi), ~ .x - r), panel = "L(r) - r, centred")
env_all <- bind_rows(eg, ef, el)
env_all$panel <- factor(env_all$panel, levels = c("G(r), nearest neighbour",
                                                  "F(r), empty space", "L(r) - r, centred"))
ggplot(env_all, aes(r)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = PAL$rule, alpha = 0.75) +
  geom_line(aes(y = theo), colour = PAL$muted, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_line(aes(y = obs), colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, scales = "free", nrow = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(scale = 1e-3, suffix = " km")) +
  labs(x = "r", y = NULL,
       title = "Against complete spatial randomness, everything is significant",
       subtitle = glue("Orange, observed. Grey band, envelope from {SO$nsim} CSR simulations. Dashed, theoretical CSR value.")) +
  theme_ex01(base_size = 9)








Figure 9: Nearest-neighbour G, empty-space F, and the centred L function, each against a complete spatial randomness envelope from 199 simulations. What I take from it: every statistic departs from the CSR envelope immediately and by an enormous margin. G rises far faster than expected, meaning nearest neighbours are much closer than random; F rises far slower, meaning empty gaps are much larger than random; L sits far above zero at every lag. Read naively this is overwhelming evidence of clustering. Read correctly it is evidence of almost nothing, because the sensor guarantees this result: a single fire produces adjacent detections. I include it to make that failure visible rather than hide it. The analysis I actually rely on is in Section 7.3.

title: Where peat burns, and how close together
section: 7.6 Extending the range, after getting it wrong
text:
7.6 Extending the range, after getting it wrong
I set the 5 km cap because long lags in an elongated window rest on few pairs. That reasoning is fine, but 5 km was more conservative than I needed. The rule I stated in Section 5 caps \(r\) at a quarter of the window’s shortest dimension, and the window is 86 km wide, so 20 km was admissible the whole time. Extending to 20 km is not me granting myself a post-hoc licence, it is me finally applying the rule I had already written down.
Two practical constraints came with that, and I am disclosing both rather than hiding them. pcfinhom offers no border correction, and the translation correction over roughly seven million pairs per pattern would not finish in a workable time for 99 simulated patterns. So my significance across the extended range rests on \(L_{inhom}\) with a border correction and a full envelope, while the shape of \(g_{inhom}\) comes from a single translation-corrected curve with no simulations. I make no significance claim for \(g_{inhom}\) beyond 3 km.


code
Lx <- EX$env_L_ext |> mutate(across(c(obs, lo, hi), ~ .x - r), ref = 0,
                             panel = "L_inhom(r) - r, with envelope")
Gx <- EX$g_obs_ext |> filter(r > 0, is.finite(trans)) |>
  transmute(r, obs = trans, lo = NA_real_, hi = NA_real_, ref = 1,
            panel = "g_inhom(r), observed only")
ggplot(bind_rows(Lx, Gx), aes(r)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = PAL$rule, alpha = 0.75, na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_line(aes(y = ref), colour = PAL$muted, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_line(aes(y = obs), colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(data = tibble(panel = "g_inhom(r), observed only",
                           x = EX$summary_ext$r_g_within_10pct_of_1),
             aes(xintercept = x), colour = PAL$cool, linetype = "12", linewidth = 0.4) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, scales = "free", nrow = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(scale = 1e-3, suffix = " km")) +
  labs(x = "r", y = NULL,
       title = "Dependence is local, but a cumulative statistic cannot say so",
       subtitle = glue("Dotted line marks {round(EX$summary_ext$r_g_within_10pct_of_1/1000, 1)} km, where g_inhom first comes within 10% of 1.")) +
  theme_ex01(base_size = 9)








Figure 14: Left, inhomogeneous centred L function to 20 km with a 99-simulation envelope. Right, the observed inhomogeneous pair correlation function over the same range, with no envelope, on a log scale. What I take from it: the two panels answer different questions and disagree in an instructive way. g_inhom, which localises scale, peaks at about 440 m and decays steadily: it is 4.3 at 1 km, 2.7 at 2 km, 1.4 at 5 km, and reaches within 10% of its asymptote of 1 at about 7.2 km. L_inhom, which is cumulative, never re-enters its envelope within 20 km. Both are correct. The excess pair density is a local phenomenon that has largely dissipated by 7 km, and because L accumulates every excess at smaller lags it remains significantly elevated far beyond the range over which anything is actually happening.
