Table 17: Observed inhomogeneous pair correlation at selected lags. A value of 1 means no excess over the inhomogeneous Poisson expectation.




I cross-checked the extended curve against my Section 7.3 estimate over the lags both cover, since both use the translation correction. The median relative difference is 0.15%, so changing the \(r\) grid has not quietly changed the estimate underneath me.
So here is my corrected answer to Q3. Residual clustering begins immediately above the sensor floor, is strongest at roughly 438 m, and only decays to within 10% of no excess by about 7.2 km. My earlier statement that the excess was exhausted by 2 km was simply an artefact of not having looked far enough, and the conclusion I drew from it, that the first-order surface was a sufficient description above 2 km, was wrong. It is not sufficient at any lag below roughly 7 km.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Geospatial Analytics for Public Safety
text:
12.2 Where my analysis is weakest
Four places, roughly in order of how much they worry me.
My event definition does the heavy lifting. Collapsing detections to cells is necessary and defensible, but it is a modelling decision presented as data preparation, and those are not the same thing. A cell that burned for three weeks and one that burned for a single overpass contribute identically to ppp_cell. Weighting by persistence or by cumulative radiative power would answer a related question, and I am not confident it would give the same scale.
My inhomogeneous null is estimated from the data I am testing. The bias runs in the conservative direction, so I am comfortable that the rejection stands. But the magnitude of the excess clustering is not reliably estimated, so anything I say about how much clustering there is should be read as ordinal rather than quantitative.
Detectability is confounded with intensity. I cannot discharge assumptions A1 and A2 within this data source. Sub-surface peat smouldering, the mode I care most about for public health, is systematically under-detected, and cloud cover is not plausibly independent of location. What I have mapped is a surface of detected fire, not of fire.
One of my decisions was simply wrong and I had to reverse it. I initially capped the r range at 5 km. Every inhomogeneous statistic sat outside its envelope across the whole of that range, which means my cap could not answer the question I set it to answer, and my first draft drew a conclusion from it that the extended analysis contradicts. I have left the cap in the record rather than quietly replacing it. A range chosen before seeing the curves and then revised when the curves demanded it is a different thing from a range chosen to produce a tidy answer, and a reader has no way to tell those apart unless I say which one happened.

title: Global Measures of Spatial Autocorrelation
text:
R spdep Moran’s I Geary’s C Correlogram
This exercise follows Global Measures of Spatial Autocorrelation, in the Spatial Weights block of the course.

title: Global Measures of Spatial Autocorrelation
text:
1. Overview
Exercise 4 built the weights matrix. This exercise finally uses it to answer a question worth asking: is Hunan’s economic development spatially clustered, or is it scattered at random across the province?
That matters because the two cases call for different policy. If wealthy counties are scattered, each one succeeded on its own terms and there is little to generalise. If they are clustered, something is spilling across county borders, and the unit of intervention is the region rather than the county.
The techniques split into two levels:

Global measures return one number for the whole map. Moran’s I and Geary’s C answer “is there clustering anywhere”.
Local measures return one number per county. LISA and Getis-Ord Gi* answer “clustering where”, which is the question a planner actually has.

I expected the local maps to be a more detailed version of the global result. They are not, and the gap between them turned out to be the most useful thing in this exercise.

title: Global Measures of Spatial Autocorrelation
text:
2. The Study Area and Data








Dataset
Description
Format




Hunan
County boundary layer for Hunan province, China, 88 counties
ESRI Shapefile (polygon)


Hunan_2012.csv
Selected local development indicators for 2012
CSV



Same data as Exercise 4, which is deliberate. Having already built and inspected the weights matrix for these 88 counties, I can attribute anything surprising here to the statistics rather than to the geography being unfamiliar.
The variable of interest is GDPPC, GDP per capita, which ranges from 8,497 to 88,656 with a mean of 24,405. That is better than a tenfold spread across a single province.

title: Global Measures of Spatial Autocorrelation
text:
5. Visualising the Distribution
Before any test, look at the map. A statistic that disagrees with the picture usually means the statistic was computed wrong.

equal <- tm_shape(hunan) +
  tm_polygons("GDPPC", fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(n = 5, style = "equal"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Equal interval")) +
  tm_borders(col_alpha = 0.5)

quantile <- tm_shape(hunan) +
  tm_polygons("GDPPC", fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(n = 5, style = "quantile"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Equal quantile")) +
  tm_borders(col_alpha = 0.5)

tmap_arrange(equal, quantile, asp = 1, ncol = 2)














NoteThe two classifications disagree about how many rich counties there are



Equal interval puts almost every county in the bottom class, because Changsha at 88,656 stretches the range so far that the other 87 counties are squeezed together. Equal quantile forces 20% into each class and shows a north-east cluster clearly.
Neither is wrong. Equal interval is honest about the magnitude of the gap; quantile is honest about the ranking. The reason this matters for the rest of the exercise is that Moran’s I works on deviations from the mean, and that mean of 24,405 is dragged upward by a handful of counties. Most of Hunan sits below its own provincial average.

title: Global Measures of Spatial Autocorrelation
text:
6. Global Measures of Spatial Autocorrelation

6.1 Computing Row-standardised Weights

wm_q <- poly2nb(hunan, queen = TRUE)
rswm_q <- nb2listw(wm_q, style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE)
rswm_q

Characteristics of weights list object:
Neighbour list object:
Number of regions: 88 
Number of nonzero links: 448 
Percentage nonzero weights: 5.785124 
Average number of links: 5.090909 

Weights style: W 
Weights constants summary:
   n   nn S0       S1       S2
W 88 7744 88 37.86334 365.9147


Queen contiguity, row-standardised, as built in Exercise 4. Average of 5.09 neighbours per county.


6.2 Moran’s I Test

moran.test(hunan$GDPPC, listw = rswm_q, zero.policy = TRUE, na.action = na.omit)


    Moran I test under randomisation

data:  hunan$GDPPC  
weights: rswm_q    

Moran I statistic standard deviate = 4.7351, p-value = 1.095e-06
alternative hypothesis: greater
sample estimates:
Moran I statistic       Expectation          Variance 
      0.300749970      -0.011494253       0.004348351 


Moran’s I is 0.3007 against an expected value of -0.0115 under spatial randomness. The z-score is 4.735 and p is about 1.1e-06.
So: positive spatial autocorrelation. Counties resemble their neighbours more than chance would produce. On the standard reading of Moran’s I, which runs roughly -1 to +1, 0.30 is moderate rather than overwhelming.


6.3 Monte Carlo Moran’s I
The analytical p-value assumes normality, and GDPPC is clearly skewed. A permutation test avoids that assumption entirely by shuffling the values across counties 999 times and asking where the observed value falls.

set.seed(1234)
bperm <- moran.mc(hunan$GDPPC, listw = rswm_q, nsim = 999, zero.policy = TRUE, na.action = na.omit)
bperm


    Monte-Carlo simulation of Moran I

data:  hunan$GDPPC 
weights: rswm_q  
number of simulations + 1: 1000 

statistic = 0.30075, observed rank = 1000, p-value = 0.001
alternative hypothesis: greater


The observed statistic ranks 1000 out of 1000, giving p = 0.001. No permutation of the data produced clustering as strong as the real arrangement. The conclusion survives dropping the normality assumption, which is the point of running it.


6.4 Visualising the Simulation

hist(bperm$res, freq = TRUE, breaks = 20, xlab = "Simulated Moran's I",
     main = "999 permutations against the observed value")
abline(v = 0, col = "grey40", lty = 2)
abline(v = bperm$statistic, col = "red", lwd = 2)








The simulated distribution sits around zero, as it should when values are scattered at random. The observed value sits outside the whole distribution.


6.5 Geary’s C Test

geary.test(hunan$GDPPC, listw = rswm_q)


    Geary C test under randomisation

data:  hunan$GDPPC 
weights: rswm_q   

Geary C statistic standard deviate = 3.6108, p-value = 0.0001526
alternative hypothesis: Expectation greater than statistic
sample estimates:
Geary C statistic       Expectation          Variance 
        0.6907223         1.0000000         0.0073364 


Geary’s C is 0.6907 against an expected 1. Values below 1 indicate positive autocorrelation, so this agrees with Moran’s I.


6.6 Monte Carlo Geary’s C

set.seed(1234)
bperm_geary <- geary.mc(hunan$GDPPC, listw = rswm_q, nsim = 999)
bperm_geary


    Monte-Carlo simulation of Geary C

data:  hunan$GDPPC 
weights: rswm_q  
number of simulations + 1: 1000 

statistic = 0.69072, observed rank = 1, p-value = 0.001
alternative hypothesis: greater


p = 0.001 again.






NoteWhy run both when they agree



Moran’s I is built on cross-products of deviations from the global mean, so it responds to the overall pattern. Geary’s C is built on squared differences between neighbouring pairs, so it is more sensitive to local differences between adjacent units.
When they agree, as here, the reading is that the pattern is not an artefact of one formulation. If Moran’s I had come back positive while Geary’s C indicated no structure, that would have pointed to a broad regional gradient without sharp neighbour-to-neighbour similarity, and would have been worth chasing. Agreement is the boring outcome, but it is only boring because it was checked.

text:
7. Spatial Correlogram
Contiguity only looks at immediate neighbours. A correlogram extends the question: how far does the similarity reach before it dies out?

7.1 Moran’s I Correlogram

MI_corr <- sp.correlogram(wm_q, hunan$GDPPC, order = 6, method = "I", style = "W")

ImportantThe sign flip is the finding, not the decay



I expected the correlation to decay toward zero as lag increases, and it does through lag 4. What I did not expect is that it goes negative at lags 5 and 6.
Decay to zero would mean influence simply fades with distance. Going negative means something stronger: counties five or six steps apart are systematically dissimilar. That is the signature of a single dominant cluster rather than a smooth gradient. Once you walk five counties away from the rich north-east, you are reliably in the poor periphery, so the correlation inverts.
A gradient across the province would have produced a slow decay that stayed positive. The negative tail says Hunan has a core and a periphery, and the boundary between them is crossed at about four steps.




7.2 Geary’s C Correlogram

GC_corr <- sp.correlogram(wm_q, hunan$GDPPC, order = 6, method = "C", style = "W")
plot(GC_corr)








Geary’s C mirrors it, rising above 1 at the longer lags, which is the same statement in the opposite direction.

section: 8. Additional Exploration: Does the Choice of Weights Change Moran’s I?
text:
8. Additional Exploration: Does the Choice of Weights Change Moran’s I?
Everything above used queen contiguity. Exercise 4 built four different weighting schemes, and I was left wondering how much of Moran’s I is the data and how much is the matrix.
First the distance-based neighbours, which need a cut-off large enough that no county is left isolated.

coords <- st_coordinates(st_centroid(st_geometry(hunan)))
k1 <- knn2nb(knearneigh(coords))
dmax <- max(unlist(nbdists(k1, coords, longlat = TRUE)))
round(dmax, 2)

[1] 61.81








WarningPass coordinates, not geometry



My first attempt passed st_centroid() output straight into knearneigh(), an sfc object rather than a coordinate matrix, and the maximum first-neighbour distance came back as 0.60 instead of 61.81. The longlat = TRUE argument is silently ignored, so spdep measures in degrees as though they were planar units.
It does not error. It produces a perfectly well-formed weights matrix that is completely wrong. I made this exact mistake in Exercise 4, wrote it up, and made it again here. What saved me was the habit the first one left behind: look at the number and ask whether 0.6 km is plausible for Chinese counties.


Now the four schemes.

d62 <- dnearneigh(coords, 0, dmax, longlat = TRUE)
wm_r <- poly2nb(hunan, queen = FALSE)
k6 <- knn2nb(knearneigh(coords, k = 6))
schemes <- list(Queen = wm_q, Rook = wm_r, `knn (k=6)` = k6, `Fixed 62km` = d62)

map_dfr(names(schemes), function(nm) {
  lw <- nb2listw(schemes[[nm]], style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE)
  m <- moran.test(hunan$GDPPC, lw, zero.policy = TRUE)
  tibble(Scheme = nm,
         `Avg neighbours` = round(mean(card(schemes[[nm]])), 2),
         `Moran's I` = round(unname(m$estimate[1]), 4),
         z = round(unname(m$statistic), 3),
         p = format.pval(m$p.value, digits = 3))
}) %>% kable()

NoteThe direction is robust. The magnitude is not.



Every scheme agrees that autocorrelation is positive, and the weakest p-value is still about 1e-06. That conclusion is safe.
Moran’s I itself ranges from 0.30 to 0.42, a swing of 40% of the lower value. Reporting “Moran’s I for Hunan GDPPC is 0.42” without naming the matrix would not be reproducible by someone who reasonably chose queen contiguity.
The mechanism is the neighbour count. The fixed-distance scheme has the fewest neighbours at 3.64, so each county is compared against a tighter and nearer set, and near neighbours are more alike. Fewer and closer neighbours means a higher measured index. Part 02 finds the same sensitivity in the local statistics, where it decides whether Hunan has any cold spots at all.
The rule I am taking from this: treat the ranking of places as more trustworthy than the absolute value of any index, and state the weights specification alongside the statistic.

title: Global Measures of Spatial Autocorrelation
text:
9. What I Take Away
Hunan’s development is spatially clustered, and the evidence is not marginal. Moran’s I of 0.3007 against an expected -0.0115 gives z = 4.735 and p near 1e-06, and the permutation test puts the observed value outside all 999 simulations. Geary’s C agrees from a different formulation. The conclusion survives dropping the normality assumption, which is the reason to run the Monte Carlo version at all.
The correlogram’s negative tail was worth plotting. Decay to zero would mean influence simply fades with distance. Turning negative at lags 5 and 6 means counties that far apart are systematically dissimilar, which is the signature of a core and a periphery rather than a smooth gradient. The boundary is crossed at about four steps.
The direction is robust, the magnitude is not. Moran’s I moves between 0.30 and 0.42 across four reasonable weighting schemes. Reporting the number without naming the matrix that produced it would not be reproducible. Fewer and nearer neighbours means a higher index, every time.
And a global statistic is an average over the whole map. It says clustering exists somewhere. It cannot say where, it cannot say whether the clustering is in the rich counties or the poor ones, and it cannot say how much of the province participates. Part 02 takes the same data apart county by county, and the answer turns out to be narrower than this number suggests.

title: Local Measures of Spatial Autocorrelation
text:
R spdep LISA Getis-Ord Gi* Cluster maps
This exercise follows Local Measures of Spatial Autocorrelation, in the Spatial Weights block of the course.

title: Local Measures of Spatial Autocorrelation
text:
1. Overview
Part 01 established that Hunan’s GDP per capita is spatially clustered: Moran’s I of 0.3007 with p near 1e-06. That is one number for 88 counties, and it cannot say where the clustering is.
This part decomposes it. Local Moran’s I (LISA) returns a statistic per county and classifies each into high-high, low-low, high-low or low-high. Getis-Ord Gi* asks a different question again: is this neighbourhood’s total unusually high or low?
I expected the local maps to be a more detailed version of the global result. They are not, and the gap between them is the most useful thing here. I also found an error in the reference code along the way, and it inverted the finding.

title: Local Measures of Spatial Autocorrelation
text:
2. Getting Started
Same packages and the same Hunan data as Part 01, re-imported so this page stands alone.

pacman::p_load(sf, spdep, tmap, tidyverse, knitr)

wm_q <- poly2nb(hunan, queen = TRUE)
rswm_q <- nb2listw(wm_q, style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE)

Queen contiguity, row-standardised, averaging 5.09 neighbours per county.

3. Local Indicators of Spatial Association
The global tests say clustering exists. They cannot say where. LISA decomposes Moran’s I into one value per county.

3.1 Computing Local Moran’s I

fips <- order(hunan$County)
localMI <- localmoran(hunan$GDPPC, rswm_q)

localMI.map <- tm_shape(hunan.localMI) +
  tm_polygons("Ii", fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "pretty"),

  tm_polygons("Pr.Ii",

Only 11 of 88 counties reach significance at the 0.05 level.


3.3 LISA Cluster Map
The cluster map classifies each significant county into one of four quadrants. This is the code the chapter gives.

quadrant <- vector(mode = "numeric", length = nrow(localMI))
hunan$lag_GDPPC <- lag.listw(rswm_q, hunan$GDPPC)
DV <- hunan$lag_GDPPC - mean(hunan$lag_GDPPC)
LM_I <- localMI[, 1] - mean(localMI[, 1])
signif <- 0.05

quadrant[DV < 0 & LM_I > 0] <- 1   # low-high
quadrant[DV > 0 & LM_I < 0] <- 2   # high-low
quadrant[DV < 0 & LM_I < 0] <- 3   # low-low
quadrant[DV > 0 & LM_I > 0] <- 4   # high-high
quadrant[localMI[, 5] > signif] <- 0

Before mapping it I checked the output against the underlying values, and it does not survive that check.

lab <- c("insignificant", "low-high", "high-low", "low-low", "high-high")

       GDPPC = hunan$GDPPC,

Wugang has a GDPPC of 12,112 against a provincial mean of 24,405, and its neighbours average 11,566. A poor county surrounded by poor counties is the definition of low-low. The code labels it low-high.






ImportantThe chapter’s quadrant code is wrong, and it inverts the finding



The second axis in that code is LM_I, the local Moran statistic itself. That cannot work, and the reason is in the formula. Local Moran’s I for county i is
\[I_i = z_i \sum_j w_{ij} z_j\]
a product of the county’s own standardised deviation and its neighbours’. When both are positive, high-high, the product is positive. When both are negative, low-low, the product is also positive. Local Moran’s I is positive for high-high and low-low alike, and negative for high-low and low-high alike. Using it as an axis therefore conflates exactly the pairs the quadrant map exists to separate.
The correct second axis is the county’s own deviation from the mean, GDPPC - mean(GDPPC), which is what a Moran scatterplot actually plots.

quadrant2 <- vector(mode = "numeric", length = nrow(localMI))
X <- hunan$GDPPC - mean(hunan$GDPPC)
Y <- hunan$lag_GDPPC - mean(hunan$lag_GDPPC)

quadrant2[X > 0 & Y < 0] <- 2   # high-low
quadrant2[X < 0 & Y < 0] <- 3   # low-low
quadrant2[X > 0 & Y > 0] <- 4   # high-high
quadrant2[localMI[, 5] > signif] <- 0


tibble(Quadrant = lab,
       `Chapter code` = map_int(0:4, ~sum(quadrant == .x)),

The asymmetry I thought I had found is still there, just smaller than the buggy version claimed. Seven counties form high-high clusters against two low-low. Wealth clusters about three times as often as poverty does.
There are also zero high-low counties, meaning no rich county sits isolated in a poor neighbourhood. Wealth in Hunan does not appear alone. Every significantly rich county has rich neighbours, which is a stronger statement about spillover than Moran’s I of 0.30 conveys on its own.
And 77 of 88 counties are locally insignificant. The global test returned p near 1e-06, yet seven eighths of the province is indistinguishable from a random arrangement. A significant global statistic does not mean most places participate in the pattern.

title: Local Measures of Spatial Autocorrelation
section: 4. Hot and Cold Spot Analysis with Getis-Ord Gi*
text:
4. Hot and Cold Spot Analysis with Getis-Ord Gi*
LISA asks whether a county resembles its neighbours. Gi* asks whether a neighbourhood’s total is unusually high or low, and answers in z-score units.

4.1 Deriving the Weights

coords <- st_coordinates(st_centroid(st_geometry(hunan)))
k1 <- knn2nb(knearneigh(coords))
k1dists <- unlist(nbdists(k1, coords, longlat = TRUE))
summary(k1dists)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  24.79   32.56   38.00   39.07   44.52   61.81 








WarningI walked into the same trap I documented last exercise



My first run passed st_centroid() output straight into knearneigh() and got a maximum first-neighbour distance of 0.60 instead of 61.81. That is the exact sfc versus coordinate-matrix mistake I wrote a callout about in Exercise 4, and I made it again within a fortnight.
Writing the lesson down was evidently not the same as learning it. What saved me was the habit the last one left behind: I looked at the number, knew 0.6 km was impossible for Chinese counties, and checked. The value of documenting a mistake was not that I stopped making it, but that I now recognise the symptom on sight.


Maximum first-nearest-neighbour distance is 61.81 km, the cut-off that guarantees every county at least one neighbour.


4.2 Gi* with Fixed Distance Weights
Gi* includes the county itself, which is what include.self() is for and what the star in the name denotes.

d62 <- dnearneigh(coords, 0, 61.81, longlat = TRUE)
gi.fixed <- localG(hunan$GDPPC, nb2listw(include.self(d62), style = "B"))
hunan.gi <- cbind(hunan, as.matrix(gi.fixed)) %>%
  rename(gstat_fixed = as.matrix.gi.fixed.)


tm_shape(hunan.gi) +
  tm_polygons("gstat_fixed",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                breaks = c(-Inf, -2, -1, 1, 2, Inf),
                values = "brewer.-rd_bu"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Gi* (fixed 62km)")) +
  tm_borders(col_alpha = 0.5)









gi_f <- as.numeric(gi.fixed)
tibble(County = hunan$County, GDPPC = hunan$GDPPC, `Gi*` = round(gi_f, 2)) %>%
  arrange(-`Gi*`) %>% head(7) %>% kable()

NoteXiangyin shows what Gi* is actually measuring



Xiangyin has a GDPPC of 33,983, which ranks 13th of 88. Its Gi* ranks 3rd, behind only Wangcheng and Changsha.
Its neighbours explain it: Wangcheng at 70,666 and Miluo at 42,497, alongside Yuanjiang, Yueyang and Taojiang. Gi* scores the neighbourhood sum including the county, so Xiangyin inherits a large score from company it keeps rather than from its own output. LISA, by contrast, leaves Xiangyin insignificant at p = 0.051.
The two statistics are answering different questions rather than giving two views of one answer. If the task is siting infrastructure to serve concentrated economic mass, Gi* is the right tool. If the task is finding counties that have fallen behind their own neighbours, LISA is.




4.3 Gi* with Adaptive Distance Weights

knn8 <- knn2nb(knearneigh(coords, k = 8))
gi.adaptive <- localG(hunan$GDPPC, nb2listw(include.self(knn8), style = "B"))
hunan.gi$gstat_adaptive <- as.numeric(gi.adaptive)

  tm_polygons("gstat_adaptive",

       `Avg neighbours` = c(round(mean(card(d62)), 2), 8),
       Minimum = round(c(min(gi_f), min(gi_a)), 2),
       Maximum = round(c(max(gi_f), max(gi_a)), 2),
       `Hot (> +2)` = c(sum(gi_f > 2), sum(gi_a > 2)),
       `Cold (< -2)` = c(sum(gi_f < -2), sum(gi_a < -2))) %>%
  kable()

ImportantWhether Hunan has any cold spots at all depends on the weights



The fixed-distance scheme finds 7 hot spots and 0 cold spots. The adaptive scheme finds 15 hot spots and 5 cold spots. Same variable, same province, same threshold.
The mechanism is the neighbour count. The fixed 62 km band averages 3.64 neighbours, and in the sparse western counties it gives very few. A Gi* z-score built from three units cannot reach far from zero, so the poor west never crosses -2. Forcing k = 8 gives those same counties a wider window, their deficit accumulates over more neighbours, and cold spots appear.
Pingjiang makes the point sharply. Its GDPPC is 17,252, below the provincial median of 20,433, so it is a genuinely poor county. Under the fixed band its Gi* is +1.95; under adaptive k = 8 it is +4.61, which would be reported as a strong hot spot. The corrected LISA classifies it as low-high, a poor county surrounded by wealth, which is the honest description.
“Hunan has no economic cold spots” is a sentence I could have written from the fixed-band map alone, and it would have been an artefact of the neighbour definition. Report the weights with the result, every time.

title: Local Measures of Spatial Autocorrelation
text:
5. What I Take Away
I caught a real error in the reference code, and only because I checked the output against the data. The chapter’s quadrant assignment uses local Moran’s I as an axis, and because that statistic is positive for high-high and low-low alike, it cannot separate them. Five of 11 significant counties were mislabelled, low-low was reported as empty when there are two, and three spurious high-low counties appeared. Running the code and mapping the result would have shown nothing wrong. Reading one row against its own values did.
The wrong answer was the more interesting one. “Hunan has no low-low clusters at all” is a better line than “seven high-high against two low-low”, and I had already written it. Findings that flatter the analysis deserve more scepticism than findings that complicate it, not less.
Global and local measures answer different questions. Part 01’s Moran’s I of 0.30 at p near 1e-06 sounds province-wide. Locally, 77 of 88 counties are indistinguishable from random and the pattern is carried by a minority around Changsha. A significant global statistic does not mean most places participate.
Two statistics can both be right and disagree. Xiangyin is 13th by GDPPC and 3rd by Gi*, and insignificant under LISA. Neither is broken; Gi* scores the neighbourhood and LISA scores the county against its neighbours. The choice belongs to the question being asked.
Weights are not a preliminary step. Whether Hunan has any cold spots at all flips between 0 and 5 on the neighbour definition alone. Exercise 4 presented weights as setup for the real analysis. They are part of the result.
And I repeated a documented mistake. The sfc versus coordinate-matrix trap cost me time in Exercise 4, I wrote it up carefully, and I made it again here. What had stuck was the sanity check rather than the rule, which is probably the realistic version of learning from a mistake.

title: Geographical Segmentation with Spatially Constrained Clustering
text:

This exercise follows Geographical Segmentation with Spatially Constrained Clustering Techniques, the reading for the Geographic Segmentation block of the course.

title: Geographical Segmentation with Spatially Constrained Clustering
text:
1. Overview
Exercises 4 and 5 asked whether values were spatially clustered. This one asks a different question: given a set of multivariate measurements attached to areal units, how do I carve the study area into a small number of internally homogeneous regions?
That is segmentation rather than detection. The practical use is planning: a telecoms regulator, a market-entry team or a ministry allocating infrastructure does not want 55 townships, it wants five or six coherent zones it can write a policy for.
The complication is that ordinary cluster analysis knows nothing about geography. It will happily place two townships at opposite ends of Shan State in the same cluster because their radio ownership happens to match. A region you cannot draw on a map is not much use as a planning unit. Two families of method address this:

SKATER, which prunes a minimum spanning tree built on the contiguity graph, so contiguity is enforced by construction;
ClustGeo, which blends an attribute dissimilarity matrix with a geographic distance matrix through a mixing parameter alpha, trading homogeneity for compactness continuously.

By the end I should be able to run all three (plain hierarchical, SKATER, ClustGeo) and say something defensible about what each one costs.

Both come from the Myanmar Information Management Unit (MIMU). The filter keeps Shan (East), Shan (North) and Shan (South), which gives 55 townships.
Shan State is a reasonable choice for this problem. It is large, internally very uneven, and the ICT variables are genuinely multivariate: radio is a legacy technology with a different geography from mobile phones, so the clustering has something to work with rather than six proxies for one underlying wealth gradient.

4.1 What Happened to Hunan Between 2005 and 2021
Before any spatial statistic, it is worth knowing what the variable did.

w <- GDPPC %>% pivot_wider(names_from = Year, values_from = GDPPC)
tibble(Measure = c("Mean GDPPC", "Coefficient of variation", "Max / min ratio"),
       `2005` = c(round(mean(w$`2005`)), round(sd(w$`2005`)/mean(w$`2005`), 3),
                  round(max(w$`2005`)/min(w$`2005`), 1)),
       `2021` = c(round(mean(w$`2021`)), round(sd(w$`2021`)/mean(w$`2021`), 3),
                  round(max(w$`2021`)/min(w$`2021`), 1))) %>% kable()

NoteEverything grew, and the gaps stayed the same shape



Mean GDP per capita rose from about 7,500 to about 50,400, a factor of 6.7 in sixteen years. That is the headline a growth statistic would report.
The dispersion measures did not move. The coefficient of variation went from 0.467 to 0.471, and the ratio of richest to poorest county actually narrowed slightly, from 7.4 to 6.4. Hunan got six times richer without meaningfully changing how unequally that wealth was distributed across counties.
This matters for what follows. Because every county grew, and grew at broadly similar proportional rates, a trend test on raw GDPPC is useless: Kendall’s tau on the raw series averages 0.97 across counties, which just says “GDP went up everywhere”. The whole point of running the trend test on Gi* rather than on GDPPC is that Gi* is a relative measure. It asks whether a county’s standing among its neighbours changed, and that is a question the raw series cannot answer.

title: Emerging Hot Spot Analysis
text:
5. Creating a Space-Time Cube
A spacetime cube pairs each location with each time period. sfdep validates that the pairing is complete, which is why the balanced-panel check above mattered.

GDPPC_st <- spacetime(GDPPC, hunan, .loc_col = "County", .time_col = "Year")
is_spacetime_cube(GDPPC_st)

[1] TRUE


TRUE confirms every county appears in every year.

title: Emerging Hot Spot Analysis
text:
6. Computing Gi* Year by Year
First derive the neighbours and weights, then compute Gi* within each year.

GDPPC_nb <- GDPPC_st %>%
  activate("geometry") %>%
  mutate(nb = include_self(st_contiguity(geometry)),
         wt = st_inverse_distance(nb, geometry, scale = 1, alpha = 1),
         .before = 1) %>%
  set_nbs("nb") %>%
  set_wts("wt")


gi_stars <- GDPPC_nb %>%
  group_by(Year) %>%
  mutate(gi = local_gstar_perm(GDPPC, nb, wt, nsim = 99)) %>%
  tidyr::unnest(gi) %>%
  ungroup()


gi_stars %>%
  group_by(Year) %>%
  summarise(Hot = sum(gi_star > 2), Cold = sum(gi_star < -2)) %>%
  pivot_longer(-Year) %>%
  ggplot(aes(Year, value, colour = name)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) + geom_point(size = 1.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Hot = "#C0392B", Cold = "#2c7bb6")) +
  labs(y = "Counties beyond |Gi*| = 2", colour = NULL,
       title = "Hot and cold counties per year") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)








The hot count is remarkably stable at around 11 counties throughout. The cold count drifts upward in the later years.

8.2 Locating the Bug
emerging_hotspot_analysis() ends with this line (sfdep 0.2.5):
res_ehs <- cbind(
  location = attr(x, "geometry")[[.loc_col]],
  do.call(rbind, lapply(split(all_gis, x[[.loc_col]]),
                        function(.x) classify_hotspot(.x, threshold)))
)






ImportantThe results are computed in alphabetical order and labelled in shapefile order



split() groups by the location column and returns those groups sorted alphabetically. That is the order the classification rows come out in.
location is taken from attr(x, "geometry")[[.loc_col]], which is the county column of the shapefile, in whatever order the file happens to store its features.
cbind() then pastes the two together positionally. The two orderings only agree if the shapefile is already sorted alphabetically. Hunan’s is not.

Row 1 of the classification block belongs to Anhua, the first county alphabetically, but gets labelled Anxiang, the first county in the shapefile. Every row is attached to the wrong county. The output is a valid-looking table of the right shape, with the labels shuffled.

  group_by(version, classification) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), `mean Gi*` = round(mean(mean_gi), 2), .groups = "drop") %>%

title: Emerging Hot Spot Analysis
text:
11. What I Take Away
Three exercises, three silent failures, and none of them threw an error. The sfc coordinate trap in Exercise 4, the quadrant axis error in Exercise 5, and now an ordering mismatch inside a published CRAN package. Every one produced output of the correct shape and plausible appearance. The only thing that caught any of them was checking a result against the values it claimed to describe.
The check that works is cheap and always the same. Join the output back to the input and ask whether it is consistent. Counties called hot spots should have high Gi*. That took one line and four seconds, and it is the difference between this exercise and a confidently wrong map.
Trusting a package is not the same as trusting a result. sfdep is on CRAN, is written by a competent author, and implements all seventeen ArcGIS EHSA classes correctly. The classification logic is fine. One cbind at the end attaches it to the wrong rows. A package being good is not evidence that a particular call to it returned what you think.
The bug is invisible on data that happens to be sorted. If Hunan’s shapefile had stored its counties alphabetically, this code would be correct and I would have found nothing. Whether an analysis is right would then depend on the storage order of a file nobody looks at. That is worth remembering when a workflow “works on my machine”.
On Hunan itself: the Changsha corridor is not an emerging hot spot, it is a permanent one, hot in all seventeen years and already established before the data begins. The change is happening in a ring of middle-income counties to its north whose relative standing is rising, and in a western periphery that has become more tightly clustered in its disadvantage. Growth of 6.7 times province-wide moved the levels and left the structure almost exactly as it found it.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Geospatial Analytics for Public Safety
text:
11.1 Two rules for comparability
S-NPP only, every year including 2026. NOAA-20 joins the record in 2018, so counting two platforms in recent years against one platform in earlier years would produce a step change in detection capability indistinguishable from a change in fire. The 2026 figure in this section is therefore smaller than the headline figure elsewhere in the report, which uses both platforms.
The identical calendar window every year, so window length cannot be confused with fire intensity.
One caveat I cannot remove: 2026 is the near-real-time product and every earlier year is the reprocessed standard product. They differ slightly, and I cannot quantify by how much, because the retention windows of the two products do not overlap anywhere in the record. The direction of the likely bias is that near-real-time retains some detections that reprocessing removes, so the 2026 figure should be read as, if anything, a little generous.

Figure 26: Burned cells in the same 87-day window, 2013 to 2026, log scale. Reading: this is the figure I could not draw before, and it reframes the whole report. 2026 is not a representative season. It ranks second of fourteen years, roughly fifty times the median, behind only the 2015 El Nino fires and ahead of 2019. The record is also violently bimodal rather than continuous: drought years produce thousands of burned cells and wet years produce single or double digits, with almost nothing in between. That matters for planning, because a capability sized to the median would be overwhelmed in a year like this one, and a capability sized to 2026 would idle for years at a time.





2026 recorded 8,164 burned cells in the window, against a 2013 to 2025 median of 150. That is 54 times the median and ranks 2 of 14, behind only 2015 (11,236 cells).
The gap is so large that the near-real-time versus standard-product caveat cannot explain it. Reprocessing shifts detection counts by a few percent, not by a factor of fifty.
There is one thing this understates rather than overstates. My window closes on 25 September because that was the last complete day before I pulled the data, and Section 11.2 shows October can be the peak month: in 2023 it carried more burned cell-days than September did. Every year in the comparison is truncated at the same point, so the ranking is fair, but the 2026 figure is a season in progress. On the 2023 pattern it could still grow substantially.

Figure 27: Monthly burned cell-days across two complete calendar years, log scale, showing the seasonal cycle the 87-day window cannot contain. What I take from it: fire here is not merely seasonal, it is close to switch-like, with wet-season months at or near zero and a dry-season peak orders of magnitude above. But it also corrects an assumption I had been carrying. My window closes on 25 September, and in 2023 the peak month was October, which alone carried more burned cell-days than September. July to September captured only 39% of the 2023 fire year against 67% of 2024. So my window is not the whole fire season, it is the first two thirds of it, and the 2026 figures should be read as a season still in progress rather than a completed total.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Geospatial Analytics for Public Safety
section: 11.3 What this does to the rest of the report
text:
11.3 What this does to the rest of the report
No second-order result is overturned. The clustering scale, the Knox interaction and the covariate relationships are estimated within 2026 and stand on their own.
The interpretation of all of them changes. I thought I was describing the spatial structure of a dry season. I was describing a severe one, second worst in fourteen years. A cluster scale near a kilometre and a containment window of days are properties of extreme conditions. Whether they survive in a median year, when the regency records a few dozen burned cells instead of eight thousand, this analysis cannot say. There may be too few events in a median year to estimate them at all.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Geospatial Analytics for Public Safety
section: 8. The correction that reframes it all
text:
8. The correction that reframes it all













I had written that I could not tell whether 2026 was severe, blaming the API’s 90-day retention.
I was wrong. The standard archive is empty for 2026 only because reprocessing lags five months. For earlier years the same endpoint serves it normally. One query against 2019 would have shown me.
2026 ranks 2 of 14, at 54x the 2013-2025 median of 150 cells.
So everything on the previous slides describes a severe season, not a typical one. And the record is bimodal, which means an average is a useless planning number here.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Geospatial Analytics for Public Safety
section: 5. Two nulls: one meaningless, one that can fail
text:
5. Two nulls: one meaningless, one that can fail













Against CSR, G, F and L all leave the envelope immediately. That persuades nobody, including me: the sensor guarantees it. g(r) is even suppressed below 375 m, which is the pixel, not fires avoiding each other.
So I changed the null. An inhomogeneous Poisson process with intensity from the 4 km kernel estimate, with the reference re-estimated for every simulated pattern. Everything my first-order analysis found is already inside it.
The departure survives. Both global tests reject at the Monte Carlo floor.
The two panels disagree, and that was the lesson. L_inhom never re-enters its envelope in 20 km; g_inhom, which localises scale, peaks at 438 m and is within 10% of no-excess by 7.2 km. My first draft capped r at 5 km and drew the wrong conclusion from exactly this.
An areal method agrees. Moran’s I on hexagons falls from 0.69 on raw counts to 0.28 once lambda-hat is removed, and to 0.07 at 5 km. Different weights, different test, same answer on scale.

title: Where peat burns, and how close together
section: 7.4 Testing isotropy, instead of just assuming it
text:
7.4 Testing isotropy, instead of just assuming it
Assumption A7 says \(K\), \(L\) and \(g\) all average over direction, and that I expected real anisotropy because peat fires spread with the wind and along canal lines. Listing an assumption and never testing it is the kind of thing that should not survive a read, so this section tests it. The test found something, but not the thing I predicted, and the first version of my own analysis missed it.
Why I did not use the packaged tools. spatstat offers Ksector and pairorient, and neither accepts a lambda argument: both assume homogeneity. Applied here they would reject isotropy for two reasons that have nothing to do with fire. The window is 86 km wide and 213 km tall, so even a perfectly isotropic process yields more north-south pairs than east-west ones purely because there is more room that way. And intensity is concentrated in a south-southeast band, so any pair drawn from inside it inherits that elongation.
I therefore built the null the way I built it for clustering: simulate from an inhomogeneous Poisson process with the same \(\hat{\lambda}\) from Section 6, which absorbs the window geometry and the first-order trend together.
Two statistics, and the second one is the point. Orientations here are axial, so I double the angles before averaging and summarise concentration by the mean resultant length \(R_2 = |n^{-1}\sum_k e^{2i\theta_k}|\), which is 0 when orientations are spread evenly and 1 when every pair lies on one axis.
Each harmonic is blind to the next one up, and I walked into that twice.
\(R_2\) detects a single preferred axis and is structurally blind to four-fold structure, because a rose with spikes at 0 and 90 degrees has its doubled angles cancel. My first version of this section reported the short range as isotropic on the strength of \(R_2\) alone, and the rose diagram contradicted it on sight. So I added \(R_4 = |n^{-1}\sum_k e^{4i\theta_k}|\).
\(R_4\) is in turn blind to eight-fold structure. Spikes at 0, 45, 90 and 135 degrees have a 45-degree period, so under \(e^{4i\theta}\) the 45 and 135 pair sits in antiphase to the 0 and 90 pair and the two cancel. That is exactly the shape a square grid produces, because a lattice offers displacements along its axes and along its diagonals. \(R_8\) is what captures it, and it turns out to be the largest directional signal anywhere in this analysis.
A harmonic statistic finds only the structure you asked it about. Two passes were needed here because I kept asking the wrong one, and each time the rose diagram was what showed me.

Figure 12: Orientation of close pairs by distance band, as a rose diagram, against the 95% interval from 199 inhomogeneous Poisson simulations. Each rose is mirrored across the origin because orientations are axial. What I take from it: the shortest band is not isotropic at all. It has eight sharp spikes on the cardinal axes and the diagonals, which is the signature of a square grid rather than of fire, and my R2 statistic scored it as isotropic because R2 cannot see four-fold structure. The figure caught what the table missed. From 750 m outward the spikes vanish and the roses sit close to their null intervals, with only a slight and growing elongation by 3 to 6 km.






7.4.1 The short-range structure is my grid, and the sensor’s
Over 375 to 750 m the eight-fold concentration is 0.087 against 0.007 under the null, < 0.005. That is more than twelve times the null value and the largest directional effect measured anywhere in this report. The four-fold term is 0.0289, also significant, and \(R_2\) is 0.0063 against a null of 0.0066, 0.475, which is nothing at all.
Three statistics on the same 36,860 pairs, and they disagree completely. The structure is spikes on the axes and on the diagonals, which is what a square lattice produces and what only the eighth harmonic can see.
My first explanation was that this is entirely my own doing. ppp_cell keeps at most one point per 375 m cell, so short-range displacements are dominated by lattice vectors: 375 m at 0 and 90 degrees, 530 m on the diagonals, 750 m at two cells. That would produce spikes exactly where they appear. The way to check it is to run the identical test on ppp_all, which keeps every detection at its own sensor coordinate and has no such lattice.

The control only half-confirms my explanation, which is more interesting than if it had confirmed it outright. Thinning multiplies the eight-fold signal by about two and a half, from 0.0336 to 0.087, so a large part of the structure is indeed my construction. But the un-thinned detections still show 0.0336 against a null of 0.0018, < 0.01, which is roughly nineteen times the null. Removing my lattice reduces the effect without removing it.
The remainder is the instrument. VIIRS reports detections on its own scan grid, organised along-scan and along-track, and for a polar orbiter those project to roughly cardinal directions on the ground. So the raw detections carry a quasi-rectangular sampling geometry before I do anything to them.
Neither component is fire. Both are instrument geometry, which is the warning from Section 1.1 applied to my own directional test.


7.4.2 At longer range, a real but negligible tilt
From 750 m outward every harmonic goes quiet. Over 750 to 1500 m, \(R_4\) is 9^{-4} (0.930) and \(R_8\) is 0.0021 (0.665), both below their nulls. That is what a lattice explanation predicts, since every lattice vector is shorter than 750 m, and it is the check that makes me believe the short-range result is geometric rather than physical.
What remains is a weak single-axis elongation that grows with distance, reaching \(R_2 =\) 0.024 over 3000 to 6000 m against a null of 0.0055. That is statistically distinguishable at the Monte Carlo floor and it is 2.4% of the way to perfect alignment, which is not a directional pattern in any sense a fire officer would recognise.


7.4.3 My stated mechanism was wrong
A7 guessed that fires would align with canal lines. They do not.

The mapped waterways run at about 113 degrees and the roads at about 38 degrees. The long-range fire axis is 77 degrees: 37 degrees off the drainage and 38 degrees off the roads, on a scale where 90 degrees is the maximum possible disagreement. Neither is a match.
So the weak long-range tilt is not canal-following. It runs closer to north-south, which is also the long axis of the regency and of the peat belt inside it. The most likely explanation is first-order structure that \(\hat{\lambda}\) at a 4 km bandwidth does not fully absorb, not a directional process in the fire. I cannot separate those two with this design and I will not claim otherwise.


7.4.4 What this changes
A7 said anisotropy was likely because fires follow canals, and that it made my clustering estimates conservative. Both claims fail.
The short-range structure is geometric. It comes from the 375 m cell grid and the sensor’s scan grid, not from wind or canals. Beyond 750 m, where the clustering lives, no harmonic finds anything. The isotropic \(K\), \(L\) and \(g\) estimate what they claim to, and there is no conservatism to claim.
One practical consequence for the rest of the report. Because the eight-fold structure is symmetric about the cardinal axes and the diagonals, it very largely cancels in any statistic that averages over direction, which is what \(K\), \(L\) and \(g\) do. So it does not bias the clustering results. It would wreck a directional analysis, and anyone extending this work should thin differently before attempting one.

9.1 What the local statistics say

lis <- bind_rows(
  LI$hex |> st_drop_geometry() |> transmute(hex_id, cluster = cl_raw, panel = "Raw counts"),
  LI$hex |> st_drop_geometry() |> transmute(hex_id, cluster = cl_resid, panel = "Residuals after lambda-hat")) |>
  left_join(LI$hex |> select(hex_id), by = "hex_id") |> st_as_sf()
cols <- c("High-High" = PAL$accent_dk, "Low-Low" = PAL$cool,
          "High-Low" = PAL$accent_lt, "Low-High" = "#8FBDC0",
          "not significant" = PAL$ground_alt)
ggplot(lis) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = cluster), colour = NA) +
  geom_sf(data = win_p, fill = NA, colour = PAL$ink, linewidth = 0.35) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, nrow = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = cols, name = NULL, drop = FALSE) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA, expand = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "The local statistics find the peat belt, and nothing beyond it") +
  theme_map(base_size = 9)








Figure 20: Local Moran clusters at 3 km, Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted across 1,252 simultaneous tests. Left, raw counts. Right, residuals after the kernel intensity is removed. What I take from it: the left map rediscovers the peat belt and nothing else. Its 105 High-High hexagons are the same southern concentration the intensity surface already shows, arrived at by a different route. The right map is empty. Not one hexagon survives correction, and the smallest adjusted p-value is 0.066. The residual autocorrelation that the global statistic detects is real but diffuse, spread thinly across the map instead of concentrated anywhere a planner could point at.






9.1.1 Reading it against the point-pattern result
The two methods agree, and that is the main value of doing both. Removing \(\hat{\lambda}\) cuts global Moran’s I from 0.69 to 0.28 at 3 km. What remains is significant (z = 16.4) and decays steeply as the hexagons grow, reaching 0.07 at 5 km. An areal method with contiguity weights and a point-pattern method with edge-corrected distance statistics both put residual structure below a few kilometres and nothing much above it.
The local statistics add a caution the global ones do not. On raw counts, 105 hexagons come out High-High, and they are the peat belt. On residuals, 0 survive correction. The residual autocorrelation is genuine in aggregate and too thin to localise.
That matters for how the earlier results should be used. Section 10.2 gives a cluster radius near a kilometre, which is a statement about typical scale. It is not a claim that particular places have persistently more clustering than the intensity surface predicts, and this section is the check that would have found such places if they existed.
Two caveats. The modifiable areal unit problem is unavoidable here, which is why three resolutions are reported instead of one; the raw-count conclusion is stable across them and the residual magnitude is not. And Benjamini-Hochberg across 1,252 tests is doing real work. Without it, an unadjusted 5% test would be expected to mark about 60 hexagons by chance alone, which would have made a convincing and entirely spurious map of residual hotspots.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Geospatial Analytics for Public Safety
section: 1.1 The problem the data handed me
text:
1.1 The problem the data handed me
A VIIRS active-fire detection is not a fire. It is a 375 m pixel where a radiometer measured a thermal anomaly during one overpass. A peat fire covering ten square kilometres fills dozens of those pixels in a single pass, and between them the two satellites pass overhead about four times a day, so the same fire is recorded again and again. The detection set samples the sensor’s view of fire. Any statistic I compute on it is partly a measurement of the instrument.
That ruins the textbook second-order question. Asking whether the pattern is clustered relative to complete spatial randomness has an answer before I compute anything: yes, overwhelmingly, and it would still be yes if fires were sited at random, because each one produces a burst of adjacent detections. I did not want to build a report on a rejection that was guaranteed.
Two changes follow, and they are the methodological content of this exercise. The unit of analysis becomes the 375 m cell, not the detection. The null becomes an inhomogeneous Poisson process, not complete spatial randomness. Section 7 is where that earns its keep.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Geospatial Analytics for Public Safety
text:
6.5 The intensity surface I report


code
kde_main <- im_df(FO$kde$main) |> mutate(v = per_1000km2(intensity))
ggplot(kde_main) +
  geom_raster(aes(x, y, fill = v)) +
  geom_sf(data = win_p, fill = NA, colour = PAL$ink, linewidth = 0.45) +
  scale_fill_intensity(v = kde_main$v) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA, expand = FALSE) +
  scalebar_layer(bb) + north_layer(bb) +
  labs(title = "Fire intensity concentrates in the drained southern peat",
       subtitle = glue("Kernel intensity estimate, sigma = {fmt_n(FO$sigma_main)} m, Diggle edge correction")) +
  theme_map() + theme(legend.position = "right", legend.key.height = unit(34, "pt"),
                      legend.key.width = unit(9, "pt"))








Figure 5: Estimated first-order intensity of burned cells, Gaussian kernel with Diggle’s edge correction, at the adopted 4 km bandwidth. What I take from it: intensity is organised as a broad south-southeast band reaching a maximum in the lower third of the regency, with a secondary extension along the eastern margin. The empty northern interior is a real absence rather than an absence of observation: the same satellites observed it on the same days. The gradient is steep, spanning roughly two orders of magnitude between the peat belt and the northern interior, which means resource allocation proportional to intensity would be very unevenly distributed. That is the operational content of a first-order surface, and it is the strongest planning-relevant thing my first-order analysis alone supports.





I also computed an adaptive estimator as a check, because a fixed bandwidth over-smooths sparse areas and under-smooths dense ones. It reproduces the same principal concentration, which is the reassurance I was after: the structure I report is not an artefact of forcing one bandwidth everywhere.

7.1 The straw man I had to test anyway

mk_env_df <- function(e, lab) e |> mutate(panel = lab)

ef <- mk_env_df(SO$env_F, "F(r), empty space")

                                                  "F(r), empty space", "L(r) - r, centred"))
ggplot(env_all, aes(r)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = PAL$rule, alpha = 0.75) +
  geom_line(aes(y = theo), colour = PAL$muted, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_line(aes(y = obs), colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, scales = "free", nrow = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(scale = 1e-3, suffix = " km")) +
  labs(x = "r", y = NULL,
       title = "Against complete spatial randomness, everything is significant",
       subtitle = glue("Orange, observed. Grey band, envelope from {SO$nsim} CSR simulations. Dashed, theoretical CSR value.")) +
  theme_ex01(base_size = 9)








Figure 9: Nearest-neighbour G, empty-space F, and the centred L function, each against a complete spatial randomness envelope from 199 simulations. What I take from it: every statistic departs from the CSR envelope immediately and by an enormous margin. G rises far faster than expected, meaning nearest neighbours are much closer than random; F rises far slower, meaning empty gaps are much larger than random; L sits far above zero at every lag. Read naively this is overwhelming evidence of clustering. Read correctly it is evidence of almost nothing, because the sensor guarantees this result: a single fire produces adjacent detections. I include it to make that failure visible rather than hide it. The analysis I actually rely on is in Section 7.3.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Geospatial Analytics for Public Safety
text:
7.3 The test that can fail
These are the statistics I trust. The null is an inhomogeneous Poisson process whose intensity is the kernel estimate from Section 6.5, so everything the first-order analysis established sits inside the null already. A departure now means residual interaction, not large-scale variation. That is Q3.


code
# An envelope built from `simulate=` has no theoretical curve, only the simulation
# mean, so the reference is set explicitly: 0 for the centred L function and 1 for
# the pair correlation function.
li <- SO$env_Linhom |> mutate(across(c(obs, lo, hi), ~ .x - r),
                              ref = 0, panel = "L_inhom(r) - r")
gi <- SO$env_pcfinhom |> filter(r > 0) |> mutate(ref = 1, panel = "g_inhom(r)")
ggplot(bind_rows(li, gi), aes(r)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = PAL$rule, alpha = 0.75) +
  geom_line(aes(y = ref), colour = PAL$muted, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_line(aes(y = obs), colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, scales = "free", nrow = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(scale = 1e-3, suffix = " km")) +
  labs(x = "r", y = NULL,
       title = "Clustering survives the honest null, and has a scale",
       subtitle = glue("Envelope from {SO$nsim} simulations of an inhomogeneous Poisson process with lambda re-estimated each time.")) +
  theme_ex01(base_size = 9)








Figure 11: Inhomogeneous centred L function and inhomogeneous pair correlation function, against envelopes from 199 simulations of an inhomogeneous Poisson process. The reference intensity is re-estimated for every simulated pattern. What I take from it: the departure survives, and it does not close. Both curves leave the envelope at about 100 m and remain outside it across the entire range plotted. g_inhom peaks near 5.9 at roughly 570 m and is still above 2 at 2.8 km, against an envelope ceiling near 1.4. So after accounting for the fact that fire is far more likely in the southern peat belt than in the north, burned cells still occur much closer together than that variation alone predicts. Note also that g_inhom falls below 1 at the shortest lags, the sensor floor surviving into the inhomogeneous statistic.

  "MAD",  "L(r)",       "complete spatial randomness",  fmt_p(SO$mad_L$p.value, 99),
  "MAD",  "L_inhom(r)", "inhomogeneous Poisson",        fmt_p(SO$mad_Linhom$p.value, 99),

Table 13: Global Monte Carlo tests. The maximum absolute deviation (MAD) and Diggle-Cressie-Loosmore-Ford (DCLF) statistics each summarise the whole curve in one number, so these p-values are not inflated by reading a band at many lags. The Monte Carlo floor is 0.01 with 99 simulations.




Both global tests reject the inhomogeneous Poisson null at the Monte Carlo floor. The pattern is clustered beyond its first-order trend, which answers the first half of Q3.
Where the clustering ends is a different matter, and here a decision of mine got in the way. I capped r at 5 km on the reasoning that longer lags in an elongated window rest on too few pairs. Across that whole range both curves sit outside the envelope. All 5 km establishes is that dependence extends at least that far. Section 7.6 extends the range.
The direction of the remaining bias matters for how confidently this can be stated. As set out in assumption A6, estimating \(\hat{\lambda}\) from the pattern under test lets it absorb part of the clustering, which widens the envelope and makes the test harder to reject. The rejection therefore stands despite a conservative procedure, not because of a permissive one.

text:
7.4 Testing isotropy, instead of just assuming it
Assumption A7 says \(K\), \(L\) and \(g\) all average over direction, and that I expected real anisotropy because peat fires spread with the wind and along canal lines. Listing an assumption and never testing it is the kind of thing that should not survive a read, so this section tests it. The test found something, but not the thing I predicted, and the first version of my own analysis missed it.
Why I did not use the packaged tools. spatstat offers Ksector and pairorient, and neither accepts a lambda argument: both assume homogeneity. Applied here they would reject isotropy for two reasons that have nothing to do with fire. The window is 86 km wide and 213 km tall, so even a perfectly isotropic process yields more north-south pairs than east-west ones purely because there is more room that way. And intensity is concentrated in a south-southeast band, so any pair drawn from inside it inherits that elongation.
I therefore built the null the way I built it for clustering: simulate from an inhomogeneous Poisson process with the same \(\hat{\lambda}\) from Section 6, which absorbs the window geometry and the first-order trend together.
Two statistics, and the second one is the point. Orientations here are axial, so I double the angles before averaging and summarise concentration by the mean resultant length \(R_2 = |n^{-1}\sum_k e^{2i\theta_k}|\), which is 0 when orientations are spread evenly and 1 when every pair lies on one axis.
Each harmonic is blind to the next one up, and I walked into that twice.
\(R_2\) detects a single preferred axis and is structurally blind to four-fold structure, because a rose with spikes at 0 and 90 degrees has its doubled angles cancel. My first version of this section reported the short range as isotropic on the strength of \(R_2\) alone, and the rose diagram contradicted it on sight. So I added \(R_4 = |n^{-1}\sum_k e^{4i\theta_k}|\).
\(R_4\) is in turn blind to eight-fold structure. Spikes at 0, 45, 90 and 135 degrees have a 45-degree period, so under \(e^{4i\theta}\) the 45 and 135 pair sits in antiphase to the 0 and 90 pair and the two cancel. That is exactly the shape a square grid produces, because a lattice offers displacements along its axes and along its diagonals. \(R_8\) is what captures it, and it turns out to be the largest directional signal anywhere in this analysis.
A harmonic statistic finds only the structure you asked it about. Two passes were needed here because I kept asking the wrong one, and each time the rose diagram was what showed me.

It has eight sharp spikes on the cardinal axes and the diagonals, which is the signature of a square grid rather than of fire, and my R2 statistic scored it as isotropic because R2 cannot see four-fold structure. The figure caught what the table missed. From 750 m outward the spikes vanish and the roses sit close to their null intervals, with only a slight and growing elongation by 3 to 6 km.






7.4.1 The short-range structure is my grid, and the sensor’s
Over 375 to 750 m the eight-fold concentration is 0.087 against 0.007 under the null, < 0.005. That is more than twelve times the null value and the largest directional effect measured anywhere in this report. The four-fold term is 0.0289, also significant, and \(R_2\) is 0.0063 against a null of 0.0066, 0.475, which is nothing at all.
Three statistics on the same 36,860 pairs, and they disagree completely. The structure is spikes on the axes and on the diagonals, which is what a square lattice produces and what only the eighth harmonic can see.
My first explanation was that this is entirely my own doing. ppp_cell keeps at most one point per 375 m cell, so short-range displacements are dominated by lattice vectors: 375 m at 0 and 90 degrees, 530 m on the diagonals, 750 m at two cells. That would produce spikes exactly where they appear. The way to check it is to run the identical test on ppp_all, which keeps every detection at its own sensor coordinate and has no such lattice.

The control only half-confirms my explanation, which is more interesting than if it had confirmed it outright. Thinning multiplies the eight-fold signal by about two and a half, from 0.0336 to 0.087, so a large part of the structure is indeed my construction. But the un-thinned detections still show 0.0336 against a null of 0.0018, < 0.01, which is roughly nineteen times the null. Removing my lattice reduces the effect without removing it.
The remainder is the instrument. VIIRS reports detections on its own scan grid, organised along-scan and along-track, and for a polar orbiter those project to roughly cardinal directions on the ground. So the raw detections carry a quasi-rectangular sampling geometry before I do anything to them.
Neither component is fire. Both are instrument geometry, which is the warning from Section 1.1 applied to my own directional test.


7.4.2 At longer range, a real but negligible tilt
From 750 m outward every harmonic goes quiet. Over 750 to 1500 m, \(R_4\) is 9^{-4} (0.930) and \(R_8\) is 0.0021 (0.665), both below their nulls. That is what a lattice explanation predicts, since every lattice vector is shorter than 750 m, and it is the check that makes me believe the short-range result is geometric rather than physical.
What remains is a weak single-axis elongation that grows with distance, reaching \(R_2 =\) 0.024 over 3000 to 6000 m against a null of 0.0055. That is statistically distinguishable at the Monte Carlo floor and it is 2.4% of the way to perfect alignment, which is not a directional pattern in any sense a fire officer would recognise.


7.4.3 My stated mechanism was wrong
A7 guessed that fires would align with canal lines. They do not.

Table 16: Orientation of the mapped drainage and road networks inside the regency, weighted by segment length, against the fire pair-orientation axis at each band. Separation is axial, so 90 degrees is the maximum possible disagreement.




The mapped waterways run at about 113 degrees and the roads at about 38 degrees. The long-range fire axis is 77 degrees: 37 degrees off the drainage and 38 degrees off the roads, on a scale where 90 degrees is the maximum possible disagreement. Neither is a match.
So the weak long-range tilt is not canal-following. It runs closer to north-south, which is also the long axis of the regency and of the peat belt inside it. The most likely explanation is first-order structure that \(\hat{\lambda}\) at a 4 km bandwidth does not fully absorb, not a directional process in the fire. I cannot separate those two with this design and I will not claim otherwise.


7.4.4 What this changes
A7 said anisotropy was likely because fires follow canals, and that it made my clustering estimates conservative. Both claims fail.
The short-range structure is geometric. It comes from the 375 m cell grid and the sensor’s scan grid, not from wind or canals. Beyond 750 m, where the clustering lives, no harmonic finds anything. The isotropic \(K\), \(L\) and \(g\) estimate what they claim to, and there is no conservatism to claim.
One practical consequence for the rest of the report. Because the eight-fold structure is symmetric about the cardinal axes and the diagonals, it very largely cancels in any statistic that averages over direction, which is what \(K\), \(L\) and \(g\) do. So it does not bias the clustering results. It would wreck a directional analysis, and anyone extending this work should thin differently before attempting one.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Geospatial Analytics for Public Safety
section: 7.6 Extending the range, after getting it wrong
text:
7.6 Extending the range, after getting it wrong
I set the 5 km cap because long lags in an elongated window rest on few pairs. That reasoning is fine, but 5 km was more conservative than I needed. The rule I stated in Section 5 caps \(r\) at a quarter of the window’s shortest dimension, and the window is 86 km wide, so 20 km was admissible the whole time. Extending to 20 km is not me granting myself a post-hoc licence, it is me finally applying the rule I had already written down.
Two practical constraints came with that, and I am disclosing both rather than hiding them. pcfinhom offers no border correction, and the translation correction over roughly seven million pairs per pattern would not finish in a workable time for 99 simulated patterns. So my significance across the extended range rests on \(L_{inhom}\) with a border correction and a full envelope, while the shape of \(g_{inhom}\) comes from a single translation-corrected curve with no simulations. I make no significance claim for \(g_{inhom}\) beyond 3 km.


code
Lx <- EX$env_L_ext |> mutate(across(c(obs, lo, hi), ~ .x - r), ref = 0,
                             panel = "L_inhom(r) - r, with envelope")
Gx <- EX$g_obs_ext |> filter(r > 0, is.finite(trans)) |>
  transmute(r, obs = trans, lo = NA_real_, hi = NA_real_, ref = 1,
            panel = "g_inhom(r), observed only")
ggplot(bind_rows(Lx, Gx), aes(r)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = PAL$rule, alpha = 0.75, na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_line(aes(y = ref), colour = PAL$muted, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_line(aes(y = obs), colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(data = tibble(panel = "g_inhom(r), observed only",
                           x = EX$summary_ext$r_g_within_10pct_of_1),
             aes(xintercept = x), colour = PAL$cool, linetype = "12", linewidth = 0.4) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, scales = "free", nrow = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(scale = 1e-3, suffix = " km")) +
  labs(x = "r", y = NULL,
       title = "Dependence is local, but a cumulative statistic cannot say so",
       subtitle = glue("Dotted line marks {round(EX$summary_ext$r_g_within_10pct_of_1/1000, 1)} km, where g_inhom first comes within 10% of 1.")) +
  theme_ex01(base_size = 9)








Figure 14: Left, inhomogeneous centred L function to 20 km with a 99-simulation envelope. Right, the observed inhomogeneous pair correlation function over the same range, with no envelope, on a log scale. What I take from it: the two panels answer different questions and disagree in an instructive way. g_inhom, which localises scale, peaks at about 440 m and decays steadily: it is 4.3 at 1 km, 2.7 at 2 km, 1.4 at 5 km, and reaches within 10% of its asymptote of 1 at about 7.2 km. L_inhom, which is cumulative, never re-enters its envelope within 20 km. Both are correct. The excess pair density is a local phenomenon that has largely dissipated by 7 km, and because L accumulates every excess at smaller lags it remains significantly elevated far beyond the range over which anything is actually happening.

I cross-checked the extended curve against my Section 7.3 estimate over the lags both cover, since both use the translation correction. The median relative difference is 0.15%, so changing the \(r\) grid has not quietly changed the estimate underneath me.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Geospatial Analytics for Public Safety
text:
10.2 How large is a cluster?
A significance test says clustering exists. A fitted cluster process says how big it is, which is the form a planner can use. Getting that number right meant discarding my first answer.
The first fit had no trend term. It returned a cluster standard deviation of 3,292 m, about 440 events per cluster, and an implied 24 parent locations across the whole regency. Twenty-three clusters of 440 events each is not a cluster scale. It is the southern peat belt re-described as a handful of enormous clusters, which is the only way a model without a trend term can represent large-scale intensity variation. Trend and interaction are not separately identifiable unless you make them so. Taken at face value the number would have given a confident and completely wrong operational radius.
The fix is to remove the trend before estimating the cluster parameters. My inhomogeneous pair correlation function already does exactly that, because it divides out \(\hat{\lambda}(u)\). So I fitted the Thomas pair correlation function
\[g(r) \;=\; 1 + \frac{1}{4\pi\kappa\sigma^{2}}\exp\!\left(-\frac{r^{2}}{4\sigma^{2}}\right)\]
directly to \(g_{inhom}\) by minimum contrast, minimising \(\sum_r \left(\hat{g}(r)^{q} - g_\theta(r)^{q}\right)^{2}\) with \(q = 1/4\) over \(r \in [200, 5,000]\) m. I set the lower limit to exclude lags governed by the 375 m sensor floor rather than by the cluster process. I wrote the fit out explicitly in R/07_cluster_scale.R rather than calling a packaged routine, because the objective function and the excluded range are the substance of the estimate and I wanted them visible.

  `sigma (m)` = round(sigma_m),
  `r95 (m)` = round(r95_m),

  `Events per cluster` = round(mu_per_cluster)) |> kable(align = "lrrrr")

The contrast between the two rows is the finding: leaving the trend in the model inflates the estimated cluster scale by a factor of two, and the implied cluster sizes become absurd.

ggplot() +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 0, xmax = TH$RMIN, ymin = 1, ymax = max(gobs$trans) * 1.05,
           fill = PAL$rule, alpha = 0.45) +

            linewidth = 0.55) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(2, 1), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(scale = 1e-3, suffix = " km")) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "r", y = "g(r), log scale",
       title = "Removing the trend halves the estimated cluster scale",
       subtitle = "Orange, observed inhomogeneous pcf. Blue, fitted Thomas models. Shaded, lags excluded from the fit.") +
  theme_ex01()








Figure 24: Observed inhomogeneous pair correlation function with the two fitted Thomas models, log scale, over the range used for fitting. The shaded band marks lags below 200 m, excluded from the fit because they are governed by the sensor’s pixel size. What I take from it: the trend-removed fit tracks the observed curve closely from the peak outward, which is the range that matters for an operational radius. The fit that retains the trend is too flat and too wide, because its cluster component is doing work that belongs to the intensity surface. Neither fit captures the observed curve beyond about 4 km, where the observed g_inhom decays more slowly than a single Gaussian cluster kernel allows. That is a real limitation of my model: the pattern has structure at more than one scale, and a one-scale model cannot represent it.





My trend-removed fit gives a cluster standard deviation of 1,055 m, so about 95% of a cluster’s events fall within roughly 2,581 m of its centre, with 67 events per cluster and about 155 cluster centres across the regency.

10.2.1 How precise is that number
Minimum contrast gives no standard error, so the estimate above was unqualified until I bootstrapped it. My first attempt resampled points with replacement. That is not a valid bootstrap for a point process: it destroys the dependence being estimated and creates coincident points, which distorts the pair correlation function at exactly the short lags the fit uses. The symptom was unmistakable. The interval excluded the point estimate entirely, and in the wrong direction.
The interval below comes from a parametric bootstrap. I simulate from the fitted inhomogeneous Thomas process, re-estimate \(\hat{\lambda}\) on each simulation, recompute \(g_{inhom}\), and refit by the same minimum contrast.

BC$boot_compare |> transmute(

  `sigma point (m)` = round(point_sigma_m),
  `median (m)` = round(median_m),
  `95% interval (m)` = glue("{round(lo95_m)} to {round(hi95_m)}"),
  `r95 interval (m)` = glue("{round(r95_lo_m)} to {round(r95_hi_m)}")
) |> kable(align = "lrrll")
