Table 25: Two bootstrap intervals on the cluster standard deviation. The non-parametric row is shown because it is wrong in an instructive way: an interval that excludes its own point estimate is a sign the resampling scheme does not respect the process.




The parametric interval puts the cluster standard deviation between 902 and 1,025 m, and the radius holding 95% of a cluster between 2.21 and 2.51 km. The refits sit a little below the point estimate, a known downward bias of minimum contrast under resimulation, so the point estimate lies just above its own interval. A cluster scale of about a kilometre, with roughly 2.2 to 2.5 km holding the bulk of one, is the summary I would defend. The kilometre-scale conclusion does not turn on which end of that range is right. That is consistent with my pair correlation function, which peaks at 438 m, and I got there by a different route: minimum contrast fitting of a mechanistic model rather than envelope testing.
Two estimates agreeing is stronger than either alone, but the agreement is only partial and I should say where it breaks. My fitted model has a single scale, and the figure below shows the observed curve decaying more slowly beyond about 4 km than a single Gaussian kernel allows. So the Thomas process describes the dominant local structure well and the longer tail of dependence out to roughly 7.2 km not at all. A multi-scale cluster process, or a log-Gaussian Cox process with a flexible covariance, would be the natural next model. Fitting one is beyond what I can do in this exercise, but it is the first thing I would try next.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Geospatial Analytics for Public Safety
section: 10.1 What is the clustering organised around?
text:
10.1 What is the clustering organised around?
Peat fire here is human in ignition and made possible by drainage. Two mapped covariates proxy those mechanisms: distance to the road network for access and ignition opportunity, distance to mapped canals and waterways for drainage-driven desiccation.
I took the covariate geometry from a dated Geofabrik OpenStreetMap extract for Kalimantan rather than a live Overpass query. That was not my first choice. Overpass refused a bounding box this size repeatedly, and once I had switched I realised the extract is better anyway: a live query returns different data every time it runs, so it cannot be part of a reproducible pipeline. The extract gave me 28,515 road features and 3,061 waterway features within a 15 km buffer of the regency.
I compute distances on that buffered frame and only then crop to the analysis window. If I had computed them on the clipped window I would have biased every distance upward for cells near the boundary, because their nearest road is often outside the regency entirely.
The same reasoning caught a bug in my first land-cover attempt, and it is worth recording because it fails quietly. distmap returns distances on the enclosing frame of whatever you hand it. Handed the union of the landuse polygons, that frame is their own bounding box, so the covariate was undefined across 98% of the regency and ppm fitted on the 2% that remained. The AIC values it returned were in the hundreds against tens of thousands for the other models, which is the only reason I looked. Evaluating distfun over the analysis window fixes it. Nothing in the report rests on the broken version, but a less absurd set of numbers would have gone unnoticed.
The 3,061 waterway features against 28,515 road features is itself my first result here, and it is a warning rather than a finding. An area defined by an abandoned canal network has fewer mapped watercourses than roads. I come back to what that does to the drainage covariate below.


code
rho_to_df <- function(rh, lab) {
  if (is.null(rh)) return(NULL)
  d <- rh
  nm <- names(d)
  tibble(x = d[[1]], rho = d[["rho"]],
         lo = if ("lo" %in% nm) d[["lo"]] else NA_real_,
         hi = if ("hi" %in% nm) d[["hi"]] else NA_real_, panel = lab)
}
rho_df <- bind_rows(
  rho_to_df(CM$rho_road,  "Distance to nearest road"),
  rho_to_df(CM$rho_water, "Distance to nearest mapped waterway"))
mean_int <- P$ppp_cell$n / (P$area_km2 * 1e6)
if (!is.null(rho_df) && nrow(rho_df)) {
  ggplot(rho_df, aes(x / 1000)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = per_1000km2(mean_int) / 1e3 * 1e3,
               colour = PAL$muted, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.35) +
    geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = per_1000km2(lo), ymax = per_1000km2(hi)),
                fill = PAL$rule, alpha = 0.6) +
    geom_line(aes(y = per_1000km2(rho)), colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.7) +
    facet_wrap(~panel, scales = "free", nrow = 1) +
    labs(x = "Distance (km)", y = "Burned cells per 1,000 km²",
         title = "Access explains a great deal, mapped drainage very little",
         subtitle = "Dashed line, mean intensity over the window.") +
    theme_ex01(base_size = 9)
} else cat("Covariate estimation unavailable; see the limitations.\n")








Figure 21: Estimated intensity as a non-parametric function of distance to the nearest road and to the nearest mapped waterway, with 95% confidence bands. The horizontal line is the mean intensity over the window. What I take from it: intensity falls steeply with distance from a road, from well above the window mean within the first kilometre to below it beyond a few kilometres. That is a strong and monotone access effect, consistent with ignition being human. The waterway relationship is weaker and less monotone. This is my more interesting negative result. It does not show drainage is unimportant, it shows OpenStreetMap’s waterway layer is a poor proxy for it, because the dense minor canal network of the former Mega Rice Project is largely unmapped. My covariate is measuring mapping effort as much as hydrology, so I read the flat curve as absence of evidence.

Table 22: Each covariate fitted on its own, so the explanatory power can be attributed rather than shared. Gain is the AIC improvement over an intercept-only model. The single-covariate models all use two parameters and are directly comparable.




Proximity to plantation and farmland is the covariate that matters. On its own it recovers 3,204 of the 3,550 AIC units the full model gains over an intercept-only model, which is about 90% of the total from a single term. Distance to road recovers 1,991 and distance to forest 1,906, both on the same two parameters.
My earlier claim that access did nearly all the work was an artefact of a thin covariate set. With only roads and waterways in the model, distance to road was the best available proxy for something it was not measuring.
The forest term is much weaker than I first reported, and I should not have read it as a mechanism. Adding forest on top of plantation buys only 267 further AIC units, and forest alone explains slightly less than roads alone. The reason is visible in the support behind it. The median burned cell sits 19.6 km from the nearest mapped forest polygon and 48% of cells are beyond 20 km, so the covariate is describing a near-regional gradient across an 86 km wide window. Plantation sits at a median of 4.1 km, which is a local relationship.

Table 23: Coefficients of the full model, on the log-intensity scale, per kilometre. A negative coefficient means intensity falls with distance from that feature. The forest coefficient is positive and precisely estimated, but see the caution below: a linear term summarises a relationship that the non-parametric curve shows is not monotone.




What the signs support, and what they do not. Intensity rises steeply as you approach plantation and farmland (coefficient -0.0519, z = -29.3). That relationship is local, monotone and carries most of the model, and for peat fire used in land clearing it is the expected pattern.
The forest coefficient is positive and has a large z, but a large z on a misspecified functional form is not evidence of a mechanism. The rhohat curve below is not monotone: intensity is moderate near mapped forest, higher at 20 to 25 km, low at 40 km and high again beyond. A single linear term across that range is a summary, not a description. What I can say is that mapped forest and fire are largely in different parts of the regency. What I cannot say is that proximity to forest suppresses fire.
The OSM caveat applies to both, with different force. Mapped forest covers 20.8% of the window and plantation or farmland 10.6%, from a few dozen polygons apiece. For plantation the effect is local and steep enough that mapping effort is an unlikely explanation. For forest, where the covariate varies over tens of kilometres, I cannot separate the two.
None of this is causal. Roads, farmland and forest edges are jointly determined by where people have cleared and worked the land. The model orders covariates by explanatory power. It does not say what would happen if any of them changed.

  d <- BC$rho_cover[[nm]]; names(d)[1] <- "x"
  d |> transmute(x, rho, lo, hi,
                 panel = ifelse(nm == "forest", "Distance to mapped forest",
                                "Distance to plantation or farmland"))
}))
ggplot(rc, aes(x / 1000)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = per_1000km2(lo), ymax = per_1000km2(hi)),
              fill = PAL$rule, alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_line(aes(y = per_1000km2(rho)), colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, scales = "free", nrow = 1) +
  labs(x = "Distance (km)", y = "Burned cells per 1,000 km\u00b2",
       title = "One curve is local and steep, the other is neither") +
  theme_ex01(base_size = 9)








Figure 22: Intensity as a non-parametric function of distance to mapped forest and to plantation or farmland, with 95% bands. What I take from it: the two panels are not equally trustworthy and the figure is the reason I stopped treating them as a pair. Plantation falls steeply over the first few kilometres and is the strongest covariate relationship in the report; the median burned cell is 4 km from mapped plantation, so the informative part of that curve is where the data is. Forest is a different matter. The curve is not monotone, rising to 20 to 25 km, dropping near 40 and rising again, and the median cell sits 20 km out with half beyond that. The positive linear coefficient in the model is a summary of that shape, not a description of it.






10.1.1 What the covariates still fail to explain


code
rk <- RK$res_K
ycol <- if ("bres" %in% names(rk)) "bres" else names(rk)[2]
ggplot(rk, aes(r, .data[[ycol]])) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = PAL$muted, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_line(colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.7) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(scale = 1e-3, suffix = " km")) +
  labs(x = "r", y = "Residual K",
       title = "The covariates explain location, not contagion",
       subtitle = glue("Model: {RK$formula}")) +
  theme_ex01()








Figure 23: Residual K function for the best-fitting Poisson model, which is the full model with road, water, forest and plantation distances. If the fitted trend explained the pattern this curve would sit on zero. What I take from it: it does not. A large positive residual remains at short lags, so the covariates account for a great deal of the first-order variation and none of the local interaction. Knowing how far a place is from cleared land tells me whether it is likely to burn. It does not tell me that burning spreads. A Poisson model cannot represent contagion by construction, which is what motivates the cluster process fitted next.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Geospatial Analytics for Public Safety
section: 18.1 The finding that governs the rest
text:
18.1 The finding that governs the rest
A satellite hotspot is not a fire, and forgetting that invalidates most of what you would otherwise conclude. A VIIRS detection is a 375 m pixel seen during one overpass. One peat fire fills dozens of them and gets re-recorded about four times a day, and I measured the consequence: the raw count overstates distinct burning locations by a factor of about 3.4. Every standard test then returns a significant result for reasons that have nothing to do with fire. Complete spatial randomness is rejected before any analysis. Moran’s I on raw counts is 0.69. The short-range rose diagram has eight sharp lobes. None of those are findings. They are the instrument and the geometry, restated.
Almost every methodological decision in this report exists to get past that.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Geospatial Analytics for Public Safety
section: 18.3 What I would tell a fire agency
text:
18.3 What I would tell a fire agency
Three things, in the order I would say them.
Allocate by intensity, not by area. Two orders of magnitude separate the southern peat belt from the northern interior. Anything distributed evenly, or in proportion to sub-district size, is mismatched to where fire actually is.
Size the response ring in kilometres and the response window in days. A cluster is about a kilometre across with 2.2 to 2.5 km holding most of one, and the raised probability of a neighbour igniting is concentrated in the first few days.
Plan for a bimodal record, not an average. Drought years produce thousands of burned cells here and wet years produce single digits. There is no average year to staff for, which argues for surge capacity keyed to seasonal drought forecasts.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Geospatial Analytics for Public Safety
section: 18.4 What I would not let them conclude
text:
18.4 What I would not let them conclude
That roads, or forest edges, are levers. They are associations, jointly determined by where people have cleared and worked land. That anything below 375 m is resolvable: it is not, and no statistic fixes that. That a quiet year will look like this one at smaller scale, which is untested and may not be estimable.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Geospatial Analytics for Public Safety
section: 18.5 The thing I would take to the next exercise
text:
18.5 The thing I would take to the next exercise
Every substantive result here came from replacing a default null with one that could actually fail, and every error I made came from not checking what a default was doing. The distance cap, the trend-free cluster fit, the thin covariate set, the harmonic that could not see the structure in front of it: each produced a confident number, and each was wrong until something forced a look. Section 15 lists all ten. The figure caught what the table missed more than once, which is the practical version of the lesson.

The regency was chosen by a rule, set before the result. Highest detection density among regencies above 5,000 km², the size floor I need for second-order estimation to a 5 km lag. Pulang Pisau wins at 3,656 per 1,000 km². Ketapang leads on raw count (65,901) but is 3x the area.
My first pass used a 7-day sample, where Pulang Pisau led on count. Over the full window it does not, so I restated the rule against the whole record.
VIIRS 375 m Collection 2, both platforms, clipped to the administrative polygon in UTM 49S, 9,759 km².
The 87-day window is set by what the REST API retains. Why that is a limit of my tooling and not of the data comes later, in the correction slide.

10. What I would take from this

What made the results credible
Every result I would defend came from replacing a default null with one that could fail. Complete spatial randomness rejects before I compute anything. Moran’s I on raw counts is 0.69. The short-range rose has eight lobes. None of those are findings: they are the instrument and the geometry, restated.
Intensity spans two orders of magnitude and is stable across four bandwidths. Clustering survives the inhomogeneous null and an areal method with different weights agrees. Scale is confirmed by two independent estimators. Land cover carries 3,204 of 3,550 AIC units from one term.


What produced the errors
Every mistake came from not checking what a default was doing. A 5 km distance cap. A cluster fit with no trend term. A covariate set of two. A harmonic that could not see the structure in front of it.
Each returned a confident number, and each was wrong until something forced a look. Ten corrections are listed in the report.
The figure caught what the table missed more than once. That is the practical version of the lesson, and the thing I would carry into the next exercise.
One caveat over all of it. Everything here was measured in a season that ranks 2 of 14, at 54x the median. These are the properties of a severe year, not a typical one.



My technical report, code and audit trail are in the repository. Data: NASA FIRMS, geoBoundaries, OpenStreetMap via Geofabrik.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Geospatial Analytics for Public Safety
section: 9. What the analysis says about fire here
text:
9. What the analysis says about fire here


Fire is concentrated, not spread. Two orders of magnitude separate the southern peat belt from the northern interior. Capability placed in proportion to sub-district area sits mostly where fire is not.
Fire is contagious, briefly. A cell that burns today raises the chance its neighbour burns tomorrow, strongest within a few hundred metres and a few days. The useful response geometry is 2.2 to 2.5 km and days, not pixels and weeks.


Fire follows cleared land. Proximity to plantation and farmland carries 3,204 of 3,550 AIC units on its own, more than roads and forest together. Burning concentrates on the agricultural frontier.
There is no average year to plan for. 2 of 14, at 54x the median, and the record is bimodal: drought years in the thousands, wet years in single digits. Staffing to the mean staffs for a year that never happens. This argues for surge capacity keyed to seasonal drought forecasts.

5. Exploratory Data Analysis

5.1 Counts versus rates

ggarrange(
  ggplot(ict_derived, aes(x = RADIO)) +
    geom_histogram(bins = 20, color = "black", fill = "light blue") +
    ggtitle("Households owning a radio (count)"),
  ggplot(ict_derived, aes(x = RADIO_PR)) +
    geom_histogram(bins = 20, color = "black", fill = "light blue") +
    ggtitle("Radio per 1,000 households"),
  ncol = 2)








The count distribution is strongly right-skewed, which is a size effect: a handful of large townships sit far out in the tail. The rate is much closer to symmetric. This is the whole justification for section 4.3 in one picture.


5.2 All six penetration rates

radio <- ggplot(ict_derived, aes(x = RADIO_PR)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, color = "black", fill = "light blue")
tv <- ggplot(ict_derived, aes(x = TV_PR)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, color = "black", fill = "light blue")
llphone <- ggplot(ict_derived, aes(x = LLPHONE_PR)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, color = "black", fill = "light blue")
mphone <- ggplot(ict_derived, aes(x = MPHONE_PR)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, color = "black", fill = "light blue")
computer <- ggplot(ict_derived, aes(x = COMPUTER_PR)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, color = "black", fill = "light blue")
internet <- ggplot(ict_derived, aes(x = INTERNET_PR)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, color = "black", fill = "light blue")

ggarrange(radio, tv, llphone, mphone, computer, internet,
          ncol = 3, nrow = 2)








Radio and TV are broad and roughly symmetric. Landline, computer and internet are all heavily right-skewed with a floor near zero, which is what low-penetration technology looks like: most townships have almost none, a few urban ones have some.


5.3 Joining geospatial and aspatial data

shan_sf <- left_join(shan_sf, ict_derived, by = c("TS_PCODE" = "TS_PCODE"))


sum(!is.na(shan_sf$TT_HOUSEHOLDS))

[1] 55


All 55 townships matched on TS_PCODE. Worth checking rather than assuming, because a left join silently produces NA rather than failing.


5.4 Choropleths: why the rate matters

  tm_polygons(fill = "TT_HOUSEHOLDS",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(n = 5, style = "jenks"),

  tm_borders(col_alpha = 0.5)

RADIO.map <- tm_shape(shan_sf) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "RADIO",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(n = 5, style = "jenks"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Radio (count)")) +
  tm_borders(col_alpha = 0.5)

tmap_arrange(TT_HOUSEHOLDS.map, RADIO.map, asp = NA, ncol = 2)








The two maps are near-identical. The count map is essentially a population map.

RADIO_PR.map <- tm_shape(shan_sf) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "RADIO_PR",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(n = 5, style = "jenks"),

tmap_arrange(TT_HOUSEHOLDS.map, RADIO_PR.map, asp = NA, ncol = 2)








Once normalised the pattern inverts in places: some of the least populous townships have the highest radio penetration. That is a real signal, and it was completely hidden in the count map.

               tl.col = "black")














NoteWhich pair actually has to go



COMPUTER_PR and INTERNET_PR correlate at 0.87, far above any other pair (MPHONE_PR–COMPUTER_PR is 0.74, TV_PR–MPHONE_PR is 0.72). In 2014 Myanmar a home internet connection almost always implied a computer, so the two are close to the same measurement. I drop INTERNET_PR and keep COMPUTER_PR, following the handout.
Worth noting what is not collinear: RADIO_PR is essentially uncorrelated with everything else (its largest correlation with any other variable is 0.15). Radio is not a proxy for wealth here, it is its own axis, and it will do real work in the clustering.

8.3 Edge costs and the minimum spanning tree
The cost of each edge is the attribute dissimilarity between the two townships it joins. Note the weights style is B, not row-standardised: these are distances, and scaling them per row would destroy their meaning.

54 edges for 55 nodes, as a spanning tree must have.

plot(st_geometry(shan_sf), border = gray(.5))
plot.mst(shan.mst, coords, col = "blue",
         cex.lab = 0.7, cex.circles = 0.005, add = TRUE)










8.4 Pruning the tree

clust6 <- spdep::skater(edges = shan.mst[,1:2],
                        data = shan_ict,
                        method = "euclidean",
                        ncuts = 5)
table(clust6$groups)


 1  2  3  4  5  6 
22 18 11  2  1  1 








ImportantSKATER buys contiguity with badly unbalanced clusters



The six groups are 22, 18, 11, 2, 1, 1. Two of the six “regions” are single townships and a third has two. Effectively this is a three-region solution with three outliers shaved off.
That is a structural property of the method, not bad luck. SKATER can only cut edges of the spanning tree, so an extreme township that sits on a leaf gets isolated by the cheapest available cut long before the algorithm will split a large interior block. If the goal is six comparably sized planning regions, SKATER at ncuts = 5 does not deliver them.

clust6$ssw

Total sum of squares is 12,613 and each of the five cuts reduces the within-cluster sum of squares, ending at 8,735. The cuts are doing real work, just unevenly.

The right-hand map is made of solid contiguous blocks. That is the entire point of SKATER, and it is visually obvious.

title: Geographical Segmentation with Spatially Constrained Clustering
text:
9. Spatially Constrained Clustering: ClustGeo

9.1 Ward-like clustering without a spatial constraint

nongeo_cluster <- hclustgeo(proxmat)
plot(nongeo_cluster, cex = 0.5)
rect.hclust(nongeo_cluster, k = 6, border = 2:5)














Importanthclustgeo() with no constraint is not the same as the hclust() above



The handout presents hclustgeo(proxmat) as doing “a typical Ward-like hierarchical clustering just like hclust()”. It is Ward-like, but it is not the same Ward.
My hclust() call in section 7.6 used method = "ward.D" and gave cluster sizes 20/4/13/6/7/5. hclustgeo(proxmat) gives 16/8/13/6/7/5. I checked where the difference comes from, and hclustgeo(proxmat) reproduces hclust(proxmat, "ward.D2") exactly, township for township, not ward.D.
The distinction is that ward.D2 squares the dissimilarities before applying the Ward update and ward.D does not, so only ward.D2 implements Ward’s actual criterion on a non-squared input distance matrix. Twelve townships move between clusters 1 and 2 as a result. It is a small difference here but it means the section 7 dendrogram and the section 9 dendrogram are not two views of one clustering.



groups <- as.factor(cutree(nongeo_cluster, k = 6))
shan_sf_ngeo_cluster <- cbind(shan_sf, as.matrix(groups)) %>%
  rename(`CLUSTER` = `as.matrix.groups.`)


qtm(shan_sf_ngeo_cluster, "CLUSTER")










9.2 Choosing the mixing parameter
D0 holds attribute dissimilarity, D1 holds geographic distance, and alpha sets how much weight goes to each.

dist <- st_distance(shan_sf, shan_sf)
distmat <- as.dist(dist)


cr <- choicealpha(proxmat, distmat, range.alpha = seq(0, 1, 0.1), K = 6, graph = TRUE)
















round(cr$Qnorm, 3)

          Q0norm Q1norm
alpha=0    1.000  0.139
alpha=0.1  0.978  0.301
alpha=0.2  0.855  0.665
alpha=0.3  0.825  0.735
alpha=0.4  0.697  0.882
alpha=0.5  0.652  0.928
alpha=0.6  0.652  0.928
alpha=0.7  0.635  0.934
alpha=0.8  0.543  0.999
alpha=0.9  0.496  0.975
alpha=1    0.252  1.000








NoteReading the alpha curves



Q0norm is the proportion of attribute homogeneity retained, Q1norm the geographic homogeneity. Moving from alpha = 0 to alpha = 0.2 costs about 14% of attribute homogeneity (1.000 → 0.855) and buys a jump in geographic homogeneity from 0.139 to 0.665. That is a very favourable exchange and it is why 0.2 is the conventional choice here.
Pushing on to alpha = 0.3 costs a further 3 points of attribute homogeneity for 7 points of geographic, still positive but clearly past the knee. I follow the handout and use 0.2.




9.3 The spatially constrained solution

clustG <- hclustgeo(proxmat, distmat, alpha = 0.2)
groups <- as.factor(cutree(clustG, k = 6))
shan_sf_Gcluster <- cbind(shan_sf, as.matrix(groups)) %>%
  rename(`CLUSTER` = `as.matrix.groups.`)
table(shan_sf_Gcluster$CLUSTER)


 1  2  3  4  5  6 
10  9  7  9 12  8 



qtm(shan_sf_Gcluster, "CLUSTER")








Much more balanced than SKATER (12/10/9/9/8/7, no singletons) and visibly more spatially coherent than the unconstrained solution, though not perfectly contiguous. Section 11 measures that.

The six profiles are interpretable:

Cluster 4 (n = 6) is the connected one: highest on TV (744), landline (99), mobile

and computer (65.5) by a wide margin. These are the urban centres.

Cluster 5 (n = 7) is the opposite on everything modern (TV 224, mobile 132, computer 6.7) but mid-range on radio. Low-penetration remote townships.
Cluster 6 (n = 5) is the interesting one: lowest radio of all (98.6) yet high mobile (468). These townships appear to have skipped radio rather than lagged on it.
Cluster 3 (n = 13) is the high-radio group (300) with solid mobile (392).

title: Geographical Segmentation with Spatially Constrained Clustering
section: 11. My Own Exploration: What Does the Spatial Constraint Actually Cost?
text:
11. My Own Exploration: What Does the Spatial Constraint Actually Cost?
Every method here claims a different balance between two things I can measure directly:

attribute homogeneity, as the total within-cluster sum of squares on standardised variables (lower is better);
spatial coherence, as the number of contiguous pieces the six clusters break into (6 is perfect, higher is worse).

The handout asserts the trade-off exists. I wanted the numbers.

11.1 Counting contiguous pieces

pieces <- function(lab, nb) {
  total <- 0
  for (k in unique(lab)) {
    idx <- which(lab == k); seen <- integer(0); comp <- 0
    for (i in idx) {
      if (i %in% seen) next
      comp <- comp + 1; stack <- i
      while (length(stack)) {
        v <- stack[1]; stack <- stack[-1]
        if (v %in% seen) next
        seen <- c(seen, v)
        nbrs <- nb[[v]]; nbrs <- nbrs[nbrs != 0]
        stack <- c(stack, intersect(nbrs[!(nbrs %in% seen)], idx))
      }
    }
    total <- total + comp
  }
  total
}

wss <- function(lab) {
  x <- scale(shan_ict)
  sum(sapply(unique(lab), function(k) {
    s <- x[lab == k, , drop = FALSE]
    if (nrow(s) < 2) return(0)
    sum(scale(s, scale = FALSE)^2)
  }))
}



11.2 The trade-off, measured

cg3 <- cutree(hclustgeo(proxmat, distmat, alpha = 0.3), 6)

solutions <- list(
  `hclust (ward.D)`   = cutree(hclust_ward, 6),
  `hclustgeo (a = 0)` = cutree(nongeo_cluster, 6),
  `ClustGeo a = 0.2`  = cutree(clustG, 6),
  `ClustGeo a = 0.3`  = cg3,
  `SKATER`            = clust6$groups
)

tibble(
  method = names(solutions),
  pieces = sapply(solutions, pieces, nb = shan.nb),
  within_SS = round(sapply(solutions, wss), 1),
  sizes = sapply(solutions, function(l)
    paste(sort(as.vector(table(l)), decreasing = TRUE), collapse = "/"))
)

# A tibble: 5 x 4
  method            pieces within_SS sizes         
  <chr>              <dbl>     <dbl> <chr>         
1 hclust (ward.D)       24      107. 20/13/7/6/5/4 
2 hclustgeo (a = 0)     28      110. 16/13/8/7/6/5 
3 ClustGeo a = 0.2      18      130. 12/10/9/9/8/7 
4 ClustGeo a = 0.3      17      134. 21/8/8/7/6/5  
5 SKATER                 6      151. 22/18/11/2/1/1








ImportantThe constraint is expensive, and ClustGeo does not actually enforce it



Three things came out of this that I did not get from the maps.
The unconstrained solutions are extremely fragmented. Six clusters break into 24 and 28 separate patches. That is roughly half of the 55 townships sitting in a patch of their own or nearly so. “Fragmented” undersells it.
SKATER’s contiguity is absolute and the price is 42%. It returns exactly 6 pieces for 6 clusters, as guaranteed by construction. Within-cluster sum of squares rises from 106.6 to 151.1, which is 42% worse attribute homogeneity. That is the real cost of mappable regions on this data, and it is not small.
ClustGeo at alpha = 0.2 does not deliver contiguity. This is the finding that surprised me. It still breaks into 18 pieces, only a third of the way from 24 to 6, while already giving up 22% of homogeneity. Raising alpha to 0.3 barely helps (17 pieces). ClustGeo pulls clusters toward geographic compactness through a distance penalty, but nothing in the algorithm forbids a cluster from being in two places at once. SKATER’s graph-based formulation is categorically different: contiguity is a constraint, not a preference.
So the two methods are not interchangeable alternatives. If the deliverable must be drawable as contiguous regions, only SKATER guarantees it. ClustGeo buys balance (no singletons, sizes 12/10/9/9/8/7 against SKATER’s 22/18/11/2/1/1) but not contiguity.




11.3 A second question: the handout standardises, then clusters on raw rates
Sections 7.2 computed both a min-max and a z-score standardisation, and then the proximity matrix in 7.3 was built from shan_ict, the unstandardised rates. All five variables are per-1,000 rates so they share a unit, which is presumably the reasoning. But sharing a unit is not the same as sharing a scale.

v <- apply(shan_ict, 2, var)
tibble(variable = names(v),
       sd = round(sqrt(v), 1),
       pct_of_total_variance = round(100 * v / sum(v), 1))

# A tibble: 5 x 3
  variable       sd pct_of_total_variance
  <chr>       <dbl>                 <dbl>
1 RADIO_PR    105.                   16  
2 TV_PR       159.                   36.6
3 LLPHONE_PR   40.7                   2.4
4 MPHONE_PR   176.                   44.4
5 COMPUTER_PR  20.5                   0.6


MPHONE_PR and TV_PR together carry 81% of the total variance. COMPUTER_PR contributes 0.6% and LLPHONE_PR 2.4%. Euclidean distance on these raw rates is therefore, to a good approximation, a distance on mobile phones and television only.

raw_k6 <- cutree(hclust(dist(shan_ict), "ward.D"), 6)
std_k6 <- cutree(hclust(dist(scale(shan_ict)), "ward.D"), 6)

adj_rand <- function(a, b) {
  t <- table(a, b); n <- sum(t)
  s <- sum(choose(t, 2))
  sa <- sum(choose(rowSums(t), 2)); sb <- sum(choose(colSums(t), 2))
  e <- sa * sb / choose(n, 2)
  (s - e) / ((sa + sb) / 2 - e)
}

tibble(raw_sizes = paste(table(raw_k6), collapse = "/"),
       z_sizes = paste(table(std_k6), collapse = "/"),
       adjusted_rand = round(adj_rand(raw_k6, std_k6), 3))

# A tibble: 1 x 3
  raw_sizes     z_sizes       adjusted_rand
  <chr>         <chr>                 <dbl>
1 20/4/13/6/7/5 11/12/9/8/9/6           0.3








ImportantStandardising changes the answer substantially



The adjusted Rand index between the raw-rate and z-scored partitions is 0.30. For reference, 1 would be identical and 0 would be the agreement expected by chance. 0.30 is weak agreement: these are largely different segmentations of Shan State, from the same variables and the same algorithm.
The z-scored version also produces much more even clusters (11/12/9/8/9/6 against 20/4/13/6/7/5), which is what I would expect once COMPUTER_PR is no longer contributing 0.6% of the distance.
I am not claiming the handout is wrong to use raw rates: if the analyst genuinely believes a 100-per-1,000 difference in mobile ownership matters more than a 100-per-1,000 difference in computer ownership, raw rates encode that belief correctly. The point is that this is a decision, it is unstated, and it moves the result a long way. Reporting the six clusters without mentioning it would make a choice look like a finding.

title: Geographical Segmentation with Spatially Constrained Clustering
section: 12. What I Take From This Exercise
text:
12. What I Take From This Exercise
Segmentation is not detection. Exercise 5 tested a hypothesis and returned a p-value. This exercise returns a partition, and there is no p-value for a partition. The gap statistic in section 7.5 pointed at k = 1, which in plain terms means these five variables do not contain strong natural groupings. Six regions is a planning decision made on top of a weak statistical signal, and that should be stated out loud rather than buried.
Contiguity costs 42% here, and I can now quantify it rather than assert it. The measurement in section 11.2 is the thing I will carry forward. Before this exercise I would have described the spatial constraint as a mild regularisation. On Shan State it raises within-cluster variance by two-fifths. Whether that is acceptable depends entirely on whether the output has to be drawn on a map and administered, which is a question about the client, not about the data.
ClustGeo and SKATER solve different problems. This is the correction I most needed. They are presented side by side as two spatially constrained methods, which made me assume they were two routes to the same place. They are not: SKATER enforces contiguity and distorts cluster sizes to do it; ClustGeo encourages compactness and preserves balance but left 18 disconnected pieces at the recommended alpha. Picking between them is picking which guarantee matters.
Two silent decisions moved the result more than any modelling choice. Dropping INTERNET_PR for collinearity was explicit and defensible. Clustering on unstandardised rates was neither, and it changed the partition to an adjusted Rand of 0.30 against the standardised alternative. The ward.D versus ward.D2 discrepancy in section 9.1 is smaller but the same species of problem: a default that quietly differs between two sections of the same analysis.
Connecting forward. The next exercise moves to geographically weighted regression, where a bandwidth plays a role structurally similar to alpha here, deciding how much geography constrains the estimate. The habit worth keeping from this exercise is to report what the constraint cost, not just that it was applied.

7.2 Local Moran’s I


code
lm <- with_geo(L$lisa) |> mutate(var = var_lab(var), cls = factor(cls, names(LISA_COLS())))
ggplot(lm) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = cls), colour = PAL$border, linewidth = 0.04) +
  geom_sf(data = states, fill = NA, colour = PAL$ink, linewidth = 0.18) +
  facet_wrap(~var, nrow = 1, labeller = label_wrap_gen(16)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = LISA_COLS(), name = NULL, drop = FALSE) +
  coord_sf(expand = FALSE, datum = NA) + theme_map(base_size = 10)








Figure 4: Local Moran’s I cluster maps, p < 0.05 by conditional permutation (999). Only significant townships are coloured. High-High: a violent township among violent neighbours. Low-Low: a quiet township among quiet neighbours. Low-High: a quiet township surrounded by violence. No High-Low outlier reaches significance for any variable.





What the maps say. For every variable the largest High-High cluster is the same block of the dry zone: southern Sagaing, northern Magway and western Mandalay. Between 52% and 88% of each variable’s High-High townships lie in those three regions. A second High-High belt runs down the eastern border from Kayin through Mon to Tanintharyi. Battles add a western belt in Chin and a northern patch in Kachin, matching the ethnic armed organisations there; violence against civilians is the most concentrated, almost entirely in the dry zone and Tanintharyi.
Low-Low clusters fall in eastern Shan (including the Wa and Mongla areas discussed above), the Ayeyarwady delta and around Yangon, and in the far north of Kachin for explosions and civilian targeting. The few Low-High townships, such as Hlaingbwe in Kayin and Mabein in Shan, are quieter places beside intense fighting: candidates for watching rather than for reassurance.
There are no significant High-Low outliers at all. Violence in Myanmar does not form isolated islands. Wherever a township is unusually violent, its neighbours are too.

7.3 Getis-Ord Gi*


code
gm <- with_geo(L$gi) |> mutate(var = var_lab(var), cls = factor(cls, names(GI_COLS())))
ggplot(gm) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = cls), colour = PAL$border, linewidth = 0.04) +
  geom_sf(data = states, fill = NA, colour = PAL$ink, linewidth = 0.18) +
  facet_wrap(~var, nrow = 1, labeller = label_wrap_gen(16)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = GI_COLS(), name = NULL, drop = FALSE) +
  coord_sf(expand = FALSE, datum = NA) + theme_map(base_size = 10)








Figure 5: Gi* hot and cold spots on log(1 + count), each township included in its own neighbourhood, p < 0.05 by conditional permutation (999).





Gi* asks a narrower question than Local Moran’s I: is the neighbourhood total unusually high or low? Because it does not separate a township from its surroundings it cannot detect outliers, and here that costs little, because there are almost none. It agrees with the Local Moran maps township for township in most places: the dry zone and the southeastern border are hot, eastern Shan, the delta and Yangon are cold. Its value is as a check that the clusters do not depend on the choice of statistic, and as the quantity EHSA tracks through time.

title: Take-home Exercise 2: Geospatial Analytics for Peace
section: 8.1 From a five-year snapshot to a time series
text:
8.1 From a five-year snapshot to a time series
The local statistics above collapse nearly five years into one number per township. To see change, I compute Gi* for every township in every one of the 19 quarters, and then test each township’s 19-value series for a monotonic trend with the Mann-Kendall test. A positive and significant tau means the township’s neighbourhood has been getting hotter relative to the rest of the country; a negative one means it has been cooling.


code
mkm <- with_geo(E$mk |> filter(var == "pv")) |>
  mutate(fill = if_else(sl < ALPHA, tau, NA_real_))
ggplot(mkm) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = fill), colour = PAL$border, linewidth = 0.05) +
  geom_sf(data = states, fill = NA, colour = PAL$ink, linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = PAL$cool, mid = PAL$ground, high = PAL$accent_dk, midpoint = 0,
                       na.value = PAL$null, limits = c(-1, 1),
                       name = "Kendall's tau (p < 0.05)") +
  scalebar_layer(bb) + north_layer(bb) +
  coord_sf(expand = FALSE, datum = NA) + theme_map() +
  theme(legend.key.width = unit(40, "pt"))








Figure 6: Mann-Kendall trend in each township’s quarterly Gi* series for all political violence, 2021 Q1 to 2025 Q3. Townships with p ≥ 0.05 are shown in grey. The trend is relative: a falling Gi* means the neighbourhood is becoming less violent compared with the rest of Myanmar.





64 townships have a significantly rising Gi* and 83 a falling one. The falling trend is overwhelmingly one city: 44 of Yangon Region’s 45 townships are cooling, the signature of the urban resistance of 2021 being suppressed or pushed out. Smaller falling patches sit in Kachin (Myitkyina, Hpakant and their neighbours) and in the city townships of Mandalay.
The rising townships form a belt across the middle of the country: Bago West, Magway, Mandalay and Bago East, with Tanintharyi in the south and a handful in Rakhine. These are the places where the war arrived late, either as the dry-zone insurgency spread south and east out of Sagaing or as new fronts opened. Sagaing itself, the largest theatre, shows almost no significant trend, because it was hot from 2021 onward and stayed hot. A trend test cannot see a level, which is exactly the gap EHSA fills.

title: Take-home Exercise 2: Geospatial Analytics for Peace
text:
8.2 EHSA classification
EHSA combines the two pieces of information above: how often a township is a significant Gi* hot or cold spot, and whether its Gi* is trending. I use sfdep’s implementation, which also lets each township’s neighbourhood in quarter t include its neighbours in quarter t − 1, so a hot spot must be hot in space and persist in time. I set the significance used inside the classification rules to 0.05, as the brief does, instead of sfdep’s default of 0.01.
Checking the labels. sfdep 0.2.5 has a defect I found in Hands-on Exercise 6: emerging_hotspot_analysis() computes results in alphabetical order of location but labels them in the geometry’s order, so whenever the two differ, the classifications land on the wrong townships with no error. I sort the townships by PCode before building the cube, assert in the script that the orders match, and then check the labels against the independently computed mean Gi* of each township:

code
em <- with_geo(E$ehsa |> filter(var == "pv")) |>
  mutate(classification = factor(classification, EHSA_LEVELS))
present <- levels(droplevels(em$classification))
em2 <- bind_rows(
  em |> mutate(panel = "All classes"),
  em |> mutate(panel = "Mann-Kendall p < 0.05 only",
               classification = if_else(p_value < ALPHA, classification, factor(NA, EHSA_LEVELS))))
ggplot(em2) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = classification), colour = PAL$border, linewidth = 0.04) +
  geom_sf(data = states, fill = NA, colour = PAL$ink, linewidth = 0.2) +
  facet_wrap(~panel) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = EHSA_COLS()[present], breaks = present, labels = ehsa_label(present),
                    name = NULL, na.value = "#FFFFFF", drop = TRUE) +
  coord_sf(expand = FALSE, datum = NA) + theme_map(base_size = 10) +
  theme(legend.position = "right", legend.key.width = unit(12, "pt"), legend.key.height = unit(10, "pt"))








Figure 7: Emerging hot spot classification of all political violence, 19 quarters, Gi* with a one-quarter time lag, 199 permutations per quarter, classification rules at α = 0.05. Left: every township’s class. Right: the same classes shown only where the Mann-Kendall trend is significant at p < 0.05, which is the filter the brief asks for.







code
eb <- E$ehsa |> filter(var == "pv") |> count(classification) |>
  mutate(classification = factor(classification, rev(EHSA_LEVELS)))
ggplot(eb, aes(n, classification, fill = classification)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = n), hjust = -0.3, size = 3, colour = PAL$ink, family = "Helvetica") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = EHSA_COLS(), guide = "none") +
  scale_y_discrete(labels = ehsa_label) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.08))) +
  labs(x = "Townships", y = NULL) + theme_ex02(grid = "x")








Figure 8: Townships in each EHSA class, all political violence.





On the brief’s filter. The right-hand panel shows only townships whose Mann-Kendall p is below 0.05, as the brief asks. It is worth seeing what that removes. A persistent hot or cold spot is defined as one that is significant in at least 90% of periods without a significant trend, so the filter deletes every persistent class by construction: all 24 persistent cold spots vanish. The filter answers “where is the pattern changing?”, which is a good question, but it should not be read as “where is the pattern significant”. I interpret the left-hand panel and use the right-hand one to pick out the townships whose trajectory is statistically clear.

8.2.1 Interpreting the hot spot classes
Intensifying hot spots (6 townships: Madaya, Yesagyo, Myingyan, Dawei, Ngazun, Seikphyu). These are the townships that have been significant hot spots in at least 90% of quarters and whose Gi* is still rising. Five of the six are in the dry zone, along the Mandalay-Magway corridor south of Sagaing, the area into which the Sagaing insurgency has expanded; the sixth, Dawei, is the main town of northern Tanintharyi. For a peace-building organisation this is the most urgent class: established violence that is not plateauing. Madaya, just north of Mandalay city, stands out with nearly 800 events and a tau of 0.71.
Consecutive hot spots (11: Kawkareik, Kyaukkyi, Myawaddy, Kyaikto, Kyaukme, Launglon, Bilin, Kyainseikgyi, Yebyu, Thayetchaung, Shwegyin). Townships that became hot spots and have stayed hot for an unbroken run up to the latest quarter, after earlier periods of not being one. They trace one geographic line: the southeastern front from Kyaukkyi and Shwegyin in Bago East, through Kyaikto and Bilin in Mon, to Kawkareik, Myawaddy and Kyainseikgyi along the Thai border, and on into Tanintharyi. Much of it is territory contested by the Karen National Union, whose 2024 offensive reached Myawaddy, the main land crossing to Thailand. Kyaukme in northern Shan, on the Operation 1027 front, is the outlier. This is the clearest evidence in the analysis of a front that has moved into new townships and stayed there.
Oscillating hot spots (48, led by Sagaing (18), Magway (8), Mandalay (5)). Hot in the latest quarter but significantly cold at some earlier point. Most are in Sagaing and Magway, which seems paradoxical for the heartland of the war. The explanation is the start of the window. EHSA classifies on its own space-time Gi*, and in that series 41 of the 48 oscillating townships were significantly cold in 2021 Q1, the quarter of the coup, before the armed resistance existed, when the conflict was still carried by the border regions. The first quarter is also the only one with no preceding quarter to lag on, so its neighbourhood is purely spatial. So “oscillating” here means “transformed”: quiet farming townships that became the war’s centre. That is a substantive finding, and a warning about reading EHSA labels off a window that starts at a regime change.
Sporadic hot spots (65, led by Shan (North) (13), Kachin (9), Mandalay (8)). On-and-off hot spots that were never cold. Northern Shan and Kachin dominate: front lines that flare with offensives and go quiet under local ceasefires, as northern Shan did after the China-brokered truce of January 2024.
Diminishing hot spot. One township, Gangaw in Magway, hot in nearly every quarter but with a significantly falling trend.
No persistent hot spots. No township was a significant hot spot in 90% of the 19 quarters. Again the reason is the window: the first quarter or two predate the resistance in exactly the places that later became its core.


8.2.2 Interpreting the cold spot classes
Cold spots are 138 townships, more than the hot spots, and they are of two kinds. The persistent cold spots (24) are almost all in the Shan hills: 21 of them in eastern, northern and southern Shan. That area contains the Wa and Mongla zones, where I argued in the data audit that zeros partly measure silence. The consecutive cold spots (8) are all in Yangon: townships that were not significantly cold in the first years and have been continuously cold since, the same cooling the Mann-Kendall map shows. The single intensifying cold spot, Kunhing in southern Shan, records only eight events.
The large sporadic cold spot group (88) is mostly the Ayeyarwady delta and Yangon, the military’s most secure territory: places that are sometimes significantly quiet relative to the national level. It would be a mistake to read “cold spot” as “safe”. A cold spot in Yangon is a place where armed clashes are rare. It is also a place where repression takes forms ACLED records as arrests and strategic developments, which I excluded.

text:
8.3 By event type


code
et <- with_geo(E$ehsa |> filter(var != "pv")) |>
  mutate(var = var_lab(var), classification = factor(classification, EHSA_LEVELS))
present_t <- levels(droplevels(et$classification))
ggplot(et) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = classification), colour = PAL$border, linewidth = 0.04) +
  geom_sf(data = states, fill = NA, colour = PAL$ink, linewidth = 0.18) +
  facet_wrap(~var, nrow = 1, labeller = label_wrap_gen(18)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = EHSA_COLS()[present_t], breaks = present_t,
                    labels = ehsa_label(present_t), name = NULL) +
  coord_sf(expand = FALSE, datum = NA) + theme_map(base_size = 10) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.key.width = unit(12, "pt"))








Figure 9: EHSA classes by event type, all classes shown. Explosions and remote violence share the dry-zone pattern of the total; battles carry a stronger border signal; violence against civilians has no intensifying hot spot at all.





The three types tell slightly different stories. Battles produce the most consecutive hot spots, front by front, and eight intensifying cold spots, all in central Yangon and the delta, where armed clashes occurred in 2021 and then stopped almost entirely. Explosions and remote violence reproduce the dry-zone pattern of the total, with its own six intensifying hot spots, consistent with the air campaign concentrating on the resistance heartland. Violence against civilians has no intensifying hot spot, and the most townships with no pattern at all: it is diffuse in time, following raids and sweeps rather than fixed fronts.

text:
8.4 Reading individual trajectories


code
pick <- c("Madaya", "Kawkareik", "Monywa", "Hlaingtharya (East)", "Gangaw", "Kunhing")
pick <- intersect(pick, tsp$TS)
tr <- G |> left_join(tsp_attr, by = "TS_PCODE") |>
  filter(TS %in% pick) |>
  left_join(ehsa_pv |> select(TS, classification), by = "TS") |>
  mutate(lab = glue("{TS}: {ehsa_label(classification)}"))
ggplot(tr, aes(period, gi)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = PAL$rule) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(COUP_DATE, OP1027_DATE), colour = PAL$muted, linewidth = 0.25, linetype = "22") +
  geom_line(colour = PAL$muted, linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = classification, alpha = p_sim < ALPHA), size = 1.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = EHSA_COLS(), guide = "none") +
  scale_alpha_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = 1, `FALSE` = 0.25), guide = "none") +
  facet_wrap(~lab, ncol = 3) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "2 years", date_labels = "%Y") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Gi*") + theme_ex02(base_size = 10)








Figure 10: The space-time Gi* series that EHSA classified, for one township from several classes. Solid points are significant at p < 0.05. The dashed lines are the coup and Operation 1027.





The trajectories make the labels concrete. Monywa and Madaya are both significantly cold in the coup quarter and hot in almost every quarter after it; Monywa’s Gi* levels off, Madaya’s keeps climbing, and that difference alone puts one in “oscillating” and the other in “intensifying”. Kawkareik is not significant through 2021 and then hot in every quarter from 2022 onward, an unbroken final run that makes it “consecutive”. Gangaw is hot almost throughout but drifting down. Hlaingtharya (East), an industrial township on Yangon’s western edge, is hot in 2021 and cold by the end. Kunhing in southern Shan is cold in all 19 quarters and getting colder.

title: Take-home Exercise 2: Geospatial Analytics for Peace
text:
8.5 Sensitivity of the classification
EHSA classes are less stable than the local statistics, and this needs saying plainly. Rebuilding the cube monthly keeps the same class for 62% of townships; using raw counts instead of log(1 + count) keeps it for 57%. At the coarser level of hot, cold or neither, agreement rises to 78% and 74%. Most of the movement is between neighbouring classes: sporadic hot spots in the quarterly cube become “no pattern” in the monthly one, because monthly noise makes an occasional significant quarter harder to reach. Intensifying hot spots either stay intensifying or become oscillating, never cold.
So I read the EHSA results at two levels. The broad geography (which townships are hot, which cold, which are trending) is robust. The fine distinctions between sporadic, oscillating and consecutive depend on parameter choices and should be used to prompt a look at the trajectory, not quoted as fact.

title: Take-home Exercise 2: Geospatial Analytics for Peace
text:
9.1 The question
EHSA describes where hot spots appear and persist. It does not say how a quiet township becomes violent. For a peace-building organisation that is the question that matters for planning: if violence spreads to neighbours, the townships to prepare are the quiet ones on the edge of active areas; if it jumps or appears independently, adjacency is no guide.
The conflict literature distinguishes contagious diffusion, where violence spreads to adjacent places, from relocation, where it moves and leaves its origin quiet (Schutte and Weidmann 2011). I test the first with a spatial Markov chain (Rey 2001).

title: Take-home Exercise 2: Geospatial Analytics for Peace
text:
9.2 Method
Each township-quarter is classified Active if it records at least 3 political-violence events (one a month, which separates sustained activity from an isolated incident) and Quiet otherwise. Each township’s neighbourhood in that quarter is classified by the share of its queen neighbours that are active: none, some (under half), or most (half or more). I then estimate the probability of being Active in the next quarter, conditional on the township’s own state and its neighbourhood. That gives 5,940 observed transitions.
If violence diffuses contagiously, a quiet township’s chance of becoming active should rise with its neighbours’ activity.

title: Take-home Exercise 2: Geospatial Analytics for Peace
text:
9.3 Result


code
pt <- D$phase_tab |> mutate(ctx = factor(ctx, D$ctx_lab))
tb2 <- D$tab |> mutate(ctx = factor(ctx, D$ctx_lab))
ggplot(tb2, aes(ctx, p_active_next)) +
  geom_col(fill = PAL$accent_lt, width = 0.62) +
  geom_point(data = pt, aes(shape = phase, colour = phase), size = 2.4,
             position = position_dodge(width = 0.38)) +
  geom_text(aes(label = glue("n = {fmt_n(n)}"), y = 0.02), vjust = 0, size = 2.6,
            colour = PAL$ink, family = "Helvetica") +
  facet_wrap(~ factor(from, c("Quiet", "Active"), c("Quiet this quarter", "Active this quarter"))) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(PAL$cool, PAL$accent_dk), name = NULL) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(16, 17), name = NULL) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_percent(), limits = c(0, 1)) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = c("None", "Some", "Most")) +
  labs(x = "Neighbours active this quarter", y = "Active next quarter") + theme_ex02()








Figure 11: Probability that a township is active in the next quarter, by its own state and its neighbours’. Bars give the full period; points split it at Operation 1027. n is the number of township-quarter transitions behind each bar.





A quiet township with no active neighbour becomes active in the next quarter 9% of the time. With most neighbours active, the figure is 36%, about four times higher. The same gradient appears for active townships: an active township with no active neighbours stays active about half the time, but one surrounded by fighting stays active 85% of the time. The likelihood-ratio test of homogeneity across neighbourhoods rejects decisively (G² = 353, 4 df).

title: Take-home Exercise 2: Geospatial Analytics for Peace
section: 9.4 Is it contagion, or just a violent region?
text:
9.4 Is it contagion, or just a violent region?
The likelihood-ratio test assumes every transition is independent, which is false: each township contributes 18 transitions, and neighbouring townships share conditions. Three checks address this.
Spatial permutation. I kept every township’s full 19-quarter history intact and shuffled which location each history sits at, 499 times, recomputing the onset gap each time. This destroys spatial arrangement while preserving every township’s temporal persistence.


code
ggplot(tibble(g = D$gap_perm), aes(g)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = PAL$null, colour = PAL$border) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = D$gap_obs, colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("text", x = D$gap_obs, y = Inf, vjust = 1.5, hjust = 1.05, size = 3,
           label = glue("observed {round(100 * D$gap_obs)} points"), colour = PAL$accent,
           family = "Helvetica") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = \(x) paste0(round(100 * x), " pts")) +
  labs(x = "Onset gap under random placement", y = NULL) + theme_ex02()








Figure 12: Onset gap (most neighbours active minus none active) under 499 spatial permutations, against the observed gap.





Not one permutation reaches the observed gap (p < 0.002). Under random placement the gap is centred slightly below zero, because shuffling places busy townships next to quiet ones.
Controlling for region and time. A logistic model of onset among quiet townships with fixed effects for each of the 18 states and regions and for each quarter, plus the township’s own activity in the previous year, still finds the neighbourhood effect (Table 8). A township with most neighbours active has 4.1 times the odds of onset of one with none, with a township-cluster bootstrap interval of 2.8 to 6.6. The effect cannot be “this is Sagaing” or “this was a violent quarter”, because those are held constant.

title: Take-home Exercise 2: Geospatial Analytics for Peace
text:
9.5 What changed with Operation 1027
Splitting the transitions at Operation 1027 (the points in Figure 11) shows a chain that is not stationary, and the way it changes is informative. Before the offensive, a quiet township with no active neighbours ignited 13% of the time; from 2023 Q4 onward, 4%. Onset next to active neighbours did not change at all (36% before, 36% after). Isolated outbreaks have become rare. New violence now appears almost only at the edge of existing violence. That is what a war of consolidated fronts and contested territory looks like, as opposed to the scattered uprising of 2021 and 2022.

In the last observed quarter, 174 townships were quiet, and 54 of them had most of their neighbours active. They cluster in Magway (7), Sagaing (6), Kachin (5), Mandalay (5): the margins of the dry-zone and southern fronts. The map is a list of where the diffusion result says to look, not a forecast, and it inherits every limitation of ACLED’s coverage.

Contents

One question in three parts: where violence clusters, how that is changing, and whether it spreads from one township to the next.

title: Take-home Exercise 2: Geospatial Analytics for Peace
section: 1. The question, the place and the data
text:
1. The question, the place and the data



53,907


political-violence events




330


townships, MIMU 9.4




19


quarters




2021-25


Jan 2021 to Sep 2025
















Where does armed conflict in Myanmar cluster, how is it changing, and does it spread? Since the coup of February 2021 the war has moved from the borderlands into the Bamar heartland, and it has kept moving.
Data. ACLED events (battles, explosions and remote violence, violence against civilians), joined by location to the 330 MIMU township polygons. Protests and strategic developments are excluded: they are not armed conflict.
Approach. Local Moran’s I and Gi* for where; a 19-quarter space-time cube with Mann-Kendall and emerging hot spot analysis for how it changes; a spatial Markov chain for whether it spreads.
Darker townships on the map have more events; the dry zone and the Thai border stand out.

title: Take-home Exercise 2: Geospatial Analytics for Peace
text:
2. Clearing the land mines


What I removed
6 events coded to the Indian Ocean.
93 events placed on a regional centroid (geo_precision 3). Kept, they would pile false violence onto whichever township holds the centroid.
111 events have no township name, so I joined every event by its coordinates, not its name. A name join would have lost all of them.


What I kept but distrust
Fatalities. The top 1% of events carry 21% of reported deaths. Analysed, never used to build the cube.
Zeros in Wa and Mongla. 8 townships record nothing in five years; seven are in ceasefire enclaves that report almost nothing. They anchor a cold spot that partly measures silence.
Skew. Counts run from 0 to 1,039. The statistics use log(1 + count), checked against raw counts.

title: Take-home Exercise 2: Geospatial Analytics for Peace
section: 3. A war that changed its means
text:
3. A war that changed its means


Violence climbed through 2021 and peaked with Operation 1027 in November 2023. Explosions and remote violence overtook battles in 2023, driven by the military’s air campaign: 88 air or drone strikes in 2021, 2,977 in 2024. An air strike lands where the military chooses, not where the fighting is.

title: Take-home Exercise 2: Geospatial Analytics for Peace
text:
4. Where violence clusters













All political violence, p < 0.05, 999 permutations.
Global Moran’s I is 0.67. A township’s violence is very well predicted by its neighbours’.
One dominant core: the dry zone of Sagaing, Magway and Mandalay, with a second belt down the Thai border through Kayin, Mon and Tanintharyi.
Cold spots: the Ayeyarwady delta, Yangon and eastern Shan.
No High-Low outliers at all. Violence in Myanmar does not form islands; it comes in neighbourhoods.
82 to 96% of townships keep their class under raw counts or 6-nearest-neighbour weights. About half survive a false discovery rate correction: the cluster cores.

title: Take-home Exercise 2: Geospatial Analytics for Peace
section: 5. Every kind of violence, the same core
text:
5. Every kind of violence, the same core


Local Moran’s I by type. Battles add the ethnic fronts in Chin, Kachin and Kayah. Violence against civilians is the most concentrated: 88% of its High-High townships are in the dry zone. Fatalities follow battles.

title: Take-home Exercise 2: Geospatial Analytics for Peace
text:
6. Which way the trends run













Mann-Kendall test on each township’s 19-quarter Gi* series, p < 0.05.
Cooling: Yangon. 44 of its 45 townships have a falling Gi*. The urban resistance of 2021 is gone from the map.
Warming: the middle belt. Bago West, Mandalay, Magway, Bago East and Tanintharyi, where the war arrived late as the dry-zone insurgency spread and new fronts opened.
Sagaing barely registers, because it was hot from 2021 and stayed hot. A trend test cannot see a level, which is the gap emerging hot spot analysis fills.

title: Take-home Exercise 2: Geospatial Analytics for Peace
text:
7. Emerging hot spots













Intensifying, the most urgent: Dawei, Yesagyo, Seikphyu, Madaya, Myingyan, Ngazun. Hot in nearly every quarter and still rising, five of six in the dry zone.
Consecutive, a front that moved and held: Kyaukkyi and Shwegyin through Kyaikto and Bilin to Kawkareik and Myawaddy on the Thai border.
Oscillating hot spots fill Sagaing and Magway. Not unstable: they were cold in the coup quarter, before the resistance existed, and have been hot since.
Persistent cold spots are the Shan hills, including Wa and Mongla.
Fine classes are fragile: 62% of townships keep their label on a monthly cube, 78% keep hot/cold/neither. Every label was checked against an independent Gi* series, because sfdep 0.2.5 can attach labels to the wrong townships.

title: Take-home Exercise 2: Geospatial Analytics for Peace
text:
8. Violence spreads to neighbours













Value-added: a spatial Markov chain. Each township-quarter is active (3 or more events) or quiet. Does a quiet township’s chance of becoming active depend on its neighbours?
Yes, by a factor of four: 9% with no active neighbour, 36% with most neighbours active.
It is not just “a violent region”. With fixed effects for state and quarter and the township’s own history, the odds ratio is 4.1 (bootstrap 2.8 to 6.6). Shuffling townships’ histories across the map never reproduces the gap (p < 0.002). It holds at 1, 3 and 6 events.
Out of sample it is a modest signal: AUC 0.73 from own history, 0.75 with neighbours.

title: Take-home Exercise 2: Geospatial Analytics for Peace
text:
9. Fronts, not sparks













Since Operation 1027, isolated outbreaks have almost stopped. A quiet township with no active neighbour ignited 13% of the time before the offensive and 4% after. Onset next to active neighbours did not change (36% and 36%).
New violence now appears at the edge of existing violence: a war of consolidated fronts rather than the scattered uprising of 2021.
The map: townships quiet in 2025 Q3, shaded by the share of neighbours active. The warmest are where the evidence says to look next, most of them in Magway, Sagaing, Kachin and Mandalay. Not a validated forecast.

title: Take-home Exercise 2: Geospatial Analytics for Peace
section: 10. What this means, and what it cannot say
text:
10. What this means, and what it cannot say


For peace-building
Prioritise the intensifying hot spots (Madaya, Myingyan, Seikphyu, Yesagyo, Ngazun, Dawei) for protection and humanitarian access: established violence that is still rising.
Watch the quiet edges, not the centres. Early warning and preparedness belong in quiet townships beside active ones.
Treat the southeast as a moving front, where cross-border routes from Thailand matter most.
Plan for air-strike exposure beyond battle lines. Battle maps alone will not locate it.


Limitations
ACLED counts reports, not violence. Hot spots partly reflect visibility; the Wa and Mongla zeros are the clearest case. A cold spot is not proof of safety.
Counts, not rates. No reliable township population exists for 2021-2025.
Scale and neighbours. Townships run from under 1 km² to over 12,000 km², and contiguity treats every border as equally permeable.
EHSA depends on the window, which starts in the coup quarter, and its fine classes move with parameter choices.
Diffusion is descriptive. An advancing front and contagion look alike at quarterly resolution.

title: Modelling Geographical Accessibility
text:
R SpatialAcc Hansen KD2SFCA SAM Eldercare
This exercise follows Modelling Geographical Accessibility, the reading for the Geographic Accessibility block of the course.

title: Modelling Geographical Accessibility
text:
1. Overview
Exercise 6 grouped places by what they contain. This one asks how easily people in one place can reach something located somewhere else: here, how far each part of Singapore is from an eldercare centre, once distance along the road network is taken into account.
Accessibility models answer questions such as which neighbourhoods are underserved, and which would lose most if a facility closed or two were merged. The exercise uses three of them, all from the SpatialAcc package, and they do not measure the same thing:

Hansen’s potential model adds up every centre’s capacity, discounted by how far away it is. It ignores demand entirely: a centre counts the same whether ten people or ten thousand share it.
KD2SFCA (kernel density two-step floating catchment area) first works out how much capacity each centre offers per unit of demand within a catchment, then sums those ratios for each origin, again discounted by distance. Competition for the same centre lowers everyone’s score.
SAM (Spatial Accessibility Measure) divides each centre’s capacity by the origin’s demand and by distance raised to a power, then sums.

The study unit is a grid of 250 m hexagons rather than planning subzones, so the result is not tied to administrative boundaries of very different sizes.

title: Modelling Geographical Accessibility
text:
2. The Data








Dataset
Description
Format




MP14_SUBZONE_NO_SEA_PL
URA Master Plan 2014 subzone boundaries, 323 subzones
ESRI Shapefile (polygon)


hexagons
3,125 hexagons of 250 m radius covering the main island
ESRI Shapefile (polygon)


ELDERCARE
120 eldercare service locations from data.gov.sg
ESRI Shapefile (point)


OD_Matrix.csv
Road network distance from every hexagon to every centre, in metres
CSV, 375,000 rows



OD_Matrix.csv has six fields: origin_id (a hexagon’s fid), destination_id (a centre’s fid), entry_cost (from the origin to the nearest road), network_cost (along the road network), exit_cost (from the road to the destination) and total_cost, the sum of the three.
The hexagons, eldercare points and distance matrix were prepared by Prof. Kam for teaching use, and everything printed below matches the handout’s own output. One thing to keep in mind: the eldercare shapefile’s metadata is dated March 2017, so it describes eldercare services as they were then, not today.

The counts match the handout: 323 subzones, 3,125 hexagons, 120 centres. The hexagons and centres are already in SVY21 / Singapore TM. The subzone layer is in SVY21 too, but without an EPSG code attached.


4.2 Updating the CRS

c(mpsz = st_crs(mpsz)$epsg,
  hexagons = st_crs(hexagons)$epsg,
  eldercare = st_crs(eldercare)$epsg)

     mpsz  hexagons eldercare 
       NA      3414      3414 



mpsz <- st_transform(mpsz, 3414)
eldercare <- st_transform(eldercare, 3414)
hexagons <- st_transform(hexagons, 3414)

c(mpsz = st_crs(mpsz)$epsg,
  hexagons = st_crs(hexagons)$epsg,
  eldercare = st_crs(eldercare)$epsg)

     mpsz  hexagons eldercare 
     3414      3414      3414 


All three layers now carry EPSG 3414.


4.3 Cleaning the attribute fields
Both layers carry many fields the models do not use. I keep the identifiers and add a capacity field to the centres and a demand field to the hexagons.

eldercare <- eldercare %>%
  select(fid, ADDRESSPOS) %>%
  mutate(capacity = 100)

hexagons <- hexagons %>%
  select(fid) %>%
  mutate(demand = 100)

As the handout says, a constant 100 stands in for real values. In practice demand would be the number of older residents in each hexagon and capacity the number of places at each centre. This one simplification shapes almost everything that follows, and I come back to it in section 9.

title: Modelling Geographical Accessibility
text:
5. Aspatial Data Wrangling

5.1 Importing the distance matrix

ODMatrix <- read_csv("data/aspatial/OD_Matrix.csv", skip = 0)


ODMatrix %>%
  summarise(rows = n(),
            origins = n_distinct(origin_id),
            destinations = n_distinct(destination_id))

# A tibble: 1 x 3
    rows origins destinations
   <int>   <int>        <int>
1 375000    3125          120


That is 3,125 origins times 120 destinations: every pair is present once.
The handout goes straight to reshaping. Before that I check one property any real distance matrix must have: the centres are spread over 40 km of island, so each hexagon should be near some of them and far from others.

od_check <- ODMatrix %>%
  group_by(origin_id) %>%
  summarise(spread_m = max(total_cost) - min(total_cost),
            nearest_m = min(total_cost))

c(origins = nrow(od_check),
  same_distance_to_every_centre = sum(od_check$spread_m == 0))

                      origins same_distance_to_every_centre 
                         3125                           159 


159 hexagons fail it. Each has one total_cost repeated for all 120 centres:

ODMatrix %>%
  filter(origin_id == 1067) %>%
  head(4)

# A tibble: 4 x 6
  origin_id destination_id entry_cost network_cost exit_cost total_cost
      <dbl>          <dbl>      <dbl>        <dbl>     <dbl>      <dbl>
1      1067              1       295.        4634.      44.0      4974.
2      1067              2       295.        4634.      44.0      4974.
3      1067              3       295.        4634.      44.0      4974.
4      1067              4       295.        4634.      44.0      4974.


For hexagon 1067 even the exit cost, from the road to the centre’s door, is the same 44 m for every centre. No road network produces that. These rows look like routing failures that were written out as if they were distances. I keep them through sections 6 to 8, as the handout does, so that my results stay comparable with it, and measure what they do in section 9.5.


5.2 Tidying the distance matrix
The file is in long format, one row per origin-destination pair. ac() needs a wide matrix with one row per origin and one column per destination. The handout uses spread() and recommends its replacement, pivot_wider(), which I use here.

distmat <- ODMatrix %>%
  select(origin_id, destination_id, total_cost) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = destination_id,
              values_from = total_cost)

ac() has no idea which row is which hexagon. It pairs row i of the matrix with element i of the demand vector and column j with element j of the capacity vector, purely by position. So before dropping the identifier column, I check that the rows are in the same order as hexagons and the columns in the same order as eldercare.

c(rows_match_hexagons = identical(distmat$origin_id,
                                  as.numeric(hexagons$fid)),
  cols_match_eldercare = identical(as.numeric(names(distmat)[-1]),
                                   as.numeric(eldercare$fid)))

 rows_match_hexagons cols_match_eldercare 
                TRUE                 TRUE 


Both are true, but it is worth knowing why. The eldercare fid values run from 1 to 133 with gaps, and pivot_wider() orders columns by first appearance, not numerically. The match holds only because the CSV happens to be sorted the same way as the shapefiles. With constant capacity a misalignment would change nothing, which is exactly why it would go unnoticed. With real capacities it would silently assign each centre another centre’s places.

distmat <- distmat %>%
  select(-origin_id)

distmat_km <- as.matrix(distmat / 1000)

The handout presents the conversion to kilometres as a change of unit. For two of the three models it is more than that, as section 9.1 shows.

title: Modelling Geographical Accessibility
section: 10. What I Take From This Exercise
text:
10. What I Take From This Exercise
Check the input matrix before trusting any accessibility model. A three-line check in section 5.1 found that 159 hexagons, five per cent of the grid, have the same distance to every centre. The models accept those rows without complaint and return plausible-looking numbers: a hexagon in Clementi ranks near the top of the island under Hansen while KD2SFCA calls it unserved. Every accessibility measure is only as good as the travel-cost matrix underneath it, and a matrix should be checked against straight-line distance before it is used.
The three models are different arguments, not three readings of one thing. Hansen asks how much capacity is nearby. KD2SFCA and SAM ask how much capacity is nearby per unit of demand. With demand and capacity both set to 100, that difference disappears and all three collapse onto distance to the nearest centre (rank correlation 0.94 to 0.997). The exercise teaches the mechanics; it cannot show what the models are for until the placeholders are replaced.
Units and defaults are modelling decisions. Converting metres to kilometres sets the bandwidth of Hansen and KD2SFCA, power means a decay rate in one family and an exponent in another, and SAM silently ignores d0. None of this is in the function’s output; it is only visible by reading the source. I would not report an accessibility map without stating the unit, the kernel and the catchment.
Joins need the same care as models. The region boxplots looked like routine plotting code, but st_intersects counted hexagons up to several times, weighted towards exactly the well-served ones, and overstated the West’s median by a factor of about three. largest = TRUE, or a join on centroids, gives one row per hexagon.
Positional matching is a silent risk. ac() pairs matrix rows and columns with demand and capacity by position. Here the orders agree, and with constant capacity a mismatch would be invisible anyway. That is the combination that lets a bug survive into a real analysis.
What I would change. Use resident population aged 65 and over per hexagon as demand (apportioned from subzone counts) and licensed places per centre as capacity, drop hexagons with no residents from the region summaries rather than letting reservoirs and industrial land define the West, set d0 from a stated travel standard, and put a floor under SAM’s distances. Then compare KD2SFCA with Hansen directly: the places where they disagree are the places where a centre is close but oversubscribed, which is the finding an accessibility study exists to produce.

text:

Hansen, W. G. (1959). How accessibility shapes land use. Journal of the American Institute of Planners, 25(2), 73-76.
