title: Modelling Geographical Accessibility
text:
6. Accessibility with Hansen’s Method

6.1 Computing Hansen’s accessibility

acc_Hansen <- data.frame(ac(hexagons$demand,
                            eldercare$capacity,
                            distmat_km,
                            #d0 = 50,
                            power = 2,
                            family = "Hansen"))

colnames(acc_Hansen) <- "accHansen"
acc_Hansen <- as_tibble(acc_Hansen)
hexagon_Hansen <- bind_cols(hexagons, acc_Hansen)

The handout then repeats the same steps in a single chunk, but with power = 0.5, and everything it maps afterwards uses that second result. I follow it, so my maps are comparable with the handout’s, and compare the two settings in section 9.1.

acc_Hansen <- data.frame(ac(hexagons$demand,
                            eldercare$capacity,
                            distmat_km,
                            #d0 = 50,
                            power = 0.5,
                            family = "Hansen"))

colnames(acc_Hansen) <- "accHansen"
acc_Hansen <- as_tibble(acc_Hansen)
hexagon_Hansen <- bind_cols(hexagons, acc_Hansen)

summary(hexagon_Hansen$accHansen)

     Min.   1st Qu.    Median      Mean   3rd Qu.      Max. 
1.080e-03 1.371e+01 8.872e+01 1.550e+02 2.399e+02 1.158e+03 




6.2 Mapping Hansen’s accessibility

mapex <- st_bbox(hexagons)


tm_shape(hexagon_Hansen,
         bbox = mapex) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "accHansen",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 10,
                values = "brewer.blues")) +
tm_shape(eldercare) +
  tm_dots(size = 0.3,
          fill = "red",
          col = "black") +
  tm_title("Accessibility to eldercare: Hansen method") +
  tm_layout(frame = TRUE) +
  tm_compass(type = "8star", size = 2) +
  tm_scalebar() +
  tm_grid(alpha = 0.2)








The pattern follows the centres closely. Half of the 120 centres are in the Central region, and accessibility is highest in the older estates around the city centre: Kallang, Bukit Merah, Toa Payoh, Geylang and Bishan. It is lowest in Tuas, the Western Islands, Lim Chu Kang and Changi.


6.3 Comparing planning regions

hexagon_Hansen <- st_join(hexagon_Hansen, mpsz,
                          join = st_intersects)


ggplot(data = hexagon_Hansen,
       aes(y = log(accHansen),
           x = REGION_N)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_point(stat = "summary",
             fun = "mean",
             colour = "red",
             size = 2)








The handout passes fun.y = "mean", which ggplot2 deprecated in version 3.3; fun is the current name and gives the same red mean markers. The plot is on a log scale because Hansen values span six orders of magnitude.
Central and North-East have the highest accessibility; West has the lowest and the widest spread. Section 9.2 shows that the join above distorts this plot.

title: Modelling Geographical Accessibility
text:
7. Accessibility with the KD2SFCA Method

7.1 Computing KD2SFCA accessibility

acc_KD2SFCA <- data.frame(ac(hexagons$demand,
                             eldercare$capacity,
                             distmat_km,
                             d0 = 5,
                             power = 2,
                             family = "KD2SFCA"))

colnames(acc_KD2SFCA) <- "accKD2SFCA"
acc_KD2SFCA <- as_tibble(acc_KD2SFCA)
hexagon_KD2SFCA <- bind_cols(hexagons, acc_KD2SFCA)

summary(hexagon_KD2SFCA$accKD2SFCA)

     Min.   1st Qu.    Median      Mean   3rd Qu.      Max. 
0.000e+00 0.000e+00 3.000e-08 3.840e-02 4.616e-03 1.476e+00 


d0 = 5 sets a 5 km catchment: a centre further away than that contributes nothing. The summary already shows the consequence. The first quartile is exactly zero.


7.2 Mapping KD2SFCA accessibility

tm_shape(hexagon_KD2SFCA,
         bbox = mapex) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "accKD2SFCA",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 10,
                values = "brewer.blues")) +
tm_shape(eldercare) +
  tm_dots(size = 0.3,
          fill = "red",
          col = "black") +
  tm_title("Accessibility to eldercare: KD2SFCA method") +
  tm_layout(frame = TRUE) +
  tm_compass(type = "8star", size = 2) +
  tm_scalebar() +
  tm_grid(alpha = 0.2)








This map needs reading with care. With 41% of hexagons tied at exactly zero, the quantile breaks pile up at zero: the legend still lists ten classes, but the first five all span zero, and floating-point noise even gives four of them negative upper bounds. Every zero hexagon lands in the fifth class. So the part of the island with no centre within 5 km is drawn in uniform mid-blue, not in the palest colour, and at a glance looks better served than it is. Section 9.4 maps the same values as percentile ranks, which avoids the problem.


7.3 Comparing planning regions

hexagon_KD2SFCA <- st_join(hexagon_KD2SFCA, mpsz,
                           join = st_intersects)


ggplot(data = hexagon_KD2SFCA,
       aes(y = accKD2SFCA,
           x = REGION_N)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_point(stat = "summary",
             fun = "mean",
             colour = "red",
             size = 2)








On the raw scale the boxes are squashed against zero and the plot is mostly outliers. What it does show is that the highest values are all in the Central region, in Bukit Merah, Toa Payoh and Geylang. The top three hexagons each have three or more centres within a kilometre by road.

title: Modelling Geographical Accessibility
text:
8. Accessibility with the SAM Method

8.1 Computing SAM accessibility

acc_SAM <- data.frame(ac(hexagons$demand,
                         eldercare$capacity,
                         distmat_km,
                         d0 = 5,
                         power = 2,
                         family = "SAM"))

colnames(acc_SAM) <- "accSAM"
acc_SAM <- as_tibble(acc_SAM)
hexagon_SAM <- bind_cols(hexagons, acc_SAM)

summary(hexagon_SAM$accSAM)

     Min.   1st Qu.    Median      Mean   3rd Qu.      Max. 
  0.07718   0.40249   0.86880   1.77638   1.82919 740.42209 




8.2 Mapping SAM accessibility

tm_shape(hexagon_SAM,
         bbox = mapex) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "accSAM",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 10,
                values = "brewer.blues")) +
tm_shape(eldercare) +
  tm_dots(size = 0.3,
          fill = "red",
          col = "black") +
  tm_title("Accessibility to eldercare: SAM method") +
  tm_layout(frame = TRUE) +
  tm_compass(type = "8star", size = 2) +
  tm_scalebar() +
  tm_grid(alpha = 0.2)








SAM has no zeros, because every centre contributes something however far away it is, so the map shades smoothly outwards from the centres. The geography is the same as Hansen’s.


8.3 Comparing planning regions

hexagon_SAM <- st_join(hexagon_SAM, mpsz,
                       join = st_intersects)


ggplot(data = hexagon_SAM,
       aes(y = accSAM,
           x = REGION_N)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_point(stat = "summary",
             fun = "mean",
             colour = "red",
             size = 2)








The y-axis is stretched by a single hexagon in the Central region scoring far above the rest. Section 9.4 explains why.

title: Modelling Geographical Accessibility
text:
9. Checks the Handout Skips

9.1 What power and the distance unit actually do
The three models share one argument name, power, but it means something different in each. Reading the source of ac() in SpatialAcc 0.1.6 gives the weight each model puts on a centre at distance d:

Hansen: exp(-power * d), an exponential decay where power is a rate.
KD2SFCA: exp(-d^power), a Gaussian-shaped kernel, cut to zero beyond d0.
SAM: d^-power, an inverse-power decay with no cut-off. d0 is accepted but never used, so the handout’s d0 = 5 has no effect.


d <- c(0.5, 1, 2, 3, 5)
tibble(distance_km = d,
       Hansen_power_2 = exp(-2 * d),
       Hansen_power_0.5 = exp(-0.5 * d),
       KD2SFCA_power_2 = exp(-d^2),
       SAM_power_2 = d^-2) %>%
  mutate(across(-distance_km, ~ signif(.x, 3)))

# A tibble: 5 x 5
  distance_km Hansen_power_2 Hansen_power_0.5 KD2SFCA_power_2 SAM_power_2
        <dbl>          <dbl>            <dbl>           <dbl>       <dbl>
1         0.5      0.368               0.779         7.79e- 1       4    
2         1        0.135               0.607         3.68e- 1       1    
3         2        0.0183              0.368         1.83e- 2       0.25 
4         3        0.00248             0.223         1.23e- 4       0.111
5         5        0.0000454           0.0821        1.39e-11       0.04 


Two things follow. First, KD2SFCA’s 5 km catchment is mostly nominal: the kernel has already fallen below 0.02 at 2 km and to about one ten-thousandth at 3 km. The effective reach is about 2 km, and d0 only decides where values become exactly zero rather than merely tiny.
Second, d enters Hansen and KD2SFCA inside an exponential, so its unit is not cosmetic. The same models run on the matrix in metres:

hansen_m <- ac(hexagons$demand, eldercare$capacity,
               as.matrix(distmat), power = 0.5, family = "Hansen")
kd2sfca_m <- ac(hexagons$demand, eldercare$capacity,
                as.matrix(distmat), d0 = 5000, power = 2, family = "KD2SFCA")

tibble(model = c("Hansen, power 0.5", "KD2SFCA, d0 5 km"),
       max_in_km = c(max(hexagon_Hansen$accHansen), max(acc_KD2SFCA$accKD2SFCA)),
       max_in_metres = c(max(hansen_m), max(kd2sfca_m, na.rm = TRUE)),
       hexagons_above_1e6_in_metres = c(sum(hansen_m > 1e-6),
                                        sum(kd2sfca_m > 1e-6, na.rm = TRUE)))

# A tibble: 2 x 4
  model             max_in_km max_in_metres hexagons_above_1e6_in_metres
  <chr>                 <dbl>         <dbl>                        <int>
1 Hansen, power 0.5   1158.     0.000000958                            0
2 KD2SFCA, d0 5 km       1.48   0                                      0








ImportantThe distance unit is a model parameter



In metres, Hansen’s accessibility is effectively zero for every hexagon and KD2SFCA’s is exactly zero everywhere, because exp(-0.5 × 2,000) underflows to nothing. SAM is the only one of the three where the unit merely rescales the result (by a factor of a million, with an identical ranking). For Hansen and KD2SFCA, choosing kilometres is choosing the bandwidth. A Hansen rate of 0.5 per kilometre means a centre’s weight halves every 1.4 km; the same number per metre would mean it halves every 1.4 m.


The handout’s two Hansen settings make the same point from the other side. At power = 2 the weight halves every 350 m, so only the nearest centre matters. At power = 0.5 centres several kilometres away still count. The rank correlation between the two is computed in section 9.4.


9.2 The region boxplots count some hexagons many times
st_join() with st_intersects returns one row for every subzone a hexagon touches. Subzones are small in the Central region and large at the edges, so this is not a rounding issue:

tibble(hexagons = n_distinct(hexagon_Hansen$fid),
       rows_after_join = nrow(hexagon_Hansen))

# A tibble: 1 x 2
  hexagons rows_after_join
     <int>           <int>
1     3125            5406



hexagon_Hansen %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  count(fid, name = "subzones_touched") %>%
  count(subzones_touched, name = "hexagons")

  subzones_touched hexagons
1                1     1603
2                2      973
3                3      384
4                4      130
5                5       27
6                6        7
7                8        1


Nearly half the hexagons appear more than once, one of them eight times. That would not matter if the repeats were random, but they are not. Hexagons that straddle many subzones tend to be closer to a centre, in every region:

hexagon_Hansen %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  count(fid, REGION_N, name = "rows") %>%
  left_join(tibble(fid = hexagons$fid,
                   nearest_km = apply(distmat_km, 1, min)),
            by = "fid") %>%
  group_by(REGION_N) %>%
  summarise(rank_corr_rows_vs_nearest = round(cor(rows, nearest_km,
                                                  method = "spearman"), 2))

# A tibble: 5 x 2
  REGION_N          rank_corr_rows_vs_nearest
  <chr>                                 <dbl>
1 CENTRAL REGION                        -0.33
2 EAST REGION                           -0.33
3 NORTH REGION                          -0.38
4 NORTH-EAST REGION                     -0.32
5 WEST REGION                           -0.51


The fix is to give each hexagon exactly one subzone, the one it overlaps most, with largest = TRUE. I collect all three measures on that clean join for the rest of this section.

nearest_km <- apply(distmat_km, 1, min)

acc <- hexagons %>%
  mutate(accHansen = acc_Hansen$accHansen,
         accHansen_p2 = ac(demand, eldercare$capacity, distmat_km,
                           power = 2, family = "Hansen"),
         accKD2SFCA = acc_KD2SFCA$accKD2SFCA,
         accSAM = acc_SAM$accSAM,
         nearest_km = nearest_km) %>%
  st_join(mpsz %>% select(REGION_N, PLN_AREA_N),
          largest = TRUE)

c(rows = nrow(acc), missing_region = sum(is.na(acc$REGION_N)))

          rows missing_region 
          3125              0 



region_compare <- left_join(
  hexagon_Hansen %>%
    st_drop_geometry() %>%
    group_by(REGION_N) %>%
    summarise(rows_handout = n(),
              median_handout = median(accHansen)),
  acc %>%
    st_drop_geometry() %>%
    group_by(REGION_N) %>%
    summarise(hexagons = n(),
              median_corrected = median(accHansen)),
  by = "REGION_N") %>%
  mutate(handout_over_corrected = round(median_handout / median_corrected, 2),
         across(starts_with("median"), ~ round(.x, 1)))

as.data.frame(region_compare)

           REGION_N rows_handout median_handout hexagons median_corrected
1    CENTRAL REGION         1392          427.3      605            353.4
2       EAST REGION          776          103.1      498             79.4
3      NORTH REGION          976           69.6      622             59.2
4 NORTH-EAST REGION          659          245.5      321            229.3
5       WEST REGION         1603           43.2     1079             15.1
  handout_over_corrected
1                   1.21
2                   1.30
3                   1.18
4                   1.07
5                   2.86








ImportantThe handout’s boxplots overweight the best-served hexagons



The join turns 3,125 hexagons into 5,406 rows. The Central region’s 605 hexagons become 1,392 rows, because its subzones are small and a hexagon often straddles several. Within each region, the hexagons counted several times are the ones nearer to centres, and the hexagons in large, empty subzones are counted once.
The effect is largest where the contrast is largest. In the West, the median Hansen accessibility in the handout’s plot is 43.2, against 15.1 when each hexagon is counted once: an overstatement of about 2.9 times. The ranking of regions survives, but the gap between the West and everywhere else is wider than the handout shows.



ggplot(acc %>% st_drop_geometry(),
       aes(x = REGION_N, y = log(accHansen))) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_point(stat = "summary", fun = "mean",
             colour = "red", size = 2) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "log(Hansen accessibility)",
       title = "Hansen accessibility by region, one row per hexagon")










9.3 Where the zeros are
KD2SFCA gives exactly zero to every hexagon with no centre within 5 km.

zero_by_area <- acc %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  filter(accKD2SFCA == 0) %>%
  count(PLN_AREA_N, sort = TRUE, name = "zero_hexagons")

c(zero_hexagons = sum(zero_by_area$zero_hexagons),
  share_of_all = round(sum(zero_by_area$zero_hexagons) / nrow(acc), 3),
  planning_areas = nrow(zero_by_area))

 zero_hexagons   share_of_all planning_areas 
       1281.00           0.41          39.00 

head(zero_by_area, 10)

                PLN_AREA_N zero_hexagons
1  WESTERN WATER CATCHMENT           271
2                     TUAS           185
3                   CHANGI           167
4          WESTERN ISLANDS           145
5  CENTRAL WATER CATCHMENT           117
6             LIM CHU KANG            77
7                  PIONEER            49
8              JURONG EAST            26
9             SUNGEI KADUT            25
10                  YISHUN            24


79% of the zero hexagons fall in seven planning areas: the two water catchments, the Tuas and Pioneer industrial estates, Changi (most of it airport land), the Western Islands (mainly Jurong Island) and Lim Chu Kang. Few people live in any of them, and they explain most of the West’s poor showing in every region plot above. Leaving them out moves the West from last to third:

acc %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  filter(!PLN_AREA_N %in% low_pop) %>%
  group_by(REGION_N) %>%
  summarise(hexagons = n(),
            median_Hansen = round(median(accHansen), 1),
            share_KD2SFCA_zero = round(mean(accKD2SFCA == 0), 3))

# A tibble: 5 x 4
  REGION_N          hexagons median_Hansen share_KD2SFCA_zero
  <chr>                <int>         <dbl>              <dbl>
1 CENTRAL REGION         605         353.               0.093
2 EAST REGION            315         153.               0.13 
3 NORTH REGION           372          78.5              0.258
4 NORTH-EAST REGION      321         229.               0.047
5 WEST REGION            384         160.               0.161


The remaining 270 are spread across 32 other planning areas, including towns such as Yishun and Tampines. Whether those particular hexagons contain housing is something this dataset cannot tell, because every hexagon has the same demand. Section 9.5 shows that some of these zeros, including about a third of those in the Western Water Catchment, come from the defective distance rows found in section 5.1 rather than from real distance.
The share of zeros depends almost entirely on the choice of d0:

map_dfr(c(2, 3, 5, 10, 20), function(d0) {
  k <- ac(hexagons$demand, eldercare$capacity, distmat_km,
          d0 = d0, power = 2, family = "KD2SFCA")
  tibble(d0_km = d0,
         zero_hexagons = sum(k == 0),
         share_zero = round(mean(k == 0), 3),
         rank_corr_with_d0_5 = round(cor(k, acc$accKD2SFCA,
                                         method = "spearman"), 3))
})

# A tibble: 5 x 4
  d0_km zero_hexagons share_zero rank_corr_with_d0_5
  <dbl>         <int>      <dbl>               <dbl>
1     2          2440      0.781               0.748
2     3          1963      0.628               0.898
3     5          1281      0.41                1    
4    10           639      0.204               0.969
5    20            96      0.031               0.965


Doubling the catchment to 10 km halves the number of zeros, yet the ranking of hexagons barely moves. Because the kernel is near zero beyond 2 to 3 km anyway, d0 mostly decides which hexagons are reported as “no access” rather than “very little”. That label matters for policy, so d0 should be set from a real travel standard, not left at a round number.


9.4 Do the three measures agree?

acc %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  select(Hansen_p0.5 = accHansen, Hansen_p2 = accHansen_p2,
         KD2SFCA = accKD2SFCA, SAM = accSAM, nearest_km) %>%
  cor(method = "spearman") %>%
  round(3)

            Hansen_p0.5 Hansen_p2 KD2SFCA    SAM nearest_km
Hansen_p0.5       1.000     0.952   0.905  0.986     -0.937
Hansen_p2         0.952     1.000   0.962  0.950     -0.997
KD2SFCA           0.905     0.962   1.000  0.909     -0.963
SAM               0.986     0.950   0.909  1.000     -0.937
nearest_km       -0.937    -0.997  -0.963 -0.937      1.000








NoteWith constant demand and capacity, all three measures mostly encode distance to the nearest centre



Every pair of measures has a rank correlation above 0.9, and each is almost a mirror image of the plain distance to the nearest centre. For Hansen at power = 2 the correlation with nearest distance is -0.997: it is very nearly a ranking by nearest distance.
That is a consequence of the inputs, not a failure of the models. Hansen never uses demand. SAM and KD2SFCA do, but with demand fixed at 100 in every hexagon, the competition they are designed to capture is competition between equal areas of land, not between people. A centre in a dense estate and a centre beside a reservoir face the same “demand” per hectare. The models only start to disagree in a useful way when real population and capacity go in.


SAM’s outlier from section 8.3 is the inverse-power kernel at work:

acc %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  arrange(desc(accSAM)) %>%
  select(PLN_AREA_N, accSAM, nearest_km) %>%
  mutate(nearest_m = round(nearest_km * 1000)) %>%
  select(-nearest_km) %>%
  head(5)

   PLN_AREA_N    accSAM nearest_m
1     KALLANG 740.42209        37
2   TOA PAYOH  80.39676       114
3 BUKIT TIMAH  48.58723       145
4   TOA PAYOH  41.52309       164
5 JURONG WEST  39.45310       197


The top hexagon is 37 m by road from a centre, so d^-2 gives it about 730 from that centre alone, nine times the next highest hexagon. With no floor on distance, SAM rewards being very close far more than distance alone justifies. Clamping distances to a minimum, say the 250 m radius of the hexagon itself, would remove the spike.
Putting the three on a common scale, each hexagon’s percentile rank within its measure, shows how similar their geography is:

acc %>%
  select(fid, Hansen = accHansen, KD2SFCA = accKD2SFCA, SAM = accSAM) %>%
  pivot_longer(c(Hansen, KD2SFCA, SAM),
               names_to = "measure", values_to = "value") %>%
  group_by(measure) %>%
  mutate(percentile = percent_rank(value) * 100) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = percentile), colour = NA) +
  geom_sf(data = eldercare, size = 0.4, colour = "black") +
  facet_wrap(~ measure, ncol = 3) +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = "Blues", direction = 1,
                       name = "Percentile") +
  theme_void() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")








The maps are close to interchangeable. Apart from KD2SFCA’s floor, where everything beyond 5 km ties at zero, the differences are systematic rather than random. Comparing each hexagon’s percentile under KD2SFCA with its percentile under Hansen, among hexagons with some KD2SFCA access:

rank_gap <- acc %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  mutate(gap = percent_rank(accKD2SFCA) - percent_rank(accHansen)) %>%
  filter(accKD2SFCA > 0) %>%
  group_by(PLN_AREA_N) %>%
  summarise(hexagons = n(), median_gap = round(median(gap), 3)) %>%
  filter(hexagons >= 15)

bind_rows(slice_min(rank_gap, median_gap, n = 5),
          slice_max(rank_gap, median_gap, n = 5))

# A tibble: 10 x 3
   PLN_AREA_N    hexagons median_gap
   <chr>            <int>      <dbl>
 1 TANGLIN             33     -0.212
 2 SERANGOON           48     -0.168
 3 NOVENA              40     -0.165
 4 MARINE PARADE       24     -0.156
 5 DOWNTOWN CORE       20     -0.114
 6 SIMPANG             22      0.225
 7 WOODLANDS           59      0.145
 8 YISHUN              72      0.14 
 9 CHOA CHU KANG       31      0.132
10 PUNGGOL             41      0.11 


The gaps follow the kernels. Hansen at power = 0.5 still credits centres 5 to 10 km away, so central areas surrounded by many centres, such as Tanglin, Serangoon and Novena, rank high under Hansen even where no centre is close, and drop under KD2SFCA. KD2SFCA’s effective reach of about 2 km instead rewards outer towns with a centre of their own, such as Woodlands, Yishun and Punggol.


9.5 159 hexagons have no real distances
Section 5.1 found 159 hexagons whose distance to every centre is the same number. To see what that does, I compare the repeated distance with the straight-line distance from each hexagon’s centroid to its nearest centre.

straight_km <- st_distance(st_centroid(hexagons), eldercare) %>%
  units::drop_units() %>%
  apply(1, min) / 1000

acc <- acc %>%
  mutate(straight_km = straight_km,
         flat = od_check$spread_m[match(fid, od_check$origin_id)] == 0,
         pct_Hansen = percent_rank(accHansen),
         pct_SAM = percent_rank(accSAM))

acc %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  group_by(rows = if_else(flat, "repeated", "normal")) %>%
  summarise(hexagons = n(),
            road_over_straight = round(median(nearest_km / straight_km), 2),
            centre_within_5km_straight = sum(straight_km < 5),
            KD2SFCA_zero = sum(accKD2SFCA == 0)) %>%
  as.data.frame()

      rows hexagons road_over_straight centre_within_5km_straight KD2SFCA_zero
1   normal     2966               1.78                       2390         1123
2 repeated      159               3.63                         94          158



ggplot(acc) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = flat), colour = NA) +
  geom_sf(data = eldercare, size = 0.5, colour = "black") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "grey88", `TRUE` = "#137C8B"),
                    labels = c("normal row", "same distance to every centre"),
                    name = NULL) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")









acc %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  filter(flat) %>%
  count(PLN_AREA_N, sort = TRUE, name = "hexagons") %>%
  head(6)

               PLN_AREA_N hexagons
1 WESTERN WATER CATCHMENT       87
2        SOUTHERN ISLANDS       19
3               PASIR RIS        7
4                    TUAS        7
5 CENTRAL WATER CATCHMENT        6
6              QUEENSTOWN        6



acc %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  filter(flat) %>%
  arrange(nearest_km) %>%
  transmute(fid, PLN_AREA_N,
            repeated_km = round(nearest_km, 2),
            straight_km = round(straight_km, 2),
            Hansen_percentile = round(100 * pct_Hansen),
            SAM_percentile = round(100 * pct_SAM),
            KD2SFCA = signif(accKD2SFCA, 2)) %>%
  head(5) %>%
  as.data.frame()

   fid              PLN_AREA_N repeated_km straight_km Hansen_percentile
1 1067                CLEMENTI        4.97        2.02               100
2  832             JURONG EAST        7.28        1.49                84
3  833             JURONG EAST        7.28        1.95                84
4  527 WESTERN WATER CATCHMENT        7.62        2.31                78
5  757             JURONG EAST        7.82        2.34                75
  SAM_percentile KD2SFCA
1             96 1.1e-07
2             82 0.0e+00
3             82 0.0e+00
4             79 0.0e+00
5             77 0.0e+00








ImportantFive per cent of the distance matrix is not distance



On normal rows the road distance to the nearest centre is a median 1.8 times the straight-line distance, which is what a road network looks like. On the repeated rows it is 3.6 times, and 94 of the 159 have a centre within 5 km in a straight line. Most of them are in the Western Water Catchment and on Sentosa and the Southern Islands.
The defect pushes the measures in opposite directions. KD2SFCA sets 158 of these hexagons to exactly zero, because the one repeated distance is beyond 5 km. Hansen and SAM inflate them, because a hexagon that is “7 km from every centre” collects all 120 centres at 7 km instead of a few near ones and many 20 to 40 km away. Hexagon 1067 in Clementi is the extreme case: its real nearest centre is 2 km away in a straight line, it is recorded as 4.97 km from all 120, and that puts it in the top 0.3% of the island under Hansen.
The handout’s maps and boxplots include all of these rows. Most fall on land where few people live, so the island-wide picture survives, but any statement about the catchment areas, Sentosa or the individual hexagons in the table above would be wrong. The fix is to drop these rows, or better, to rerun the network routing for them.

title: Floating Catchment Accessibility with catchment
text:
1. Overview
Hands-on Exercise 7 computed accessibility to eldercare with SpatialAcc. catchment, from the University of Virginia’s Biocomplexity Institute, covers the floating catchment area (FCA) family with one function, catchment_ratio().

title: Floating Catchment Accessibility with catchment
text:
2. Getting Started
catchment is not on CRAN. It installs from GitHub:

remotes::install_github("uva-bi-sdad/catchment")


pacman::p_load(sf, tidyverse, tmap, catchment)

title: Floating Catchment Accessibility with catchment
text:
3. Data Preparation
The data and every preparation step are the same as in Hands-on Exercise 7: URA’s 2014 subzones, 3,125 hexagons of 250 m radius, 120 eldercare centres, and the road distance from every hexagon to every centre.

3.1 Importing the geospatial data

title: Floating Catchment Accessibility with catchment
text:
4. Reproducing Hands-on Exercise 7 First
Before trusting a new package, I check it against the old one. SpatialAcc’s KD2SFCA weights a centre at distance d by exp(-d^2) and drops it beyond d0. catchment’s Gaussian weight is exp(-d^2 / (2 * scale^2)). The two are the same function when 2 * scale^2 = 1, that is scale = 1 / sqrt(2), and catchment’s max_cost plays the part of d0.

kd_spatialacc <- ac(hexagons$demand, eldercare$capacity, distmat_km,
                    d0 = 5, power = 2, family = "KD2SFCA")

kd_catchment <- catchment_ratio(consumers, providers, distmat_km,
                                weight = "gaussian", scale = 1 / sqrt(2),
                                max_cost = 5)

twosfca_spatialacc <- ac(hexagons$demand, eldercare$capacity, distmat_km,
                         d0 = 5, family = "2SFCA")

twosfca_catchment <- catchment_ratio(consumers, providers, distmat_km,
                                     weight = 5)

c(KD2SFCA_max_abs_difference = max(abs(kd_spatialacc - kd_catchment)),
  `2SFCA_max_abs_difference` = max(abs(twosfca_spatialacc - twosfca_catchment)))

KD2SFCA_max_abs_difference   2SFCA_max_abs_difference 
              4.440892e-16               0.000000e+00 


Both agree to floating-point precision. This matters beyond reassurance: it pins down that the two packages express the same kernel with different parameters. A scale of 5 in catchment would not mean what a d0 of 5 means in SpatialAcc, and copying numbers between them without this check would silently change the model.

title: Floating Catchment Accessibility with catchment
section: 5. Four Models on the Same Data
text:
5. Four Models on the Same Data
From here on I use the clean matrix cost_km. The four models differ only in weight:








Model
weight
Catchment




2SFCA
5
everyone within 5 km counts fully, no one beyond


E2SFCA
list(c(1.5, 1), c(3, 0.68), c(5, 0.22))
steps: full weight to 1.5 km, 0.68 to 3 km, 0.22 to 5 km


KD2SFCA
"gaussian", scale = 1/sqrt(2), max_cost = 5
smooth decay, as in Hands-on Exercise 7


3SFCA
as KD2SFCA, plus normalize_weight = TRUE
a hexagon’s demand is shared out among the centres it can reach



The E2SFCA step weights 1, 0.68 and 0.22 are the ones Luo and Qi (2009) used for 10, 20 and 30-minute drive zones. Placing their edges at 1.5, 3 and 5 km is my choice, made so that the outer edge matches the 5 km catchment of the other models.

fca <- hexagons %>%
  mutate(
    `2SFCA` = catchment_ratio(consumers, providers, cost_km,
                              weight = 5),
    E2SFCA = catchment_ratio(consumers, providers, cost_km,
                             weight = list(c(1.5, 1), c(3, 0.68), c(5, 0.22))),
    KD2SFCA = catchment_ratio(consumers, providers, cost_km,
                              weight = "gaussian", scale = 1 / sqrt(2),
                              max_cost = 5),
    `3SFCA` = catchment_ratio(consumers, providers, cost_km,
                              weight = "gaussian", scale = 1 / sqrt(2),
                              max_cost = 5, normalize_weight = TRUE),
    flat = fid %in% flat_ids)

catchment gives the masked hexagons a score of 0, as if they had no centre in range. That is not what we know about them: their distances are unknown, not long. So I record them as missing.

models <- c("2SFCA", "E2SFCA", "KD2SFCA", "3SFCA")

fca <- fca %>%
  mutate(across(all_of(models), ~ if_else(flat, NA_real_, .x)))

fca %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  pivot_longer(all_of(models), names_to = "model") %>%
  group_by(model = factor(model, levels = models)) %>%
  summarise(zero = sum(value == 0, na.rm = TRUE),
            missing = sum(is.na(value)),
            median = signif(median(value, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
            max = signif(max(value, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
            places_allocated = sum(value * 100, na.rm = TRUE))

# A tibble: 4 x 6
  model    zero missing      median   max places_allocated
  <fct>   <int>   <int>       <dbl> <dbl>            <dbl>
1 2SFCA    1123     159 0.0257      0.227           12000.
2 E2SFCA   1123     159 0.0157      0.358           12000.
3 KD2SFCA  1123     159 0.000000223 1.48            12000 
4 3SFCA    1123     159 0.000000286 1.74            12000.


The scores are in places per unit of demand: with 100 places per centre and 100 units of demand per hexagon, a 2SFCA score of 0.1 means the hexagon can draw on 0.1 places for each unit of its demand. Every model gives zero to the same hexagons, the ones with no centre within 5 km. The last column is the subject of section 7.1.

fca %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  filter(!flat) %>%
  mutate(nearest_km = apply(cost_km[as.character(fid), ], 1, min)) %>%
  select(all_of(models), nearest_km) %>%
  cor(method = "spearman") %>%
  round(3)

            2SFCA E2SFCA KD2SFCA  3SFCA nearest_km
2SFCA       1.000  0.982   0.917  0.917     -0.884
E2SFCA      0.982  1.000   0.964  0.962     -0.931
KD2SFCA     0.917  0.964   1.000  0.999     -0.970

The step and kernel versions sit between plain 2SFCA and distance to the nearest centre: the more a model discounts the far edge of the catchment, the more its ranking looks like a ranking by nearest distance. 3SFCA barely reorders KD2SFCA (rank correlation 0.999), because with equal demand everywhere, sharing a hexagon’s demand among its centres changes the levels much more than the order.

6. Mapping the Four Models
Hands-on Exercise 7’s KD2SFCA map used ten quantile classes, and with 41% of hexagons tied at zero the classes collapsed and drew “no access” in mid-blue. Here all four models share one set of breaks, zero gets its own grey class, and the masked hexagons are shown as missing.

fca_long <- fca %>%
  select(fid, all_of(models)) %>%
  pivot_longer(all_of(models), names_to = "model", values_to = "access") %>%
  mutate(model = factor(model, levels = models))

# tmap facets every layer, so the centres need one copy per model
eldercare_long <- map_dfr(models, ~ mutate(eldercare,
                                           model = factor(.x, levels = models)))

tm_shape(fca_long) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "access",
              col = NA,
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                breaks = c(0, 1e-9, 0.001, 0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 2),
                labels = c("0, no centre within 5 km", "under 0.001",
                           "0.001 to 0.01", "0.01 to 0.05", "0.05 to 0.1",
                           "0.1 to 0.2", "0.2 and above"),
                values = c("grey85", "#deebf7", "#c6dbef", "#9ecae1",
                           "#6baed6", "#3182bd", "#08519c"),
                value.na = "white",
                label.na = "no valid distance"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Places per unit of demand")) +
  tm_shape(eldercare_long) +
  tm_dots(size = 0.15, fill = "red") +
  tm_facets_wrap(by = "model", ncols = 2) +
  tm_layout(frame = FALSE)








The four maps agree on where access is zero, since that depends only on the 5 km edge. Inside the catchments, 2SFCA is the flattest, because every centre within 5 km counts in full; the kernel models concentrate access close to the centres.

title: Floating Catchment Accessibility with catchment
section: 7. What catchment Shows That SpatialAcc Does Not
text:
7. What catchment Shows That SpatialAcc Does Not

7.1 Every model hands out exactly 12,000 places
The places_allocated column in section 5 is 12,000 for every model, which is the total capacity of 120 centres with 100 places each. That is not a coincidence. With \(P_i\) the demand of hexagon \(i\), \(S_j\) the capacity of centre \(j\) and \(W_{ij}\) the catchment weight, an FCA score is
\[A_i = \sum_j W_{ij} R_j, \qquad R_j = \frac{S_j}{\sum_k P_k W_{kj}},\]
so the demand-weighted total is
\[\sum_i P_i A_i = \sum_j R_j \sum_i P_i W_{ij} = \sum_j S_j.\]
Whatever the weights, each centre’s capacity is shared out once among the demand in its catchment, as long as every centre has some demand within reach (here every centre does). This is what makes FCA scores interpretable in a way Hansen’s are not: added up over any area, they give the number of places that area can draw on. Section 8 uses this.


7.2 2SFCA counts each hexagon’s demand many times over
return_type = "demand" returns the first step of the model: the demand each centre faces. Under 2SFCA a hexagon within 5 km of ten centres is counted, in full, in all ten catchments. Normalising the weights, the “3” in 3SFCA, splits it among them instead. With binary weights the effect can be counted exactly.

demand_2sfca <- catchment_ratio(consumers, providers, cost_km,
                                weight = 5, return_type = "demand")

demand_3sfca <- catchment_ratio(consumers, providers, cost_km,
                                weight = 5, normalize_weight = TRUE,
                                return_type = "demand")

centres_in_range <- rowSums(cost_km < 5, na.rm = TRUE)

c(actual_demand_within_5km = 100 * sum(centres_in_range > 0),
  demand_counted_by_2SFCA = sum(demand_2sfca),
  demand_counted_by_3SFCA = sum(demand_3sfca),
  mean_centres_within_5km = round(mean(centres_in_range[centres_in_range > 0]), 1))

actual_demand_within_5km  demand_counted_by_2SFCA  demand_counted_by_3SFCA 
                184300.0                1588800.0                 184300.0 
 mean_centres_within_5km 
                     8.6 








Important2SFCA inflates demand by a factor of 8.6



The hexagons within 5 km of a centre hold 184,300 units of demand. 2SFCA counts 1,588,800, because the average hexagon in range is within 5 km of 8.6 centres and is counted in every one of their catchments. 3SFCA’s normalised weights count each hexagon once, and the total comes back to exactly 184,300.
This is the demand inflation that Páez, Higgins and Vivona (2019) describe. Section 7.1 showed that the total supply still balances, so the inflation does not change the island-wide sum. What it changes is which centres look crowded.



crowding <- eldercare %>%
  st_join(mpsz %>% select(PLN_AREA_N)) %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  transmute(fid, PLN_AREA_N,
            demand_2SFCA = demand_2sfca,
            demand_3SFCA = round(demand_3sfca),
            rank_2SFCA = min_rank(desc(demand_2sfca)),
            rank_3SFCA = min_rank(desc(demand_3sfca)))

crowding %>% arrange(rank_2SFCA) %>% head(5)

  fid PLN_AREA_N demand_2SFCA demand_3SFCA rank_2SFCA rank_3SFCA
1  23  TOA PAYOH        18600         1243          1         60
2  46     ROCHOR        18100          966          2         81
3 127 ANG MO KIO        18100         1932          2         35
4  26    KALLANG        17400         1006          4         79
5 106 ANG MO KIO        17000         1581          5         46

crowding %>% arrange(rank_3SFCA) %>% head(5)

  fid    PLN_AREA_N demand_2SFCA demand_3SFCA rank_2SFCA rank_3SFCA
1  82        YISHUN        12800         4883         74          1
2  93   BUKIT TIMAH        14900         4324         25          2
3  84        YISHUN        11900         4033         91          3
4  32      CLEMENTI        14400         3838         31          4
5  78 CHOA CHU KANG        11200         3784        103          5


The two models disagree about which centres are under the most pressure. Under 2SFCA, the most crowded centres are in TOA PAYOH, ROCHOR, ANG MO KIO, KALLANG: central estates where many centres sit close together, so every hexagon nearby is counted by all of them. Under 3SFCA those hexagons are shared, and the most crowded centres are instead in YISHUN, BUKIT TIMAH, CLEMENTI, CHOA CHU KANG, where a centre is the only option for a large surrounding area. The rank correlation between the two crowding measures across all 120 centres is 0.04.

crowding_sf <- eldercare %>%
  select(fid) %>%
  left_join(crowding, by = "fid") %>%
  mutate(`2SFCA` = 100 * demand_2SFCA / sum(demand_2SFCA),
         `3SFCA` = 100 * demand_3SFCA / sum(demand_3SFCA)) %>%
  pivot_longer(c(`2SFCA`, `3SFCA`),
               names_to = "model", values_to = "share")

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = mpsz, fill = "grey96", colour = "grey85", linewidth = 0.1) +
  geom_sf(data = crowding_sf, aes(size = share),
          shape = 21, fill = "#137C8B", colour = "white", alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 7, name = "Share of all\ndemand counted (%)") +
  facet_wrap(~ model) +
  theme_void()








For a planner deciding where to add places, this is the difference between expanding in Toa Payoh and expanding in Yishun. Neither answer is trustworthy with constant demand, but the exercise shows that the choice of model, not just the data, decides it.


7.3 Alignment by ID
Hands-on Exercise 7 noted that SpatialAcc::ac() pairs the matrix with demand and supply purely by position, which is harmless here only because capacity is constant. To see what ID alignment buys, I give the centres different capacities and shuffle their order.

set.seed(626)
providers_varied <- providers %>%
  mutate(count = sample(50:150, n(), replace = TRUE))

shuffled <- providers_varied %>%
  slice_sample(prop = 1)

reference <- catchment_ratio(consumers, providers_varied, cost_km, weight = 5)
by_id <- catchment_ratio(consumers, shuffled, cost_km, weight = 5)
by_position <- catchment_ratio(consumers$count, shuffled$count, cost_km, weight = 5)

c(data_frames_match_reference = isTRUE(all.equal(by_id, reference)),
  plain_vectors_match_reference = isTRUE(all.equal(by_position, reference)))

  data_frames_match_reference plain_vectors_match_reference 
                         TRUE                         FALSE 


Passed as data frames, the shuffled centres are matched to their columns by ID and the result is unchanged. Passed as plain vectors, the same shuffle silently gives every centre another centre’s capacity, and nothing warns about it. The safe habit is to always pass consumers and providers as tables with IDs.

title: Floating Catchment Accessibility with catchment
text:
8. Regional Summary with catchment_aggregate()
Hands-on Exercise 7 compared regions with boxplots, and found that its st_join() counted many hexagons several times. catchment_aggregate() does the comparison the FCA way: it adds up access × demand over the hexagons in each region and divides by the region’s demand. I assign each hexagon to one region with largest = TRUE and give the masked hexagons zero demand, so they drop out of both sums.

hex_region <- st_join(hexagons, mpsz %>% select(REGION_N), largest = TRUE) %>%
  st_drop_geometry()

region_map <- split(as.character(hex_region$fid), hex_region$REGION_N)
regions <- data.frame(GEOID = names(region_map))

aggregate_model <- function(model) {
  from <- fca %>%
    st_drop_geometry() %>%
    transmute(GEOID = as.character(fid),
              access = replace_na(.data[[model]], 0),
              population = if_else(flat, 0, demand))
  list(
    per_100 = 100 * catchment_aggregate(from, regions, map = region_map),
    places = catchment_aggregate(from, regions, map = region_map,
                                 return_type = "region"))
}

agg_2 <- aggregate_model("2SFCA")
agg_3 <- aggregate_model("3SFCA")

region_summary <- tibble(
  region = names(region_map),
  hexagons = lengths(region_map),
  places_per_100_2SFCA = round(agg_2$per_100[region], 2),
  share_of_places_2SFCA = round(100 * agg_2$places[region] / 12000, 1),
  share_of_places_3SFCA = round(100 * agg_3$places[region] / 12000, 1))

as.data.frame(region_summary)

             region hexagons places_per_100_2SFCA share_of_places_2SFCA

2       EAST REGION      498                 3.04                  12.4
3      NORTH REGION      622                 1.89                   9.6
4 NORTH-EAST REGION      321                 5.07                  13.5
5       WEST REGION     1079                 1.94                  15.8
  share_of_places_3SFCA
1                  50.7
2                  11.6
3                   7.6

Because the regions partition the island and FCA conserves supply, each share column adds up to 100%: it is a split of the 12,000 places. Under 2SFCA the Central region, with 605 of the 3,125 hexagons, can draw on 48.8% of all places, and the West, with 1079 hexagons, on 15.8%. The regional shares barely move between 2SFCA and 3SFCA, because sharing demand reshuffles pressure between neighbouring centres more than between regions.

title: Floating Catchment Accessibility with catchment
section: 9. What I Take From This Exercise
text:
9. What I Take From This Exercise
Reproduce before you extend. catchment and SpatialAcc implement the same KD2SFCA with different parameters (scale = 1/sqrt(2) against power = 2), and only an explicit side-by-side run showed that they agree to floating-point precision. Without that check I would have had no way to know whether a difference between the packages was a modelling difference or a translation error.
FCA scores are allocations, and that makes them auditable. Every FCA model here hands out exactly the 12,000 places in the system. That identity is a free test of any implementation and is what allows regional totals to be read as shares of supply. Hansen’s potential has no such property.
The choice between 2SFCA and 3SFCA changes the policy answer. 2SFCA counts each hexagon’s demand in every catchment it touches, inflating total demand by a factor of 8.6. That makes clustered central centres look the most crowded; once demand is shared, the most pressured centres are isolated ones in outer towns. Hexagon-level access barely changes, but the question “where should places be added?” gets a different answer.
Pass tables with IDs, never bare vectors. catchment aligns by ID when it is given IDs and by position when it is not. The second mode reproduces exactly the silent misalignment risk of SpatialAcc.
Missing is not zero. catchment turns an unknown distance into “no connection”, which scores as zero access. For the 159 hexagons with defective distances that would have reported unknown access as no access, so they are masked back to missing.
What I would change. The same as in Hands-on Exercise 7: real demand and capacity. With resident counts aged 65 and over as demand and licensed places as capacity, the 2SFCA and 3SFCA crowding maps in section 7.2 would become a usable shortlist of centres to expand, rather than a demonstration that the method decides the answer.

title: Market Area Analysis with the Huff Model

R MCI Huff model Trade area Taichung
This exercise follows Market Area Analysis for Retail and Service Locations using Huff model, the hands-on notes for the Market Area Analysis lesson of the course.

title: Market Area Analysis with the Huff Model
text:
1. Overview
Exercise 7 asked how easily people in one place can reach a service. This one asks the question from the store’s side: given where people live and where the stores are, how much of each neighbourhood’s custom does each store get?
The setting is a fast-food franchise with 28 stores in Taichung City. The task is to delineate each store’s trade area, the area it draws customers from, and to estimate store sales from where the population lives.
The Huff model (Huff, 1963) treats a shopper’s choice of store as a probability rather than a certainty. The probability that a resident of village i uses store j is
\[
P_{ij} = \frac{A_j^{\gamma} \, d_{ij}^{\lambda}}{\sum_{k} A_k^{\gamma} \, d_{ik}^{\lambda}}
\]
where \(A_j\) is the store’s attractiveness (usually its size), \(d_{ij}\) the distance, \(\gamma\) the sensitivity to attractiveness and \(\lambda\) a negative distance decay. The denominator runs over every store, so each village’s probabilities sum to one: a store gains share only by taking it from the others. Multiplying by each village’s population and summing over villages gives a store’s expected customers.
The lesson also covers the MCI (multiplicative competitive interaction) model, which estimates \(\gamma\), \(\lambda\) and further store attributes from observed market shares. The handout uses the MCI package for the Huff step only. Section 9.5 explains why the course data cannot support an MCI fit.

pop2019.csv has households (H_CNT), total population (P_CNT), males (M_CNT) and females (F_CNT). Its INFO_TIME of 108Y12M is December of year 108 in the Republic of China calendar, which is 2019.
The handout’s data list names the layers STORES_TN and VILLAGE_TN; the files and the code use _TC. The folder also ships a sixth file, storeCD.csv, which the handout never reads. It gives every store a capacity of 50, so it carries no more information than the constant store size used below.
The data was prepared by Prof. Kam for teaching use. I checked it against the handout’s own printed output: the feature counts, the summary() tables and the final correlation all match, apart from one quartile of the sales summary that prints as 26,702 here and 26,703 in the handout, a rounding difference.

title: Market Area Analysis with the Huff Model
text:
6. Computing the Distance Matrix
The handout says it uses each village’s centroid, but its code uses st_point_on_surface(). That is the better choice: a centroid can fall outside an irregular polygon, while a point on surface is always inside it. The distances are straight lines, in metres.

village_center <- st_point_on_surface(village)
distmat <- st_distance(village_center, stores)


rownames(distmat) <- village$`VILLCODE`
colnames(distmat) <- stores$`Store_CD`
distmat_long <- distmat %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  rownames_to_column(var = "VILLCODE") %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -VILLCODE,
    names_to = "Store_CD",
    values_to = "distance"
  ) %>%
  mutate(distance = as.numeric(distance))

title: Market Area Analysis with the Huff Model
text:
7. Preparing the Interaction Matrix

interaction_matrix <- distmat_long %>%
  left_join(
    stores %>%
      st_drop_geometry() %>%
      select(Store_CD, Store_size),
    by = "Store_CD") %>%
  relocate(
    distance, .after = last_col())


summary(interaction_matrix)

   VILLCODE           Store_CD           Store_size     distance      
 Length:17276       Length:17276       Min.   :100   Min.   :  108.5  
 Class :character   Class :character   1st Qu.:100   1st Qu.: 6678.7  
 Mode  :character   Mode  :character   Median :100   Median :11965.3  
                                       Mean   :100   Mean   :12762.7  
                                       3rd Qu.:100   3rd Qu.:18122.3  
                                       Max.   :100   Max.   :41395.4  


That is 617 villages times 28 stores, 17,276 pairs. The closest pair is 108 m apart and the furthest 41 km.

title: Market Area Analysis with the Huff Model
text:
8. Computing the Huff Model

huff_share <- huff.shares(
  interaction_matrix, "VILLCODE", "Store_CD",
  "Store_size", "distance")


8.1 Trade area analysis for a single store
The handout’s text says it selects store TG, but its code and its map use BT. I follow the code.

market_share <- huff_share %>%
  filter(Store_CD == "BT")


Trade_area <- village %>%
  left_join(market_share)


selected_store <- stores %>%
  filter(Store_CD == "BT")


tm_shape(Trade_area) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "p_ij",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 10,
                values = "brewer.blues"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                title = "Patronage Probability")) +
  tm_shape(selected_store) +
    tm_dots(size = 0.3,
            fill = "red",
            col = "black") +
  tm_title("Distribution of Patronage Probability of Store BT by village") +
  tm_layout(frame = TRUE) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_compass(type = "8star", size = 2) +
  tm_scalebar() +
  tm_grid(alpha = 0.2)








BT’s share is highest in the central villages around it and falls away with distance. Two things on this map are easy to misread. First, the quantile classes compress the top of the range: the darkest class runs from under 0.07 to 0.94, so a village where BT is one option among many is coloured the same as one where it is nearly the only option.
Second, the large villages in the south-east come out in the second-darkest class, although they are not BT’s territory. In the 31 villages in that corner of the map (east of 224,000 m and south of 2,682,000 m), BT is a median 13.7 km away and typically only the 7th-nearest store. These villages have no store of their own and every store lies to their west, so their custom is spread thinly over many stores: the leading store’s median share there is only 0.19. BT’s slice of 0.042 is above the 1/28 = 0.036 of an even split, and that is enough to rank in the top fifth of a quantile scale. Section 9.4 maps the leading store’s share on fixed breaks, which shows this directly.


8.2 Store sales analysis
The model can also estimate each store’s sales from village population.

huff_share_pp <- huff_share %>%
  left_join(village %>%
      st_drop_geometry() %>%
      select(VILLCODE, P_CNT),
    by = "VILLCODE") %>%
  relocate(
    distance, .after = last_col())


huff_total <- shares.total(
  huff_share_pp, "VILLCODE", "Store_CD",
  "p_ij", "P_CNT")


store_sales_est <- stores %>%
  left_join(huff_total,
            by = join_by(
              "Store_CD" == "suppliers_single"))


store_sales_nongeom <- store_sales_est %>%
  st_drop_geometry()

ggscatterstats(
  store_sales_nongeom,
  x = sum_E_j,
  y = Total_Sales)








This matches the handout: r = 0.58, with a 95% confidence interval of 0.26 to 0.78. Population allocated by distance alone accounts for about a third of the variation in sales across the 28 stores (r² = 0.33).
The handout ends by reshaping the shares to one row per village and one column per store, the form to join back to the village layer or export:

huff_share_wider <- huff_share %>%
  select(VILLCODE, Store_CD, p_ij) %>%
    pivot_wider(names_from = Store_CD,
                values_from = p_ij)

dim(huff_share_wider)

[1] 617  29

title: Market Area Analysis with the Huff Model
text:
9. Checks the Handout Skips

9.1 What the defaults assume
The handout calls huff.shares() with no model parameters, so everything rests on its defaults:

args(huff.shares)

function (huffdataset, origins, locations, attrac, dist, gamma = 1, 
    lambda = -2, atype = "pow", dtype = "pow", gamma2 = NULL, 
    lambda2 = NULL, check_df = TRUE) 
NULL


gamma = 1, lambda = -2, and power functions for both attractiveness and distance. Three consequences follow.

Distance is the only input. Every store has Store_size 100, so \(A_j^{\gamma}\) is the same for all stores and cancels between the numerator and the denominator. The model knows nothing about the stores except where they are, and gamma has no effect.
The decay is assumed, not estimated. \(\lambda = -2\) is the inverse-square law of the gravity-model tradition and the package default. Section 9.2 tests it against the sales.
The “estimated sales” are residents. Each village’s population is shared out among the stores, so the estimates add up to the population exactly:


c(sum_E_j = sum(huff_total$sum_E_j),
  population = sum(village$P_CNT))

   sum_E_j population 
   2804359    2804359 


The scatter plot in section 8.2 therefore compares residents with a sales amount. Only the correlation is meaningful. To predict sales, the estimates need converting, for example by giving each store its share of the 28 stores’ combined sales.
One contrast with Exercise 7 is worth recording. There, converting metres to kilometres changed Hansen and KD2SFCA, because distance sat inside an exponential. Here it does not:

interaction_matrix_km <- interaction_matrix %>%
  mutate(distance = distance / 1000)

huff_share_km <- huff.shares(
  interaction_matrix_km, "VILLCODE", "Store_CD",
  "Store_size", "distance")

max(abs(huff_share_km$p_ij - huff_share$p_ij))

[1] 7.771561e-16


huff.shares() has to be given a named data frame, because its input check looks the argument up by name; passing a piped expression fails.






NoteWith a power decay, the distance unit really is cosmetic



Rescaling every distance by a constant c multiplies every term by \(c^{\lambda}\), which cancels between the numerator and the denominator. The shares in metres and in kilometres differ only by floating-point error. That holds for dtype = "pow" only; an exponential decay (dtype = "exp") would make the unit part of the model again.




9.2 Calibrating the distance decay
The lesson outline lists calibrating the Huff model; the handout uses the defaults. The sales data allows a direct test of \(\lambda\). For each candidate value I compute expected customers per store, convert them to predicted sales by giving each store its share of the 28 stores’ combined sales, and measure the mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) against actual sales.
Two baselines frame the result. An even split predicts every store at the average. At the other extreme, allocating each village wholly to its nearest store is the limit of a very steep decay (\(\lambda \to -\infty\)).

village_pop <- village %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  select(VILLCODE, P_CNT)

actual <- stores %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  select(Store_CD, Total_Sales)

huff_sales <- function(lambda) {
  huff.shares(interaction_matrix, "VILLCODE", "Store_CD",
              "Store_size", "distance", lambda = lambda) %>%
    left_join(village_pop, by = "VILLCODE") %>%
    group_by(Store_CD) %>%
    summarise(E_j = sum(p_ij * P_CNT)) %>%
    left_join(actual, by = "Store_CD") %>%
    mutate(predicted = E_j / sum(E_j) * sum(Total_Sales))
}

mape <- function(predicted, actual) mean(abs(predicted - actual) / actual)

lambdas <- seq(-0.25, -4, by = -0.25)
fits <- map(lambdas, huff_sales)

calibration <- tibble(
  lambda = lambdas,
  r = map_dbl(fits, ~ cor(.x$E_j, .x$Total_Sales)),
  MAPE = map_dbl(fits, ~ mape(.x$predicted, .x$Total_Sales)))


nearest_alloc <- interaction_matrix %>%
  group_by(VILLCODE) %>%
  slice_min(distance, n = 1) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  left_join(village_pop, by = "VILLCODE") %>%
  group_by(Store_CD) %>%
  summarise(E_j = sum(P_CNT)) %>%
  right_join(actual, by = "Store_CD") %>%
  mutate(E_j = replace_na(E_j, 0),
         predicted = E_j / sum(E_j) * sum(Total_Sales))

baselines <- tibble(
  model = c("Even split", "Nearest store only", "Huff, lambda = -2"),
  r = c(NA, cor(nearest_alloc$E_j, nearest_alloc$Total_Sales),
        calibration$r[calibration$lambda == -2]),
  MAPE = c(mape(mean(actual$Total_Sales), actual$Total_Sales),
           mape(nearest_alloc$predicted, nearest_alloc$Total_Sales),
           calibration$MAPE[calibration$lambda == -2]))

baselines %>% mutate(across(c(r, MAPE), ~ round(.x, 3)))

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  model                   r  MAPE
  <chr>               <dbl> <dbl>
1 Even split         NA     0.486
2 Nearest store only  0.217 0.49 
3 Huff, lambda = -2   0.576 0.376



best <- calibration %>% slice_min(MAPE, n = 1)

ggplot(calibration, aes(lambda, MAPE)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = baselines$MAPE[1], linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = baselines$MAPE[2], linetype = "dotted", colour = "grey50") +
  annotate("text", x = -3.9, y = baselines$MAPE[1], label = "even split",
           vjust = 1.5, hjust = 0, size = 3.2, colour = "grey40") +
  annotate("text", x = -3.9, y = baselines$MAPE[2], label = "nearest store only",
           vjust = -0.6, hjust = 0, size = 3.2, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_line(colour = "#137C8B") +
  geom_point(colour = "#137C8B") +
  geom_point(data = filter(calibration, lambda == -2), colour = "red", size = 3) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Distance decay (lambda)", y = "MAPE of predicted store sales",
       title = "The handout's lambda = -2 (red) is steeper than the sales support") +
  theme_minimal()








The error is lowest at \(\lambda\) = -1, a much gentler decay than the default. To see how firmly 28 stores support that, I resample the stores with replacement and find the best \(\lambda\) in each resample:

set.seed(626)
best_lambda <- map_dbl(1:2000, function(b) {
  idx <- sample(28, replace = TRUE)
  errors <- map_dbl(fits, ~ mape(.x$predicted[idx], .x$Total_Sales[idx]))
  lambdas[which.min(errors)]
})

c(share_best_at_minus_2 = mean(best_lambda == -2),
  share_weaker_than_minus_2 = mean(best_lambda > -2),
  quantile(best_lambda, c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95)))

    share_best_at_minus_2 share_weaker_than_minus_2                        5% 
                    0.002                     0.961                    -1.500 
                      50%                       95% 
                   -1.000                    -0.750 



fit_m2 <- fits[[which(lambdas == -2)]]
fit_best <- fits[[which(lambdas == best$lambda)]]
ape_m2 <- abs(fit_m2$predicted - fit_m2$Total_Sales) / fit_m2$Total_Sales
ape_best <- abs(fit_best$predicted - fit_best$Total_Sales) / fit_best$Total_Sales

c(stores_improved = sum(ape_best < ape_m2),
  paired_wilcoxon_p = round(wilcox.test(ape_m2, ape_best, paired = TRUE)$p.value, 3))

  stores_improved paired_wilcoxon_p 
            17.00              0.09 








Importantlambda = -2 is a default, not an estimate



Against actual sales, the handout’s setting predicts with a MAPE of 37.6%, better than an even split (48.6%). At \(\lambda\) = -1 the error falls to 33.6%. In bootstrap resamples of the stores, \(\lambda = -2\) was the best value 0.2% of the time and a weaker decay 96% of the time, with the middle 90% of best values between -1.5 and -0.75.
The evidence is directional rather than precise. Only 17 of the 28 stores individually improve, and a paired test of the two error sets gives p = 0.09. Twenty-eight stores can rule out treating \(-2\) as given; they cannot pin \(\lambda\) down to one decimal place.
The probabilistic part of the model earns its keep, though. Allocating each village wholly to its nearest store correlates with sales at only r = 0.22 and predicts no better than an even split (MAPE 49%). Customers spread across several stores, as Huff assumed.


Because \(\lambda\) is chosen and scored on the same 28 stores, the in-sample error is a little optimistic. With a single parameter the optimism is small, and the bootstrap above shows how much the choice itself moves.


9.3 Which stores the model misses
With every store equally attractive, the gap between a store’s actual and predicted sales absorbs everything the model leaves out. At the calibrated \(\lambda\):

gaps <- fit_best %>%
  mutate(actual_over_predicted = round(Total_Sales / predicted, 2)) %>%
  arrange(actual_over_predicted) %>%
  select(Store_CD, Total_Sales, predicted, actual_over_predicted) %>%
  mutate(across(c(Total_Sales, predicted), ~ round(.x / 1e6, 2)))

bind_rows(head(gaps, 5), tail(gaps, 5))

# A tibble: 10 × 4
   Store_CD Total_Sales predicted actual_over_predicted
   <chr>          <dbl>     <dbl>                 <dbl>
 1 QH              2.97      6.71                  0.44
 2 TG              1.75      4.02                  0.44
 3 EH              1.48      3.19                  0.46
 4 SQ              2.36      5.05                  0.47
 5 ZS              2.77      5.7                   0.49
 6 ZK              6.75      5.32                  1.27
 7 JW              8.13      6.33                  1.28
 8 WF              5.09      3.95                  1.29
 9 DD              6.86      4.76                  1.44
10 SA              6.74      4.65                  1.45


Sales are in millions. The five stores at the top of the table sell about half of what their location predicts, and the stores at the bottom up to half as much again. The model cannot say why. The gap combines store size, seating, drive-through, parking, competing brands nearby and whether the store traded for the whole period. The sales file has no dates, so a store that opened partway through would look exactly like an underperformer. This gap is where real attractiveness data, or the MCI model, would go to work.


9.4 How contested each village is
A single-store map shows one store’s share. The question a trade-area analysis usually needs answering is how much any store dominates each village. For every village I take the highest probability across all 28 stores, under the handout’s settings:

top_share <- huff_share %>%
  group_by(VILLCODE) %>%
  summarise(top_p = max(p_ij),
            top_store = Store_CD[which.max(p_ij)],
            nearest_m = min(distance))

contested <- village %>%
  select(VILLCODE, P_CNT) %>%
  left_join(top_share, by = "VILLCODE")


tm_shape(contested) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "top_p",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                breaks = c(0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1),
                values = "brewer.blues"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                title = "Highest store share"),
              col_alpha = 0.3) +
  tm_shape(stores) +
    tm_dots(size = 0.3,
            fill = "red",
            col = "black") +
  tm_title("How much the leading store dominates each village") +
  tm_layout(frame = TRUE) +
  tm_compass(type = "8star", size = 2) +
  tm_scalebar()








Each store holds a small dark core of villages. Two kinds of village are contested: the outer villages, far from every store, and the city centre itself, where several stores sit close enough together that none of them dominates.

contested %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  mutate(nearest_store = cut(nearest_m, c(0, 500, 1000, 2000, 5000, Inf),
                             labels = c("under 0.5 km", "0.5 to 1 km", "1 to 2 km",
                                        "2 to 5 km", "over 5 km"))) %>%
  group_by(nearest_store) %>%
  summarise(villages = n(),
            median_top_share = round(median(top_p), 2))

# A tibble: 5 × 3
  nearest_store villages median_top_share
  <fct>            <int>            <dbl>
1 under 0.5 km        56             0.93
2 0.5 to 1 km        132             0.65
3 1 to 2 km          186             0.38
4 2 to 5 km          164             0.31
5 over 5 km           79             0.18








NoteMost residents do not belong to any one store’s trade area



59% of residents live in villages where no store has even half of the expected custom. A village within 500 m of a store gives that store a median share of 0.93; beyond 5 km the leading store’s median share is 0.18. Huff trade areas are overlapping gradients, not territories. Drawing one boundary per store, for example nearest-store polygons, would throw away the overlap the model exists to measure, and section 9.2 shows that the overlap is what makes the sales predictions work.




9.5 Why the course data cannot support an MCI fit
The MCI model estimates \(\gamma\), \(\lambda\) and the effect of other store attributes from observed market shares: how much of each origin’s spending goes to each store. mci.fit() in the MCI package needs exactly that table. The sales file has a field that might provide it, because every store’s sales are broken down by POD code:

store_sales %>%
  filter(`Store Code` %in% stores$Store_CD) %>%
  distinct(`Store Code`, `POD code`) %>%
  count(`POD code`, name = "stores_using_code", sort = TRUE) %>%
  head(8)

# A tibble: 8 × 2
  `POD code` stores_using_code
  <chr>                  <int>
1 Others                    28
2 X-98                      28
3 99                        26
4 X-99                      24
5 E-05                      20
6 G-05                      20
7 E-04                      19
8 F-04                      18


The same code appears under as many as 20 of the 28 stores, which are up to 32 km apart, alongside catch-all codes such as Others and X-98 under nearly all of them. So the codes are not one shared set of zones, the handout does not document them, and without a key or boundaries they cannot be placed on the map, which leaves no origin to measure distance from. With a boundary layer for the codes, mci.fit() could estimate the decay and each store’s attractiveness from what customers actually did, instead of assuming both.

title: Market Area Analysis with the Huff Model
section: 10. What I Take From This Exercise
text:
10. What I Take From This Exercise
The defaults are the model. With equal store sizes and \(\lambda = -2\), the Huff model here is a distance-only allocation with an inverse-square decay. Neither choice was estimated, and neither appears in the output. Before reading a trade-area map I would want to know the attractiveness measure and the decay it assumes.
Test the decay against outcomes when they exist. The sales file allows a one-parameter calibration in a few lines, and it says the default decay is too steep for these stores: MAPE falls from 37.6% to 33.6%, and \(-2\) was the best value in fewer than 1% of resamples. Twenty-eight stores cannot fix \(\lambda\) precisely, but they are enough to stop treating \(-2\) as given.
Check joins in both directions. summary() after a left join shows polygons without data, never data without polygons. An anti_join() found a whole district, Heping, missing from the map. Here it holds 0.4% of the population; in another city the same silent drop could remove a market.
Trade areas overlap, and the maps should show it. Most residents live in villages that no single store dominates. Quantile classes on one store’s share hide that; fixed breaks on the leading store’s share show it.
What I would change. Use real attractiveness (floor area, seats, drive-through) so that \(\gamma\) means something, road or travel-time distance instead of straight lines, and the competing stores just outside the city boundary. Calibrate \(\lambda\), and \(\gamma\) once attractiveness varies, against sales. If the POD codes can be located, fit the MCI model to observed shares and compare its estimates with the calibrated Huff model.

title: Market Area Analysis with the Huff Model
text:
